title: Withholding under correlated reward shocks
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: What is the optimal withholding strategy for a self-interested miner when exceptional rewards arrive in correlated bursts, decay with delay, and differ across private mempool views? A formal answer would extend the general stochastic-reward model to richer information structures and model uncertainty.
status: This problem lies beyond the 2025 general stochastic-reward framework of Bahr, Neuder and Weinberg (2025) (*Selfish Mining under General Stochastic Rewards*, arXiv:2502.20360), which does not handle correlated bursty rewards, delay decay, or heterogeneous private mempool information. Related evidence that mempool statistics matter appears in Sarenche et al. (2025) (*Bitcoin under Volatile Block Rewards: How Mempool Statistics Can Influence Bitcoin Mining*, arXiv:2411.11702). No solution currently exists; robust stochastic optimization is a related technique.
solved_when: A characterization of optimal withholding is derived under rewards that are correlated across time, decay with delay, and differ across private mempools — going beyond the 2025 general stochastic-reward framework.
why: Average fee levels conceal economically important reward timing; understanding how correlated, decaying, privately observed rewards shape withholding clarifies when selfish mining is rational in practice.
key_works: Bahrani, Neuder and Weinberg (2025), *Selfish Mining under General Stochastic Rewards*, arXiv:2502.20360; Sarenche et al. (2025), *Bitcoin under Volatile Block Rewards: How Mempool Statistics Can Influence Bitcoin Mining*, arXiv:2411.11702.

title: Foreknowledge-free whale-transaction attacks
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: How much is advance knowledge of pending "whale" transactions actually worth to an attacker? This calls for attack comparisons run under identical observable information and with no leakage of future transaction arrivals, so that any advantage can be attributed to foreknowledge alone.
status: The research target was sharpened by a 2025 analysis (Sarenche et al., 2025, arXiv:2411.11702) identifying implicit reward predictability in WeRLman’s model (Bar-Zur et al., 2023, *WeRLman: To Tackle Whale (Transactions), Go Deep (RL)*, DOI:10.1109/SP46215.2023.10179444).
solved_when: An experimental evaluation isolates the value of advance transaction information — attacks compared with identical observable information and no future-arrival leakage produce a quantified measure of that value.
why: Information leakage in simulators can exaggerate the apparent feasibility of withholding attacks, so clean measurements determine whether reported attack profits are real or artifacts of the experimental setup.
key_works: Bar-Zur et al. (2023), *WeRLman: To Tackle Whale (Transactions), Go Deep (RL)*, DOI:10.1109/SP46215.2023.10179444; Sarenche et al. (2025), arXiv:2411.11702.

title: Security under abrupt hashpower migration
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can we give meaningful confirmation guarantees for proof-of-work blockchains while an adversary times sudden hashpower changes to coincide with retarget boundaries — using only quantities a node can conservatively observe? Formally, the goal is bounds on settlement error that remain valid under adversarially scheduled hashrate migrations across difficulty-adjustment epochs.
status: This is an open research target extending the 2017 variable-difficulty backbone analysis of Garay, Kiayias and Leonardos (2017), *The Bitcoin Backbone Protocol with Chains of Variable Difficulty* (IACR ePrint:2016/1048), and the fixed-rate latency–security bounds of Guo and Ren (2022), *Bitcoin's Latency–Security Analysis Made Simple* (arXiv:2203.06357); related tools include change-point detection and nonstationary stochastic processes.
solved_when: Tight confirmation guarantees (settlement-error bounds) are derived that hold under abrupt, adversarially timed hashpower changes at retarget boundaries, expressed via conservatively observable quantities.
why: During mining shocks, confirmation counts otherwise lose their meaning, so honest nodes cannot tell when a transaction is actually settled.
key_works: Garay, Kiayias and Leonardos (2017), *The Bitcoin Backbone Protocol with Chains of Variable Difficulty*, IACR ePrint:2016/1048; Guo and Ren (2022), *Bitcoin’s Latency–Security Analysis Made Simple*, arXiv:2203.06357.

title: Adaptive GHOSTDAG parameter calibration
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can the GHOSTDAG protocol adjust its concurrency tolerance parameter on the fly, based on observed network behavior, in a way that is both safe and not exploitable? Formally, this asks for an update rule that recalibrates the security parameter from observations without relying on estimates an attacker can manipulate and without passing through unsafe intermediate settings.
status: This remains a research target beyond the 2021 GHOSTDAG construction of Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG: A Scalable Generalization of Nakamoto Consensus*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990. DAG KNIGHT, by Sutton and Sompolinsky (2023), *The DAG KNIGHT Protocol*, IACR ePrint:2022/1494, sidesteps the issue via a different parameterless approach rather than solving adaptive calibration. Related techniques appear in adversarial online learning and adaptive control.
solved_when: A mechanism exists that updates the GHOSTDAG concurrency tolerance from live observations while provably avoiding attacker-controlled estimates and unsafe parameter transitions, with security analysis for the resulting protocol.
why: Propagation assumptions underlying the fixed-parameter 2021 construction change as participation in the network changes; adaptive calibration would let the protocol track those conditions rather than rely on a static guess.
key_works: Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG: A Scalable Generalization of Nakamoto Consensus*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990; Sutton and Sompolinsky (2023), *The DAG KNIGHT Protocol*, IACR ePrint:2022/1494.

title: Searcher-oracle mechanisms for large transactions
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can transaction-fee mechanisms be designed so that users, including searchers submitting MEV-informed transactions or bundles, are incentivized to bid truthfully and cannot gain through false-name strategies, even when their demands consume substantial fractions of block capacity? The goal is a mechanism with provable welfare guarantees beyond the small-transaction regime.
status: The state of the art is SAKA (Bahrani, Garimidi and Roughgarden, 2024, *Transaction Fee Mechanism Design in a Post-MEV World*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2024.29), which achieves an approximately half-optimal welfare guarantee for small transactions and a matching deterministic limitation. Extending truthful, false-name-resistant welfare guarantees to large transactions remains an open research target; a related literature is budget-feasible procurement with large projects.
solved_when: A mechanism is exhibited with truthful, false-name-resistant behavior and a welfare guarantee for transactions or bundles occupying substantial fractions of block capacity, improving on the approximately half-optimal guarantee known for small transactions.
why: Large indivisible bundles violate the small-item assumptions underlying existing guarantees, so current results simply do not apply when a single MEV-informed transaction or bundle dominates block space — precisely the regime where MEV is most consequential.
key_works: Bahrani, Garimidi and Roughgarden (2024), *Transaction Fee Mechanism Design in a Post-MEV World*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2024.29.

title: Shared-discount EIP-1559 conjecture
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Does a modification of EIP-1559 in which all transactions share a common discount rate still achieve near-optimal welfare? Formally, settle the March 2026 conjecture by proving or refuting near-optimal welfare for this shared-discount variant, and quantify the welfare loss as a function of the available capacity slack.
status: An explicit March 2026 conjecture; the shared-discount case remains open. Fully patient guarantees are established, as are impossibility results for heterogeneous discounts (Babaioff and Nisan, 2025–2026, *On the Welfare of EIP-1559 with Patient Bidders*, arXiv:2502.20031).
solved_when: A proof or counterexample for near-optimal welfare under a common transaction discount rate is given, together with an explicit quantification of the welfare loss relative to capacity slack.
why: It would extend EIP-1559's welfare guarantees from fully patient bidders to settings where transaction value decays while waiting in the mempool, which is the realistic case for fee mechanisms.
key_works: Babaioff and Nisan (2025–2026), *On the Welfare of EIP-1559 with Patient Bidders*, arXiv:2502.20031.

title: Efficient selection of fee dimensions
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: Which small set of transaction-fee dimensions best approximates a resource-capacity region as it evolves over time, and can such a set be found efficiently with provable approximation guarantees?
status: The question became a concrete research target after 2025 work by Lavee et al. (2025), *Does Your Blockchain Need Multidimensional Transaction Fees?* (arXiv:2504.15438), which characterized one-dimensional approximation and proved NP-completeness of general optimal dimension selection. Relatedly, low-dimensional approximation of production polytopes has been studied.
solved_when: An algorithm (or hardness result) is given for selecting a small set of fee dimensions that approximates the evolving capacity region with a stated, provable approximation guarantee.
why: It identifies which fee dimensions are actually worth their implementation complexity, separating useful multidimensional fee structures from unnecessary overhead.
key_works: Lavee et al. (2025), *Does Your Blockchain Need Multidimensional Transaction Fees?*, arXiv:2504.15438.

title: Execution-ticket capital concentration
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: When buyers of execution tickets differ in financing costs and risk tolerance, how concentrated can ownership of advance rights become? Formally, what bounds can be placed on the equilibrium concentration of execution tickets when participants face heterogeneous capital costs and risk preferences?
status: Research target since 2024 analysis identified concentration and restrictive conditions for complete MEV capture; see Burian, Crapis and Saleh (2024), *MEV Capture and Decentralization in Execution Tickets*, arXiv:2408.11255.
solved_when: A characterization — upper or lower bounds — of ticket-ownership concentration under heterogeneous financing costs and risk tolerances is established, including identification of conditions under which concentration becomes extreme (monopolization) or remains bounded.
why: Buyers with access to cheap financing could monopolize advance rights, undermining the decentralization that execution tickets are meant to provide.
key_works: Burian, Crapis and Saleh (2024), *MEV Capture and Decentralization in Execution Tickets*, arXiv:2408.11255.

title: Fair-order evidence at validator scale
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can we make fair transaction ordering cheap enough to audit at the scale of large, constantly changing validator committees, without giving up fault tolerance or relying on a trusted coordinator? Concretely, this asks for fair-order evidence whose cost falls below Quick Order Fairness's quadratic amortized communication while preserving its optimal resilience guarantees.
status: The state of the art is Quick Order Fairness (Cachin et al., 2022, arXiv:2112.06615), which achieves optimal resilience with quadratic amortized communication; reducing evidence costs below this at validator scale remains an open research target, with succinct distributed audit trails noted as a related direction.
solved_when: A protocol produces auditable fair-order evidence for large, changing committees that is sub-quadratic in amortized communication, maintains the fault tolerance of Quick Order Fairness (2022), and requires no trusted coordinator.
why: Current costs make fair ordering impractical as validator sets grow; cheaper evidence would make fairness affordable at larger scale and let fair-ordering protocols keep functioning as committees churn.
key_works: Cachin et al. (2022), *Quick Order Fairness*, arXiv:2112.06615.

title: Counterfactual ground truth for MEV detectors
subfield: MEV measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can we construct a corpus of blockchain-execution traces that serves as independently verified ground truth for MEV detection, separating what value was extractable, what profit was actually realized, and what harm users suffered — and including both detector failures and benign transactions that merely look like MEV?
status: A data target extending measurements begun in 2019 (Daian et al. (2019), *Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning, Transaction Reordering, and Consensus Instability in Decentralized Exchanges*, arXiv:1904.05234); the counterfactual scope and uncertainty of such traces require explicit certification.
solved_when: A released dataset of traces exists in which each event carries independently checked labels distinguishing extractable value, realized profit, and user harm, with counterfactual scope and uncertainty explicitly certified, and coverage of detector failures and benign lookalikes.
why: It frees MEV-detector evaluation from circularity: today heuristics are scored against their own labels, so their true accuracy is unknown.
key_works: Daian et al. (2019), *Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning, Transaction Reordering, and Consensus Instability in Decentralized Exchanges*, arXiv:1904.05234.

bib.title: Counterfactual ground truth for MEV detectors

title: Joint vault-and-holder peg equilibrium
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: When can a stablecoin peg remain stable if both the vaults backing it and the holders using it behave strategically — vaults choosing their leverage, and heterogeneous holders deciding whether to enter, redeem, or switch to another currency? Formally, characterize the joint equilibrium of vault leverage choices and holder participation, redemption, and currency-switching decisions, and determine when the peg is stable in that equilibrium.
status: This remains an open research target that goes beyond the 2020–2022 stochastic results on stable and unstable regimes, notably Klages-Mundt and Minca (2022), *While stability lasts: A stochastic model of noncustodial stablecoins*, DOI:10.1111/mafi.12357. Related directions include mean-field games with entry and interacting-bank systemic risk.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the joint vault-and-holder equilibrium — covering strategic vault leverage choice together with heterogeneous holders' entry, redemption, and currency-switching behavior — identifying the conditions on vault leverage and holder populations under which the peg is stable versus unstable.
why: It replaces fixed-demand peg arguments, which assume holders passively stay put, with a model in which participation itself is strategic — so stability claims actually hold when users can leave and vaults can over-lever.
key_works: Klages-Mundt and Minca (2022), *While stability lasts: A stochastic model of noncustodial stablecoins*, DOI:10.1111/mafi.12357.

title: Tenfold payment-channel capital efficiency
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a payment-channel network route an order of magnitude more completed payment volume per coin of locked capital than today's designs, while preserving comparable safety, latency, and robustness to churn? Formally, the target is a tenfold increase in completed volume per locked coin, evaluated on published asymmetric workloads.
status: This is a moonshot target building on rebalancing techniques from 2017 and congestion-control routing from 2020; no design has yet achieved it. Key works include Sivaraman et al. (2020), [*High Throughput Cryptocurrency Routing in Payment Channel Networks*](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi20-paper-sivaraman.pdf), and Khalil and Gervais (2017), *Revive*, IACR ePrint:2017/823.
solved_when: A routing and rebalancing design demonstrably achieves tenfold completed volume per locked coin on published asymmetric workloads, with safety, latency, and churn robustness comparable to existing systems.
why: It would sharply lower the working capital required to operate noncustodial payment channels, making self-custodied payments economically viable at scale.
key_works: Sivaraman et al. (2020), [*High Throughput Cryptocurrency Routing in Payment Channel Networks*](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi20-paper-sivaraman.pdf); Khalil and Gervais (2017), *Revive*, IACR ePrint:2017/823.

title: Fair exchange across heterogeneous finality
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can collusion-resistant fair exchange be extended to ledgers whose settlement guarantees differ — unequal rollback risks and unequal censorship risks — and if so, how much collateral and what outside incentives are needed to keep it secure?
status: This remains a research target beyond Rapidash's 2022 preprint and its FC 2025 user–miner-collusion guarantees (Chung, Masserova, Shi and Thyagarajan, 2022; IACR ePrint:2022/1063); no treatment of heterogeneous finality exists yet.
solved_when: A construction (with proof) achieves collusion-resistant exchange across ledgers with heterogeneous rollback and censorship risks, together with bounds on the required collateral and outside incentives.
why: It would align exchange security guarantees with the settlement paths that actually exist between real, unequal ledgers, rather than assuming uniform finality.
key_works: Chung, Masserova, Shi and Thyagarajan (2022; FC 2025), *Rapidash: Atomic Swaps Secure under User-Miner Collusion*, IACR ePrint:2022/1063.

title: Bayesian Sybil reserve prices in proof auctions
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can an auction mechanism for proof markets set reserve prices that provably limit the expected gains of provers who submit fake bids under a known distribution of valuations? The goal is a distribution-aware (Bayesian) characterization of such Sybil bidding and a mechanism design that bounds the resulting expected profit.
status: Open; listed as an explicit future direction in the 2025 revision of Prooφ (Wang, Zhou, Yaish, Zhang, Fisch and Livshits, *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism*, arXiv:2404.06495). Related literature includes false-name-proof double auctions and reserve manipulation.
solved_when: A mechanism is given whose expected Sybil gains are bounded, with a formal characterization of fake-user bidding under the assumed valuation distribution.
why: Without it, suppliers in proof markets can fabricate hidden price floors through fake identities, distorting auction outcomes and extracting excess revenue.
key_works: Wang, Zhou, Yaish, Zhang, Fisch and Livshits (2025), *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism*, arXiv:2404.06495.

bib.title: Bayesian Sybil reserve prices in proof auctions

title: Paid verification when fraud is vanishingly rare
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can a proof market sustain genuine independent verification in equilibrium when deterrence itself makes successful fraud — and hence the rewards for catching it — vanishingly rare? The question is to design an incentive structure that remains robust despite free riding by honest verifiers and by attackers with no stake in the system.
status: The problem has been a research target since the verifier's dilemma was articulated in 2015 by Luu, Teutsch, Kulkarni and Saxena, *Demystifying Incentives in the Consensus Computer* (IACR ePrint:2015/702). It connects to inspection games and to the volunteer's dilemma with rare disasters.
solved_when: A mechanism is exhibited in which independent verification is an equilibrium behavior even as successful-fraud events become arbitrarily rare, with free riding and outside attackers both accounted for.
why: Without it, the verification assumption underlying proof markets is economically hollow: rational verifiers stop checking, and the security of the underlying system silently degrades.
key_works: Luu, Teutsch, Kulkarni and Saxena (2015), *Demystifying Incentives in the Consensus Computer*, IACR ePrint:2015/702.

bib.title: Paid verification when fraud is vanishingly rare

title: Optimal deterministic scheduling with weak discounting
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: What is the best possible competitive ratio achievable by a deterministic online algorithm for packet scheduling when the value of a packet decays geometrically with a discount factor λ in the range roughly 0.770018 < λ < 1? More precisely, determine the optimal deterministic competitive ratio for all λ in this intermediate regime.
status: The problem is explicitly left open in the 2026 revision of Gafni and Yaish (2024; revised 2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549. Bounds already match for smaller values of λ, and the undiscounted endpoint λ = 1 (the classical case) is solved; the intermediate regime remains open.
solved_when: The optimal deterministic competitive ratio is pinned down (matching upper and lower bounds) for every λ with approximately 0.770018 < λ < 1.
why: It closes the gap between the solved small-λ regime and the classical undiscounted endpoint, yielding sharp performance guarantees for settings where job value decays over time, as with financially decaying or perishable goods.
key_works: Gafni and Yaish (2024; revised 2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549.

bib.title: Optimal deterministic scheduling with weak discounting

title: Heterogeneous discounting with batch capacity
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Is there a tight competitive ratio for online scheduling when jobs differ in size and decay law and must be packed into capacity-constrained batches? A formal answer would characterize the best achievable guarantee in this heterogeneous-discount, bounded-batch setting.
status: This target lies beyond the current state of the art, the common-discount unit-service model of Gafni and Yaish (2024–2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549. Related settings include online knapsack with deadlines and perishable-job scheduling.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio are established for jobs with heterogeneous sizes and heterogeneous discount laws under batch capacity constraints, generalizing the common-discount unit-service model.
why: Block space and compute-market allocation involve jobs of varying size whose value decays under different laws, so tight guarantees here would directly inform real allocation mechanisms.
key_works: Gafni and Yaish (2024–2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549.

title: Network-aware optimal block withholding
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we compute provably optimal block-withholding strategies for a selfish miner once block propagation actually depends on the network at hand — its topology, block sizes, congestion, and the attacker's choice of when and where to release blocks? A satisfactory answer would take the form of certified optimal policies for a Markov decision process whose transition structure encodes these network realities.
status: Current results are MDP-based treatments from 2015–2020, including Sapirshtein, Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Optimal Selfish Mining Strategies in Bitcoin* (arXiv:1507.06183) and Gervais et al. (2016), *On the Security and Performance of Proof of Work Blockchains* (DOI:10.1145/2976749.2978341); their optimality guarantees concern simplified network models, leaving the network-aware setting open.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that computes withholding policies with optimality guarantees valid under network-dependent propagation — i.e., propagation determined by topology, block size, congestion, and selective release — rather than under a simplified network abstraction.
why: It would make the profitability thresholds of selfish mining defensible for actual deployed networks, rather than for idealized models whose guarantees may not transfer.
key_works: Sapirshtein, Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Optimal Selfish Mining Strategies in Bitcoin*, arXiv:1507.06183; Gervais et al. (2016), *On the Security and Performance of Proof of Work Blockchains*, DOI:10.1145/2976749.2978341.

title: Many-miner private-fork equilibria
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: When many heterogeneous miners each selfishly withhold and privately fork blocks, what does an equilibrium look like? The goal is to characterize equilibrium withholding and release policies for arbitrarily many such miners under incomplete information.
status: A research target extending 2016 mining games (Kiayias et al. (2016), *Blockchain Mining Games*, arXiv:1607.02420); 2026 multi-attacker experiments (Perešíni et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.02984) compare specified strategies in multi-attacker scenarios without solving general equilibria.
solved_when: A characterization of equilibrium withholding and release policies exists for arbitrarily many heterogeneous miners maintaining private forks under incomplete information.
why: Competing attackers can invalidate single-attacker predictions, so existing selfish-mining results may not describe what actually happens once multiple withholders coexist.
key_works: Kiayias et al. (2016), *Blockchain Mining Games*, arXiv:1607.02420; Perešíni et al. (2026), *Selfish Mining in Multi-Attacker Scenarios: An Empirical Evaluation of Nakamoto, Fruitchain, and Strongchain*, arXiv:2601.02984.

title: Dynamic withholding coalitions
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we design blockchain protocols that remain robust when the attacking coalition is not a fixed set of pools but an overlapping, shifting group of economic entities that privately share withheld blocks and redistribute rewards via unobservable side payments?
status: No constructions are known beyond bounded-coalition guarantees; FruitChains (Pass and Shi, 2017, DOI:10.1145/3087801.3087809) and FairChain, along with the reward-allocation analysis of Aumayr et al. (2026, arXiv:2503.10185), establish important equilibria under specified models, but none handle dynamic, unobservable coalitions.
solved_when: A protocol is proven robust (e.g., with stated equilibrium or safety guarantees) against coalitions that may overlap, change membership over time, and coordinate through private block sharing and unobservable side payments — going beyond existing bounded-coalition guarantees under a specified model.
why: Pool identities do not reveal which economic entities are actually coordinating, so defenses keyed to observable pool structure can be circumvented by hidden coalitions.
key_works: Pass and Shi (2017), *FruitChains: A Fair Blockchain*, DOI:10.1145/3087801.3087809; Aumayr et al. (2026), *Optimal Reward Allocation via Proportional Splitting*, arXiv:2503.10185.

title: Capital-constrained time to profitability
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: When a selfish miner's bankroll is finite and borrowing is costly, how long must they endure losses before the attack pays off, and what is the trade-off between expected profit, break-even time, and risk of ruin? Formally, optimize selfish-mining strategies under capital, financing-cost, and ruin constraints and characterize the resulting profit–break-even-time–risk frontier.
status: This target goes beyond the 2018 profit-lag analysis of Grunspan and Pérez-Marco (*On profitability of selfish mining*, arXiv:1805.08281) and 2026 results by Finkbeiner, Shaw and Almashaqbeh (*When Does Being Selfish Pay Off? Temporal Composability and Profitability in Selfish Mining*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.29) distinguishing profit-maximizing from time-minimizing strategies.
solved_when: A characterization (exact or optimal within a stated strategy class) of selfish-mining strategies under finite bankrolls, financing costs, and ruin constraints, together with the derived frontier relating expected profit, time to profitability, and ruin risk.
why: A selfish-mining attack that is profitable in expectation may require interim losses so large that no realistically capitalized miner can sustain it — so classical profitability thresholds overstate the attack's practical feasibility.
key_works: Grunspan and Pérez-Marco (2018), *On profitability of selfish mining*, arXiv:1805.08281; Finkbeiner, Shaw and Almashaqbeh (2026), *When Does Being Selfish Pay Off? Temporal Composability and Profitability in Selfish Mining*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.29.

title: Attack composition with endogenous miner exit
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: When a miner launches a withholding or selfish-mining attack, how do rival miners' entry, exit, and relocation of hashpower reshape the profitability of that same attack over time? Formally, characterize the switching equilibrium among withholding, honest mining, and withdrawal in a market where competitors respond endogenously to the attacker's regime.
status: The problem emerged as a research target following 2025–2026 temporal analyses of attack revenue and efficiency; current understanding is that adaptive market equilibria require modeling endogenous competitor responses. Key works: Doger and Ulukus (2025), *Incentive Attacks in BTC: Short-Term Revenue Changes and Long-Term Efficiencies*, arXiv:2511.11538; Finkbeiner et al. (2026), DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.29.
solved_when: A model exists that endogenizes competing miners' entry, exit, and hashpower relocation, and yields checkable conditions (or an equilibrium characterization) for when a miner switches between withholding, honest mining, and withdrawal.
why: Attacks are not performed against a fixed environment: they alter the very market conditions — competitor behavior and hashpower distribution — that determine their own profitability, so static attack analysis can misjudge both feasibility and harm.
key_works: Doger and Ulukus (2025), *Incentive Attacks in BTC: Short-Term Revenue Changes and Long-Term Efficiencies*, arXiv:2511.11538; Finkbeiner et al. (2026), DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.29.

bib.title: Attack composition with endogenous miner exit

title: Competing mining-bribery markets
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: What happens to blockchain mining incentives when several bribers compete for the same hash power at once, each able to make contingent offers, counteroffers, and payments that may fail? A satisfying answer would characterize the equilibria of such a multi-briber mining game, allowing strategic acceptance by miners and unreliable payment channels.
status: This target goes beyond profitable bribery constructions developed in 2023–2025, notably Bar-Zur et al. (2023), *Deep Bribe: Predicting the Rise of Bribery in Blockchain Mining with Deep RL*, IACR ePrint:2023/472, and Sarenche, Nikova and Preneel (2025), *Mining Power Destruction Attacks in the Presence of Petty-Compliant Mining Pools*, arXiv:2502.07410; no analysis of the competing-briber setting is known.
solved_when: A solution is a game-theoretic model (and equilibrium analysis) of mining with multiple contingent bribers, incorporating counteroffers and possibly failed payments, with provable characterizations of rational miner behavior.
why: Defending against a single briber can itself create counterbribery incentives, so single-briber defenses may be unstable once competition among bribers is accounted for.
key_works: Bar-Zur et al. (2023), *Deep Bribe: Predicting the Rise of Bribery in Blockchain Mining with Deep RL*, IACR ePrint:2023/472; Sarenche, Nikova and Preneel (2025), *Mining Power Destruction Attacks in the Presence of Petty-Compliant Mining Pools*, arXiv:2502.07410.

title: Measuring petty compliance
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we empirically measure how real miners actually respond to competing tips, fees, and bribes, rather than assuming they are uniformly honest or uniformly bribe-responsive?
status: This is an open experimental target. Models from 2023–2025 established that outcomes are strongly sensitive to these behavioral assumptions: Bar-Zur et al. (2023), *Deep Bribe*, IACR ePrint:2023/472, and Sarenche et al. (2025), *Mining Power Destruction Attacks in the Presence of Petty-Compliant Mining Pools*, arXiv:2502.07410. No field measurement yet exists.
solved_when: An empirical estimate (or measurement methodology) of miners' behavioral response to competing tips, fees, and bribes exists, without imposing uniform honesty or uniform bribe-responsiveness assumptions.
why: Whether the attack thresholds predicted by bribe and withholding models actually bind in practice hinges entirely on which behavioral regime miners occupy in the field.
key_works: Bar-Zur et al. (2023), *Deep Bribe*, IACR ePrint:2023/472; Sarenche et al. (2025), *Mining Power Destruction Attacks in the Presence of Petty-Compliant Mining Pools*, arXiv:2502.07410.

title: Separating withholding from outages
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we tell, from on-chain evidence alone, that a miner is deliberately withholding blocks — as opposed to an honest miner who simply went offline, moved hashpower, lost a propagation race, or was misattributed to the wrong pool? A sharper version asks for a detection procedure that isolates the causal signature of withholding while keeping the false-positive rate from these benign confounds under control.
status: Current state of the art consists of statistical tests for selfish mining in proof-of-work systems (Li, Campajola and Tessone, 2024, DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3) and the reconstruction of the Qubic selfish mining campaign on Monero (Lee and Kim, 2026, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28). The target exceeds both, since anomalous forks still require causal interpretation, which neither provides.
solved_when: A statistical test exists that detects selfish/withholding behavior with a controlled false-positive rate against outages, hashpower migration, propagation races, and pool misattribution, going beyond the existing 2024 statistical tests and the 2026 Qubic reconstruction by providing causal interpretation of anomalous forks.
why: Without separating withholding from benign causes, anomaly signals cannot be acted on; with it, attack attribution becomes credible and defensible.
key_works: Li, Campajola and Tessone (2024), *Statistical detection of selfish mining in proof-of-work blockchain systems*, DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3; Lee and Kim (2026), *Inside Qubic’s Selfish Mining Campaign on Monero: Evidence, Tactics, and Limits*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28.

title: Profit versus statistical detectability
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: How much mining advantage can an attacker gain before their behavior becomes statistically distinguishable from honest network variation? Formally, this asks for minimax bounds on profitable withholding strategies under constraints on the detector's false-positive rate and detection delay.
status: This is a research target opened after January 2026, when hybrid attacks demonstrated revenue–forking tradeoffs without establishing general minimax bounds; Wang et al. (2026, online), *To be detected or not: a hybrid selfish mining attack and countermeasures*, DOI:10.1007/s11704-026-51791-9, and Li et al. (2024), DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3, are the key works; related lines include hypothesis-testing lower bounds and covert communication.
solved_when: A general minimax bound is established on mining advantage as a function of detector false-positive and delay constraints, and the set of attacks that remain statistically indistinguishable from honest network variation is characterized.
why: It determines the limits of monitoring-based defenses, showing where statistical detection can and cannot protect an honest network against profitable deviations.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026, online), *To be detected or not: a hybrid selfish mining attack and countermeasures*, DOI:10.1007/s11704-026-51791-9; Li et al. (2024), DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3.

title: Proof-producing attack discovery
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we take a learned mining policy and automatically produce a machine-checkable certificate of its profitability, rather than a numerical estimate that must be trusted? Formally, the goal is a pipeline that converts learned policies into verified profitability certificates or certified upper bounds, with rigorous control of both truncation errors and errors from continuous state spaces.
status: This is an engineering research target that would connect 2020 MDP analysis methods (Bar-Zur, Eyal and Tamar, 2020, *Efficient MDP Analysis for Selfish-Mining in Blockchains*, arXiv:2007.05614) with 2025 automated DAG-based analysis (Keller, 2025, *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888); no such certified pipeline currently exists.
solved_when: A method exists that takes a learned mining policy and outputs a machine-checkable profitability certificate or certified upper bound, explicitly accounting for truncation error and continuous-state error, so that attack and security claims derived from it are independently verifiable.
why: It makes claims about attack profitability and protocol security independently checkable, so that conclusions about selfish-mining and withholding strategies no longer rest on unverifiable numerical computations.
key_works: Bar-Zur, Eyal and Tamar (2020), *Efficient MDP Analysis for Selfish-Mining in Blockchains*, arXiv:2007.05614; Keller (2025), *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888.

title: Comparable mining-attack benchmarks
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can the blockchain-security community agree on a common experimental standard for evaluating mining attacks, so that selfish-mining and withholding strategies are compared on equal footing?
status: An open research target following the 2025 selfish-mining SoK (Finkbeiner et al. (2025), *SoK: Time to be Selfless?! Demystifying the Landscape of Selfish Mining Strategies and Models*, IACR ePrint:2025/043) and improved short- versus long-run profitability accounting by Doger and Ulukus (2025), arXiv:2511.11538.
solved_when: A published benchmark specification fixes elapsed time, cost, realized revenue, difficulty phase, information access, and termination rules, and is adopted across mining-attack evaluations so results are directly comparable.
why: Incompatible denominators can reverse attack rankings, making published profitability comparisons unreliable.
key_works: Finkbeiner et al. (2025), *SoK: Time to be Selfless?! Demystifying the Landscape of Selfish Mining Strategies and Models*, IACR ePrint:2025/043; Doger and Ulukus (2025), arXiv:2511.11538.

title: Composing pool infiltration and private forks
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: What is the optimal strategy for an adversary who simultaneously infiltrates pools, withholds blocks on a private chain, and selectively releases them, under realistic payout rules, identity changes, and detection responses? A full answer would characterize the joint policy and its payoff, rather than treating each attack component in isolation.
status: This is a research target extending stubborn mining (Nayak et al., 2016, *Stubborn Mining: Generalizing Selfish Mining and Combining with an Eclipse Attack*, DOI:10.1109/EuroSP.2016.32) and fork-after-withholding attacks (Kwon et al., 2017, *Be Selfish and Avoid Dilemmas: Fork After Withholding (FAW) Attacks on Bitcoin*, arXiv:1708.09790); no composed analysis exists yet.
solved_when: A strategy and payout analysis is given that composes pool infiltration, private-chain withholding, and selective release while accounting for pool payout rules, attacker identity changes, and defender detection responses, yielding a provable optimality (or rationality) characterization for the composed attack.
why: Because these attacks share computational and informational resources, separate analyses can miss composition effects that change optimal behavior and payoff.
key_works: Nayak et al. (2016), *Stubborn Mining: Generalizing Selfish Mining and Combining with an Eclipse Attack*, DOI:10.1109/EuroSP.2016.32; Kwon et al. (2017), *Be Selfish and Avoid Dilemmas: Fork After Withholding (FAW) Attacks on Bitcoin*, arXiv:1708.09790.

title: Incentive-compatible defense adoption
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: How can we design activation mechanisms that make rational miners voluntarily adopt withholding defenses even while competitors keep their existing behavior? Formally, the question is to characterize mechanisms for which adoption is incentive-compatible at (or below) the defense's adoption threshold.
status: This has been a research target since early tie-breaking defenses, and deployment feasibility and adoption incentives remain distinct requirements; the line of work runs from Zhang and Preneel (2017), *Publish or Perish: A Backward-Compatible Defense Against Selfish Mining in Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-52153-4_16, to Finkbeiner et al. (2025), IACR ePrint:2025/043.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified for which voluntary adoption by miners is an equilibrium (or dominant strategy) against competitors retaining existing behavior, with a proof of its adoption incentives; deployment feasibility is a separate requirement and need not be shown.
why: Defenses may fail before reaching their adoption threshold, so a mechanism that never clears that bar delivers no protection regardless of its technical soundness.
key_works: Zhang and Preneel (2017), *Publish or Perish: A Backward-Compatible Defense Against Selfish Mining in Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-52153-4_16; Finkbeiner et al. (2025), IACR ePrint:2025/043.

title: Stability of mining counterstrategies
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: When a selfish-mining pool faces retaliation from other pools, what repeated-game equilibria emerge — and does punishing deviators restore honest mining or merely concentrate effective mining power in the punishers?
status: The target was sharpened by 2025 counterstrategy results (Gal, Szabo and Rottenstreich, 2025, *Majority is not Needed: A Counterstrategy to Selfish Mining*, DOI:10.1109/ICBC64466.2025.11114470) showing that sufficiently large pools can exploit another deviator; the repeated-game backdrop draws on Kiayias et al. (2016), *Blockchain Mining Games*, arXiv:1607.02420.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the repeated-game outcomes when pools retaliate against withholding strategies, specifying the conditions under which retaliation restores honesty and those under which it concentrates effective power.
why: Punishing attackers can itself weaken decentralization, so understanding when counterstrategies backfire determines whether retaliation is a viable defense for protocol design.
key_works: Gal, Szabo and Rottenstreich (2025), *Majority is not Needed: A Counterstrategy to Selfish Mining*, DOI:10.1109/ICBC64466.2025.11114470; Kiayias et al. (2016), *Blockchain Mining Games*, arXiv:1607.02420.

title: Disruptive mining without reward gains
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: When can a miner rationally sustain a disruptive strategy like selfish mining even though it earns no more in mining rewards than honest behavior? The question is to characterize when non-revenue motives — publicity, harm to competitors, or external contracts — make sabotage profitable in aggregate, and to bound the resulting incentives.
status: The Qubic study (Lee and Kim, 2026, *Inside Qubic's Selfish Mining Campaign on Monero: Evidence, Tactics, and Limits*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28) documents disruption occurring without a campaign-wide mining-reward advantage, establishing this as an explicit 2026 frontier; the classic revenue-based analysis traces to Eyal and Sirer (2013), *Majority is not Enough*, arXiv:1311.0243.
solved_when: A model or empirical criterion exists that identifies when disruption without a campaign-wide mining-reward advantage is rational, quantifying how publicity, competitor harm, or external side-payments must compensate for lost mining revenue.
why: Revenue-only rationality models can miss economically motivated sabotage, leaving protocols judged secure against attacks that real actors have incentives to run.
key_works: Lee and Kim (2026), *Inside Qubic’s Selfish Mining Campaign on Monero: Evidence, Tactics, and Limits*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28; Eyal and Sirer (2013), *Majority is not Enough*, arXiv:1311.0243.

title: Short-window reward-equilibrium guarantees
subfield: Selfish mining, withholding strategies and attack rationality
open: Can we prove how strongly proportional reward splitting discourages deviation when the observation window is short and the workshare estimates it relies on are noisy? The goal is tight finite-window incentive guarantees that account for noisy workshare estimation and an explicit overhead budget.
status: A research target opened by FairChain's 2026 theorem and its modeled 38% deviation threshold at six confirmations; no finite-window guarantees under noise and overhead budgets are known yet. Key works: Aumayr et al. (2026), *Optimal Reward Allocation via Proportional Splitting*, arXiv:2503.10185; Szalachowski et al. (2019), *StrongChain: Transparent and Collaborative Proof-of-Work Consensus*.
solved_when: Tight finite-window incentive guarantees for reward splitting are derived under noisy workshare estimates with explicit overhead budgets, sharpening (or confirming) the modeled 38% deviation threshold at six confirmations.
why: Such guarantees would let practitioners set reward-system parameters from proofs rather than simulations, knowing exactly when deviations stop paying within realistic windows.
key_works: Aumayr et al. (2026), *Optimal Reward Allocation via Proportional Splitting*, arXiv:2503.10185; Szalachowski et al. (2019), [*StrongChain: Transparent and Collaborative Proof-of-Work Consensus*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/szalachowski).

title: Joint timestamp and withholding optimization
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can an attacker optimally manipulate a proof-of-work chain by choosing timestamps, timing the release of a privately mined fork, and allocating hashpower across difficulty periods all at once, subject to the protocol's exact validity and rounding rules? The question is whether this joint optimization admits a tractable characterization of the optimal adversarial strategy.
status: The target combines the 2015 selfish-withholding optimization of Sapirshtein et al. (2015, arXiv:1507.06183) with the distinct timestamp manipulation established by Yaish, Tochner and Zohar (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing: Manipulating Time for Your Best Interest* (DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250); the joint problem itself remains open.
solved_when: A solution gives optimal (or provably near-optimal) joint strategies for timestamp choice, private-fork release timing, and hashpower allocation over multiple difficulty periods, incorporating the protocol's exact validity and rounding rules rather than relaxations of them.
why: Difficulty adjustment reads timestamps and fork releases as separate threats, but the clock rules and fork rules can interact profitably for an attacker; without a joint analysis, protocol designers cannot bound how much reward a combined manipulation extracts.
key_works: Yaish, Tochner and Zohar (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing: Manipulating Time for Your Best Interest*, DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250; Sapirshtein et al. (2015), arXiv:1507.06183.

title: Robust difficulty control with strategic supply
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can a difficulty adjustment algorithm be designed that is simultaneously robust to timestamp manipulation, hashpower shocks, and strategic changes in mining supply? In formal terms, this asks for a controller whose stability and manipulation-resistance guarantees hold when miners act strategically rather than as exogenous noise.
status: This remains an open research target beyond classical control analysis of difficulty adjustment (Kraft 2016, *Difficulty control for blockchain-based consensus systems*, DOI:10.1007/s12083-015-0347-x) and beyond the supply-response model of Noda, Okumura and Hashimoto (2026), *An Economic Analysis of Difficulty Adjustment Algorithms in Proof-of-Work Blockchain Systems*, DOI:10.1111/iere.70028. Related tools include robust control and strategic system identification.
solved_when: A difficulty adjustment algorithm is proposed with provable guarantees of joint robustness against timestamp manipulation, hashpower shocks, and strategic supply responses — going beyond classical control analysis and the supply-response model of the 2025-online/2026-journal literature.
why: Fast recovery from shocks and resistance to manipulation pull the controller in opposing directions, so we currently lack a design principle that achieves both; such an algorithm would let protocols set difficulty without inviting gaming.
key_works: Kraft (2016), *Difficulty control for blockchain-based consensus systems*, DOI:10.1007/s12083-015-0347-x; Noda, Okumura and Hashimoto (2026), *An Economic Analysis of Difficulty Adjustment Algorithms in Proof-of-Work Blockchain Systems*, DOI:10.1111/iere.70028.
