title: Coalition bounds on clock distortion
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: How much can a shifting coalition of validators or miners distort a blockchain's sense of time through crafted timestamps, even when the protocol defends itself with median-time rules and future-time limits? A satisfying answer would bound the sustained clock distortion achievable by changing coalitions, and account for the cost of inducing block races as part of the attacker's budget.
status: This remains a research target beyond the specific 2022–2023 manipulation strategies; no general bound is known. Key works: Yaish et al. (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing*, DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250; Yaish, Stern and Zohar (2023), *Uncle Maker: (Time)Stamping Out The Competition in Ethereum*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674.
solved_when: A quantitative bound exists on the sustained timestamp distortion attainable by changing coalitions under median-time and future-time restrictions, with the cost of inducing races explicitly incorporated into the attacker's cost model.
why: Timestamps govern reward allocation and contractual deadlines, so a provable bound on their manipulation directly protects the fairness of consensus payments and the reliability of time-sensitive contracts.
key_works: Yaish et al. (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing*, DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250; Yaish, Stern and Zohar (2023), *Uncle Maker: (Time)Stamping Out The Competition in Ethereum*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674.

title: Retargeting under coordinated coin hopping
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can a difficulty-adjustment mechanism remain stable when miners strategically hop between compatible chains, receiving information with delay and facing costs to switch? Formally, is there a coupled retargeting design for which the switched multi-chain system converges despite coordinated, cost-burdened migration?
status: The target lies beyond current work, which documents observed cyclicality in throughput (Ilie et al. (2021), *Unstable Throughput: When the Difficulty Algorithm Breaks*, arXiv:2006.03044), incentive attacks in BTC (Doger and Ulukus (2025), *Incentive Attacks in BTC*, arXiv:2511.11538), and stability results for the single-chain case. Related mathematical tools include coupled oscillators and switched dynamical systems.
solved_when: A retargeting rule (or a proof of impossibility) is given for the coupled system under delayed information and switching costs, establishing stability — or a precise characterization of when stability fails — beyond the single-chain setting.
why: Coordinated migration between chains creates service instability and opens attack windows, so a stable design would close these vulnerabilities in multi-chain deployments.
key_works: Ilie et al. (2021), *Unstable Throughput: When the Difficulty Algorithm Breaks*, arXiv:2006.03044; Doger and Ulukus (2025), *Incentive Attacks in BTC*, arXiv:2511.11538.

title: Economically robust permissionless clocks
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can a permissionless blockchain maintain a reliable consensus clock when participants are rational, join and leave freely, and their local clocks drift? More precisely, construct a clock robust to incentive-driven timestamp manipulation, intermittent participation, and local drift, and identify the minimal external timing assumptions such a construction requires.
status: A research target beyond 2021 dynamic clock synchronization work, extending it with economic incentives; the state of the art includes Badertscher et al. (2021), *Dynamic Ad Hoc Clock Synchronization* (DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-77883-5_14), and Yaish et al. (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing* (DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250).
solved_when: A construction (or an impossibility result) is given for a permissionless consensus clock that tolerates rational timestamp manipulation, intermittent participation, and local drift, together with a characterization of the weakest external timing assumptions under which it works.
why: It would make the timing trust underlying consensus protocols explicit and minimal, replacing implicit assumptions about honest time reporting with ones that hold even when timestamp manipulation is profitable.
key_works: Badertscher et al. (2021), *Dynamic Ad Hoc Clock Synchronization*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-030-77883-5_14; Yaish et al. (2022), *Blockchain Stretching & Squeezing*, DOI:10.1145/3490486.3538250.

title: Merged-mining difficulty stability
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Prove when merged mining stabilizes coupled chains, allowing unequal rewards, selective withholding and partial portfolio abandonment.
status: Explicit in the 2025-online/2026-journal paper: a stabilizing contribution to Litecoin is conjectured.
why: Shared hardware couples otherwise separate security systems.
key_works: Noda, Okumura and Hashimoto (2026), *An Economic Analysis of Difficulty Adjustment Algorithms in Proof-of-Work Blockchain Systems*, DOI:10.1111/iere.70028.

title: Difficulty-upgrade incentive conflicts
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can a Proof-of-Work blockchain adopt a more stable difficulty-adjustment rule when the miners who must adopt it are precisely those who profit from the current rule's volatility? A satisfactory answer would model participation decisions and strategic blocking, and yield a rule that is stable and adoptable despite veto-playing miners.
status: The problem is explicitly flagged as future work in the 2025-online/2026-journal difficulty-adjustment analysis of Noda, Okumura and Hashimoto (2026), *An Economic Analysis of Difficulty Adjustment Algorithms in Proof-of-Work Blockchain Systems* (DOI:10.1111/iere.70028); see also Ilie et al. (2021), arXiv:2006.03044. No solution exists yet.
solved_when: A difficulty-adjustment rule is specified, together with a game-theoretic model incorporating miner participation and strategic blocking, in which the rule is both more stable than existing algorithms and adopted in equilibrium.
why: Without an adoption mechanism, any stability improvement to difficulty adjustment remains a paper proposal that no profitable miner has an incentive to accept; this connects the algorithmic question to the political economy of reform and bargaining with veto players.
key_works: Noda, Okumura and Hashimoto (2026), *An Economic Analysis of Difficulty Adjustment Algorithms in Proof-of-Work Blockchain Systems*, DOI:10.1111/iere.70028; Ilie et al. (2021), arXiv:2006.03044.

title: Cross-client timestamp-defense validation
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can a differential-testing methodology demonstrate that timestamp-manipulation defenses behave consistently across the major maintained blockchain clients and their descendant protocols, including under edge cases such as races, rounding, and chain reorganizations?
status: An open engineering research target arising after the 2023 "Uncle Maker" analysis (Yaish, Stern and Zohar, 2023, *Uncle Maker: (Time)Stamping Out The Competition in Ethereum*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674), which exposed timestamp-manipulation attacks and led to a mitigation; no cross-client validation effort has been reported. Related techniques include differential testing and refinement verification (cf. Garay et al. 2017, IACR ePrint:2016/1048).
solved_when: A differential test suite covering timestamp defenses across maintained clients and descendant protocols is built and run, with cases exercising races, rounding, and reorganizations, and it either confirms consistent behavior or surfaces concrete implementation discrepancies.
why: Sound incentive arguments for timestamp-based difficulty adjustment can be defeated in practice by small implementation discrepancies between clients, so validation across real implementations is what turns those arguments into deployable security.
key_works: Yaish, Stern and Zohar (2023), *Uncle Maker: (Time)Stamping Out The Competition in Ethereum*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674; Garay et al. (2017), IACR ePrint:2016/1048.

title: Ground-truth timestamp-manipulation corpus
subfield: Difficulty adjustment, timestamps and consensus clocks
open: Can we assemble a ground-truth corpus of blockchain timestamps paired with independently observed data — block arrival times, stale blocks, and mining behavior — including documented cases of honest clock failures and labels for timing uncertainty? Such a dataset would let researchers distinguish genuine timestamp manipulation from artifacts of measurement error.
status: This remains a research target; no such corpus exists beyond retrospective evidence reported in 2023. Related work includes Yaish, Stern and Zohar (2023), *Uncle Maker*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674, and Li, Campajola and Tessone (2024), *Statistical detection of selfish mining*, DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3.
solved_when: A publicly available dataset exists in which timestamps are linked to independent arrival observations and stale-block/mining-behavior records, with honest clock failures and uncertainty labels explicitly annotated, sufficient to serve as ground truth for manipulation-detection methods.
why: It separates real timestamp manipulation from measurement artifacts, which is what current detection approaches lack, as they must otherwise rely on retrospective evidence without ground truth.
key_works: Yaish, Stern and Zohar (2023), *Uncle Maker*, DOI:10.1145/3576915.3616674; Li, Campajola and Tessone (2024), *Statistical detection of selfish mining*, DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-55348-3.

title: Tight MAD-DAG security bounds
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: How tight can the security guarantees of MAD-DAG be made? Specifically, can the gap between its conservative MDP-based bound and the full attack model be closed while keeping certification of the bound tractable?
status: Left as explicit future work in 2025 (Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal (2025), *MAD-DAG: Protecting Blockchain Consensus from MEV*, arXiv:2511.21552; building on Bar-Zur, Eyal and Tamar (2020), arXiv:2007.05614). The known MDP bound is conservative, and this reward accounting can substantially loosen the computed bounds; approaches such as abstract interpretation and state-space quotienting are noted as related techniques.
solved_when: A security bound for MAD-DAG is established that matches the full attack model (removing the looseness introduced by conservative reward accounting) and remains computationally tractable to certify.
why: Tighter bounds directly improve the protocol's usable parameters, or else expose hidden weaknesses in the current guarantees that the conservative analysis masks.
key_works: Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal (2025), *MAD-DAG: Protecting Blockchain Consensus from MEV*, arXiv:2511.21552; Bar-Zur, Eyal and Tamar (2020), arXiv:2007.05614.

title: MAD-DAG with competing coalitions
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can a MAD-DAG ledger remain safe and incentive-compatible when several mining coalitions act strategically at once, under heterogeneous network delays and shifting coalition membership — that is, does the mutual-assured-destruction argument survive competition among multiple coordinating attackers?
status: This is a research target beyond the 2025 single-rational-miner analysis of MAD-DAG (Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal (2025), *MAD-DAG*, arXiv:2511.21552); related work on selfish mining in multi-attacker scenarios exists (Perešíni et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.02984), and coalition-proof stochastic games are a relevant framework.
solved_when: A formal analysis establishes safety and incentive properties of MAD-DAG in the multi-attacker setting with heterogeneous delays and changing coalitions, generalizing the single-rational-miner analysis.
why: In practice several strategic mining organizations may coexist, so the single-attacker guarantee does not describe the deployed environment; without a multi-coalition analysis the ledger's security rests on an assumption real deployments violate.
key_works: Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal (2025), *MAD-DAG*, arXiv:2511.21552; Perešíni et al. (2026), *Selfish Mining in Multi-Attacker Scenarios*, arXiv:2601.02984.

title: Liveness under content-destruction defenses
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: When attackers repeatedly trigger equal-length competing chains in content-destruction protocols, how much exclusion and wasted execution can honest participants be forced to suffer? Formally, the question is to bound these quantities under MAD-DAG-style ledger rules.
status: This is a research target following MAD-DAG's 2025 ledger rule (Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal 2025, arXiv:2511.21552); reward-extraction resistance leaves inclusion as a separate, unaddressed objective, building on inclusive chain protocols (Lewenberg, Sompolinsky and Zohar 2015, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_33).
solved_when: A quantitative bound on exclusion and wasted execution caused by equal-length competing-chain attacks is established for content-destruction protocols.
why: It prevents incentive defenses against reward extraction from becoming a cheap tool for suppressing honest content.
key_works: Bar-Zur, Tamar and Eyal (2025), *MAD-DAG*, arXiv:2511.21552; Lewenberg, Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Inclusive Block Chain Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_33.

title: Practical epsilon-sure mining equilibria
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can the Colordag-style best-response guarantees — where following the protocol is an equilibrium with high probability — be achieved with confirmation times and storage overheads small enough for real deployments, even when mining rewards vary over time? Formally: find a DAG-ledger protocol whose epsilon-sure equilibrium holds under variable rewards while keeping the confirmation and storage parameters small.
status: This is an open research target going beyond Colordag's 2023 epsilon-sure equilibrium (Abraham, Dolev, Eyal and Halpern (2023), *Colordag: An Incentive-Compatible Blockchain*, arXiv:2308.11379); FairChain (Aumayr et al. (2026), arXiv:2503.10185) provides a different, practical guarantee rather than the high-probability best-response property sought here.
solved_when: A protocol is exhibited that preserves a high-probability (epsilon-sure) equilibrium for miners under variable rewards, with confirmation and storage parameters that are small — i.e., practical — compared to those required by Colordag's 2023 construction.
why: It would turn equilibrium-based incentive compatibility from a theoretical possibility into a construction usable at realistic scales, where confirmation latency and storage cost actually matter.
key_works: Abraham, Dolev, Eyal and Halpern (2023), *Colordag: An Incentive-Compatible Blockchain*, arXiv:2308.11379; Aumayr et al. (2026), arXiv:2503.10185.

title: Security-preserving PHANTOM approximations
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can the expensive graph-selection rule at the heart of GHOSTDAG be replaced by a cheaper approximation that still provably preserves its Byzantine security and confirmation guarantees? Formally, the question is to construct approximations that remain sound on adversarially chosen DAGs, not just typical ones.
status: This is a research target beyond GHOSTDAG's greedy construction as given by Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990; the approximation–security frontier remains to be characterized. Related work includes Keller (2025), *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888, with connections to approximation algorithms and parameterized graph complexity.
solved_when: An approximation algorithm for the GHOSTDAG graph-selection rule is given, together with a proof that it preserves the explicit Byzantine security and confirmation guarantees of the original construction on adversarial DAGs, at reduced computational cost.
why: Consensus inputs are chosen by attackers, so any speedup that silently weakens guarantees on adversarial DAGs opens the door to exploitation; without a security-preserving approximation, DAG ledgers pay the full cost of the greedy GHOSTDAG construction.
key_works: Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990; Keller (2025), *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888.

title: Resource-bounded responsive DAG consensus
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can we build a DAG consensus protocol that adapts its latency to network conditions while provably bounding the CPU, memory, and communication it consumes, even when an adversary inflates the DAG's growth rate?
status: This is an open engineering research target building on DAG KNIGHT's 2022–2023 design (Sutton and Sompolinsky, 2023, *The DAG KNIGHT Protocol: A Parameterless Generalization of Nakamoto Consensus*, IACR ePrint:2022/1494), adding the missing ingredient of explicit resource limits; it also draws on the throughput-focused DAG lineage of Bagaria et al. (2019), *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092.
solved_when: A working implementation of latency-adaptive DAG consensus exists with explicit, proven bounds on CPU, memory, and communication under adversarial graph growth.
why: Responsiveness — the ability to commit quickly when the network is fast — must survive hostile workloads; without resource bounds, an adversary can degrade a DAG ledger's performance by flooding it with graph structure.
key_works: Sutton and Sompolinsky (2023), *The DAG KNIGHT Protocol: A Parameterless Generalization of Nakamoto Consensus*, IACR ePrint:2022/1494; Bagaria et al. (2019), *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092.

title: Fork choice under asymmetric partitions
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: How secure is a DAG-based fork-choice rule when the network persistently delays some valid branches and delivers others, so that honest nodes hold systematically different views of the ledger? A precise bound is wanted on both the security degradation and the strategic advantage an attacker can gain by exploiting such asymmetric partitions and selective delivery.
status: This is a research target extending the GHOST analysis of Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Secure High-Rate Transaction Processing in Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_32, and the routing attacks demonstrated by Apostolaki, Zohar and Vanbever (2017), *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524. It relates to Byzantine agreement on directed networks.
solved_when: A quantitative bound is established on fork-choice security and on the strategic advantage available to attackers under persistent asymmetric delays and selective delivery of valid DAG branches.
why: It would tell us whether DAG fork-choice rules like GHOST remain safe when routing-level adversaries give honest nodes systematically different views, connecting consensus theory to demonstrated Internet-routing attacks.
key_works: Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Secure High-Rate Transaction Processing in Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_32; Apostolaki, Zohar and Vanbever (2017), *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524.

title: Fast conflict resolution for SPECTRE-style ledgers
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can a DAG-based ledger achieve SPECTRE-style fast confirmation for independent payments while still providing bounded-time resolution for conflicting transactions and an explicitly priced fallback to total order when full ordering is required?
status: This is a research target that has been open since SPECTRE's known ordering limitations were identified in 2016; key works include Sompolinsky, Lewenberg and Zohar (2016), *SPECTRE: Serialization of Proof-of-work Events: Confirming Transactions via Recursive Elections*, IACR ePrint:2016/1159, and Bagaria et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.08092. Related ideas include serializability and optimistic concurrency control.
solved_when: A protocol is specified and analyzed that confirms independent transactions at SPECTRE-like speed, resolves conflicts within a stated bound, and defines a cost (explicit price) for invoking total-order fallback, with security guarantees for each component.
why: Fast conflict-blind confirmation only serves payments that do not interact; general applications with dependent transactions need those dependencies resolved without giving up the speed advantage.
key_works: Sompolinsky, Lewenberg and Zohar (2016), *SPECTRE: Serialization of Proof-of-work Events: Confirming Transactions via Recursive Elections*, IACR ePrint:2016/1159; Bagaria et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.08092.

bib.title: Fast conflict resolution for SPECTRE-style ledgers

title: Succinct adversarial DAG pruning proofs
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can a DAG ledger be equipped with compact, verifiable proofs that pruning its history leaves fork choice, transaction validity, and work accounting intact — all without assuming any trusted checkpoint?
status: This is an engineering research target extending the 2020 succinct-chain verification approach to richer DAG histories. Key works: Bünz et al. (2020), *FlyClient: Super-Light Clients for Cryptocurrencies*, IACR ePrint:2019/226; Sompolinsky et al. (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990. Related directions include streaming verification and authenticated graph summaries.
solved_when: A construction exists that produces succinct pruning proofs for rich DAG histories (not just chains), preserving fork choice, transaction validity, and work accounting, with no trusted checkpoints; storage does not grow indefinitely.
why: Without such proofs, nodes verifying a DAG ledger face either unboundedly growing storage or a growing dependence on trusted parties for checkpointing history.
key_works: Bünz et al. (2020), *FlyClient: Super-Light Clients for Cryptocurrencies*, IACR ePrint:2019/226; Sompolinsky et al. (2021), *PHANTOM GHOSTDAG*, DOI:10.1145/3479722.3480990.

title: DAG fork choice with unavailable payloads
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: When block headers arrive on a DAG ledger but their payloads—or those of referenced ancestors—are selectively withheld, does the fork-choice rule still select a chain whose transactions are actually available and valid? Formally, prove that availability, validation, and fork choice compose correctly under this stronger, adversarial delivery model.
status: This is an open research target extending inclusive and separated-function architectures—Lewenberg, Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Inclusive Block Chain Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_33, and Bagaria et al. (2019), *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092—to stronger delivery assumptions. Related tools include data availability and erasure-coded distributed storage.
solved_when: A proof (or a construction with a proof) that the fork-choice rule over the DAG produces, under selective withholding of payloads and ancestors, a consistent ledger containing only available, validated transactions; or a counterexample showing the composition fails.
why: Without it, apparent consensus progress can yield ledgers whose transactions cannot be executed or verified, so nominal finality delivers nothing usable to users.
key_works: Lewenberg, Sompolinsky and Zohar (2015), *Inclusive Block Chain Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_33; Bagaria et al. (2019), *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092.

bib.title: DAG fork choice with unavailable payloads

title: Fair rewards across heterogeneous propagation
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can a DAG-ledger reward scheme be designed so that an honest miner with slow or poorly connected propagation suffers no meaningful disadvantage, while a miner who deliberately withholds or delays blocks cannot profit from doing so — and can the resulting trade-offs between reward fairness, bandwidth use, and latency be characterized jointly?
status: This remains a research target beyond the improvements of StrongChain and Tailstorm (Szalachowski et al., 2019; Keller et al., 2023, arXiv:2306.12206) over 2019–2023.
solved_when: A reward structure for DAG ledgers is given, together with proofs bounding the disadvantage of honest slow miners and showing no profitable deviation via deliberate delay, plus explicit joint bounds on reward, bandwidth, and latency.
why: Throughput improvements can amplify connectivity advantages; without such a scheme, faster-connected miners capture disproportionate rewards as DAG ledgers scale.
key_works: Szalachowski et al. (2019), *StrongChain: Transparent and Collaborative Proof-of-Work Consensus*; Keller et al. (2023), *Tailstorm: A Secure and Fair Blockchain for Cash Transactions*, arXiv:2306.12206.

title: Reproducible adversarial DAG benchmark
subfield: DAG ledgers, fork choice and reward structure
open: Can we build a reproducible benchmark suite that lets different DAG-ledger protocols be compared on equal footing under adversarial network conditions — specifically workloads with executable withholding, partition, payload-starvation, pruning, and variable-reward behavior under common resource budgets?
status: This remains a research target beyond current capabilities, exceeding 2025 automated tooling (Keller (2025), *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888) and 2026 multi-attacker simulations (Perešíni et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.02984).
solved_when: A published benchmark exists that runs withholding, partition, payload-starvation, pruning, and variable-reward workloads against multiple DAG protocols under common budgets, and its artifacts are executable and reproducible by third parties.
why: Without a common benchmark, published comparisons of DAG protocols rest on incompatible setups and cannot be reproduced or trusted; a standard suite makes protocol comparisons verifiable rather than anecdotal.
key_works: Keller (2025), *Automated Selfish Mining Analysis for DAG-Based PoW Consensus Protocols*, arXiv:2501.10888; Perešíni et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.02984.

title: Measuring endogenous tie-winning advantage
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can we measure, from observable network data, how much of a tie-winning advantage each mining organization actually enjoys as a result of its relay access, geography, and block size — while honestly accounting for what remains unknown about their private infrastructure? A rigorous answer would take the form of per-organization advantage estimates with quantified uncertainty.
status: This is an open experimental target: it would connect network-measurement results accumulated since Decker and Wattenhofer (2013), *Information Propagation in the Bitcoin Network* (DOI:10.1109/P2P.2013.6688704), and Gervais et al. (2016), *On the Security and Performance of Proof of Work Blockchains* (DOI:10.1145/2976749.2978341), with attacker-specific incentive models; related methodological threads include network tomography and causal performance measurement. No such estimates exist yet.
solved_when: A measurement methodology produces per-mining-organization estimates of tie-winning advantage attributable to relay access, geography, and block size, each with a quantified uncertainty that explicitly captures the unobserved private infrastructure.
why: Treating tie-winning advantage as a fixed network parameter hides the fact that some miners systematically win ties and others systematically lose them; measuring it per organization exposes this unequal power.
key_works: Decker and Wattenhofer (2013), *Information Propagation in the Bitcoin Network*, DOI:10.1109/P2P.2013.6688704; Gervais et al. (2016), *On the Security and Performance of Proof of Work Blockchains*, DOI:10.1145/2976749.2978341.

title: Strategic block-relay service
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can a block-relay service be designed so that its relaying behavior is publicly verifiable and its operators have no profitable way to favor some nodes over others — through preferential delay, selective forwarding, or undisclosed private fast paths?
status: SABRE (Apostolaki et al., 2019, arXiv:1808.06254) provides infrastructure-level protections against routing attacks, but verifiable relay arrangements against strategic manipulation remain an open research target; the strategic-relay concern builds on Eyal and Sirer (2013), *Majority is not Enough*, arXiv:1311.0243.
solved_when: A relay arrangement (protocol plus verification mechanism) exists with a formal guarantee that deviations such as preferential delay, selective forwarding, and undisclosed private fast paths are either detectable or unprofitable for the relay operator.
why: Relay services that intermediate block propagation can accumulate consensus power beyond their nominal role, enabling the kinds of strategic manipulation identified in selfish-mining analyses.
key_works: Apostolaki et al. (2019), *SABRE: Protecting Bitcoin against Routing Attacks*, arXiv:1808.06254; Eyal and Sirer (2013), *Majority is not Enough*, arXiv:1311.0243.

title: Compact relay under adversarial mempool divergence
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: How well can compact block relay perform when peers deliberately present misleading mempool states? Specifically, the goal is to bound the reconstruction delay and bandwidth costs of BIP 152-style compact relay against adversarially divergent mempools, and to design prefill and recovery strategies that remain efficient when peers are misleading.
status: This is an open research target going beyond deployed practice: BIP 152 (Corallo, 2016, [*BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0152.mediawiki)) specifies only a standard recovery procedure, and related work on efficient transaction relay (Naumenko et al., 2019, *Erlay: Efficient Transaction Relay for Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237) does not address adversarial mempool divergence; no robust bound or optimized recovery against misleading peers exists yet.
solved_when: An analysis or protocol design gives explicit bounds on reconstruction delay and bandwidth under adversarial mempool divergence, together with optimized prefill and recovery mechanisms robust to misleading peers.
why: Compression is only useful if it survives hostile conditions; without such bounds, compact relay's bandwidth savings can be negated precisely during adversarial congestion, when block propagation matters most.
key_works: Corallo (2016), [*BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0152.mediawiki); Naumenko et al. (2019), *Erlay: Efficient Transaction Relay for Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237.

bib.title: Compact relay under adversarial mempool divergence

title: Downgrade-resistant Bitcoin transport migration
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can Bitcoin's encrypted V2 transport be deployed so that an active adversary cannot force peers back onto the unencrypted legacy transport, while honest peers can still discover each other's capabilities, interoperate across versions, and recover from failed negotiations?
status: This is a research target opened by a May 2026 analysis of V2 downgrade and sustained-eclipse paths; no solution is recorded. Foundational work includes Mehta et al., [*BIP 324: Version 2 P2P Encrypted Transport Protocol*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0324.mediawiki) and Ndolo and Tschorsch (2026), *Security Analysis of Bitcoin's V2 Transport Protocol*, arXiv:2605.19715.
solved_when: A concrete transport-migration design exists in which downgrade attempts are detectable or non-exploitable, and safe capability discovery, interoperability, and recovery are preserved; success is judged against the downgrade and sustained-eclipse attack paths identified in the May 2026 security analysis.
why: Without downgrade resistance, encryption negotiation becomes the weak point of the transport layer: an attacker who can force legacy fallback strips the confidentiality and authentication guarantees BIP 324 was designed to provide.
key_works: Mehta et al., [*BIP 324: Version 2 P2P Encrypted Transport Protocol*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0324.mediawiki); Ndolo and Tschorsch (2026), *Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s V2 Transport Protocol*, arXiv:2605.19715.

title: Eclipse resistance with uncertain AS ownership
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: How should a node select peers for eclipse resistance when it cannot verify which autonomous systems actually control the addresses it sees? The question is to design peer selection that remains robust despite stale routing data, correlated operators, and adversarial claims of network diversity.
status: This remains a research target beyond 2015 eclipse defenses (Heilman et al., 2015, [Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity15/technical-sessions/presentation/heilman)) and continuing ASmap work ([ASmap project](https://opensats.org/projects/asmap)); related directions include robust diversity selection and correlated-failure models.
solved_when: A peer-selection method exists (with analysis) that provably bounds eclipse risk when AS ownership information is uncertain, stale, or adversarially falsified — i.e., diversity claims by distinct identifiers cannot be spoofed into implying independent adversaries.
why: Distinct identifiers need not imply independent adversaries; without accounting for this, eclipse defenses can be defeated by an attacker who fakes network diversity.
key_works: Heilman et al. (2015), [*Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin’s Peer-to-Peer Network*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity15/technical-sessions/presentation/heilman); [ASmap project](https://opensats.org/projects/asmap).

bib.title: Eclipse resistance with uncertain AS ownership

title: Detecting selective delay through encrypted transport
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can a relay or peer detect that its consensus traffic is being deliberately slowed down — rather than merely passing through ordinary congestion — using only encrypted-transport observations, with bounded false alarms and without learning the traffic's content? A sharper formulation asks for a sequential detector that distinguishes adversarial selective delay from benign congestion while preserving the privacy guarantees of the encrypted channel.
status: The target has been sharpened by 2026 V2 message-length inference and isolation analysis (Ndolo and Tschorsch (2026), *Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s V2 Transport Protocol*, arXiv:2605.19715), building on earlier routing-level attack work (Apostolaki et al. (2017), *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524).
solved_when: A detection method exists that identifies deliberate slowing of consensus traffic with a bounded false-alarm rate under non-adversarial congestion, and without exposing message content; demonstrated experimentally on encrypted transport.
why: Encryption protects confidentiality but says nothing about timely delivery, so an adversary can degrade consensus participation without breaking any cryptographic guarantee; detection is the prerequisite for any response.
key_works: Ndolo and Tschorsch (2026), *Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s V2 Transport Protocol*, arXiv:2605.19715; Apostolaki et al. (2017), *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524.

bib.title: Detecting selective delay through encrypted transport

title: Path diversity against adaptive routing adversaries
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can we construct peer and relay path sets for a blockchain network whose connectivity survives route changes, hidden transit dependencies, and partial deployment of the solution — that is, paths that remain independently survivable even when an adaptive routing adversary manipulates BGP-level paths?
status: This is an open engineering research target situated beyond the 2017 BGP-hijacking attacks on Bitcoin (Apostolaki, Zohar and Vanbever, 2017, *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524) and the 2019 SABRE protections (Apostolaki et al., 2019, arXiv:1808.06254); no construction meeting the goal is recorded.
solved_when: A construction exists that maintains independently survivable peer and relay paths under adaptive route changes, does not rely on unobservable transit links being diverse, and remains effective under partial deployment.
why: Without it, many apparently independent peers can silently share a single effective failure point, so an adversary controlling that point can partition or eclipse large parts of the network at once.
key_works: Apostolaki, Zohar and Vanbever (2017), *Hijacking Bitcoin*, arXiv:1605.07524; Apostolaki et al. (2019), *SABRE*, arXiv:1808.06254.

bib.title: Path diversity against adaptive routing adversaries

title: Trust-minimized eclipse detection
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: What can a node that has been isolated from the honest network still learn about its situation, using only its own authenticated observations and a bounded-drift clock — and what is the weakest additional connectivity assumption under which eclipse detection becomes possible?
status: The problem is an open research target, rooted in the 2015 eclipse attacks of Heilman et al. (2015), *Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network*, and the 2020 Erebus attack of Tran et al. (2020), *A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network* (DOI:10.1109/SP40000.2020.00027); it connects to failure-detector impossibility and distributed observability.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the inferences available to an isolated node from authenticated observations and bounded clocks alone, together with an identification of the weakest extra connectivity assumption that suffices for useful eclipse detection (or a proof that no such assumption short of full connectivity helps).
why: Wallet-side eclipse alarms can only be built on observability assumptions that provably hold; without such a characterization, alarms are either blind to real eclipses or trip on false positives.
key_works: Heilman et al. (2015), *Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin’s Peer-to-Peer Network*; Tran et al. (2020), *A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network*, DOI:10.1109/SP40000.2020.00027.

title: Bootstrap security after prolonged disconnection
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: How can a node that has been offline for a long time rejoin a peer-to-peer network securely, when its cached peers, seed service results, and routing metadata may all be stale or attacker-controlled? A satisfactory answer should characterize how expensive it is for an adversary to subvert the rejoining process and what recovery guarantees an honest node can obtain.
status: Proposed as a research target extending the 2015–2020 line of network-partition attacks, including Heilman et al. (2015), *Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network*, and Tran et al. (2020), *A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network*, DOI:10.1109/SP40000.2020.00027; no solution yet exists.
solved_when: A bootstrapping mechanism is specified under which a returning node establishes reliable connectivity despite stale caches, seeds, and routing metadata, together with a quantification of attacker costs and the recovery guarantees the node achieves.
why: Intermittent participants are vulnerable to eclipse before they learn reliable network state, so prolonged disconnection directly opens the door to the partitioning attacks of recent years.
key_works: Heilman et al. (2015), *Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin’s Peer-to-Peer Network*; Tran et al. (2020), *A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network*, DOI:10.1109/SP40000.2020.00027.

title: Adversarially robust transaction reconciliation
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can a transaction reconciliation protocol be made to provably withstand an adversary who poisons the differences it is asked to reconcile, stalls rounds, and repeatedly reconnects? The goal is to bound the CPU, bandwidth, and delay the protocol incurs under such attacks.
status: The target lies beyond the current state of the art, which consists of Erlay's honest-case bandwidth results (Naumenko et al., 2019, *Erlay: Efficient Transaction Relay for Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237) and the message specification of BIP 330 (Naumenko and Wuille, [*BIP 330: Transaction announcements reconciliation*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0330.mediawiki)); no adversarial analysis currently covers poisoned differences, stalled rounds, or repeated reconnections.
solved_when: A reconciliation protocol is specified whose CPU cost, bandwidth use, and delay remain bounded under poisoned differences, stalled reconciliation rounds, and repeated reconnections.
why: Honest-case efficiency should not create cheap amplification; without adversarial bounds, an attacker can exploit reconciliation machinery to exhaust node resources.
key_works: Naumenko et al. (2019), *Erlay: Efficient Transaction Relay for Bitcoin*, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237; Naumenko and Wuille, [*BIP 330: Transaction announcements reconciliation*](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0330.mediawiki).

title: Private relay with deadline guarantees
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can a block-propagation protocol simultaneously guarantee source privacy and a strict delivery deadline for every honest message, even when an adaptive adversary launches Sybil attacks, observes network timing, and selectively drops messages? In other words, is there a relay scheme with Dandelion++-style anonymity guarantees whose latency bound survives this stronger adversary and churn model?
status: This is an open research target aiming to extend Dandelion++ (Fanti et al., 2018, *Dandelion++: Lightweight Cryptocurrency Networking with Formal Anonymity Guarantees*, arXiv:1805.11060) to stronger observation and churn models; related propagation-efficiency work includes Erlay (Naumenko et al., 2019, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237), and the problem connects to anonymous communication and mix-network latency bounds.
solved_when: A protocol (with proof) achieves both source-privacy guarantees at least as strong as Dandelion++'s formal anonymity guarantees and a stated propagation deadline for honest messages, under adaptive Sybils, timing observation, and selective message dropping.
why: Privacy mechanisms that delay or randomize propagation risk missing inclusion deadlines; without a scheme achieving both, deployable source privacy in block relay networks remains blocked by the fear that timeliness guarantees collapse.
key_works: Fanti et al. (2018), *Dandelion++: Lightweight Cryptocurrency Networking with Formal Anonymity Guarantees*, arXiv:1805.11060; Naumenko et al. (2019), *Erlay*, DOI:10.1145/3319535.3354237.

title: Validation work versus propagation priority
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: How should untrusted validation work — such as verifying speculatively relayed blocks or transactions — be scheduled so that a peer's expensive or malicious computational load cannot crowd out the processing of consensus-critical traffic? Formally, the question is to design a work-scheduling and resource-isolation discipline that maintains consensus liveness across heterogeneous client implementations under adversarial input.
status: An open research target in the wake of Yaish et al.'s 2024 demonstration of speculative denial-of-service attacks in Ethereum; related practical context comes from Corallo (2016), *BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*, whose speculative relay mechanisms motivate the scheduling question. Adjacent areas include adversarial scheduling and operating-system resource isolation.
solved_when: A scheduling scheme is specified (and implemented or evaluated) that prevents speculative validation work from starving consensus message processing, robust across heterogeneous clients, with liveness preserved against adversaries of the kind demonstrated by Yaish et al. (2024).
why: Computation exhaustion can cause consensus liveness failures, so without such a discipline an attacker can stall block propagation and consensus progress using only speculative work requests.
key_works: Yaish et al. (2024), [*Speculative Denial-of-Service Attacks in Ethereum*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/yaish); Corallo (2016), *BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*.

title: Privacy-preserving mining-topology measurement
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can we measure the topology of influential mining operations in Bitcoin while quantifying how much of that topology is unobserved, and without leaking information that would help an attacker target specific miners?
status: This remains a research target beyond TxProbe's 2019 testnet reconstruction of Bitcoin's network topology (Delgado-Segura et al., 2019, arXiv:1812.00942; Decker and Wattenhofer, 2013, DOI:10.1109/P2P.2013.6688704); private mining connectivity is still a separate, unsolved measurement challenge.
solved_when: A measurement methodology yields mining-topology data with an explicit quantification of missingness, alongside a demonstrated bound or audit showing that disclosures enabling targeted attacks are minimized.
why: It produces security evidence about the network's most influential participants without handing adversaries a targeting directory.
key_works: Delgado-Segura et al. (2019), *TxProbe: Discovering Bitcoin’s Network Topology Using Orphan Transactions*, arXiv:1812.00942; Decker and Wattenhofer (2013), DOI:10.1109/P2P.2013.6688704.

title: Durable stale-block observatory
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can the research community sustain a long-lived, geographically distributed observatory that records stale blocks, reorganizations, and first-seen observations — with authenticated provenance, durable retention, and independent access for outside researchers?
status: Current artifacts are case-specific, such as the 2026 Qubic dataset (Lee and Kim (2026), *Inside Qubic's Selfish Mining Campaign on Monero*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28; [Qubic study artifacts](https://github.com/shlee-lab/Qubic-selfish-mining-study)). No general observatory exists; this remains a funding target in the area of scientific observatory funding and durable research infrastructure.
solved_when: A funded, continuously operating observatory exists that maintains geographically distributed stale-block, reorganization, and first-seen records with authenticated provenance, retention guarantees, and independent access — going beyond case-specific artifacts.
why: Canonical chains discard important attack evidence; without durable records, incidents like selfish-mining campaigns cannot be independently verified or studied after the fact.
key_works: Lee and Kim (2026), *Inside Qubic’s Selfish Mining Campaign on Monero*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.28; [Qubic study artifacts](https://github.com/shlee-lab/Qubic-selfish-mining-study).

title: Hundredfold relay-efficiency frontier
subfield: Block propagation and network-layer security
open: Can block relay achieve a hundredfold improvement in throughput or communication efficiency on fixed consumer hardware while keeping explicit adversarial guarantees? That is, can the techniques of compact relay and Prism-style blockchain deconstruction be combined into a provably secure system meeting this target?
status: This moonshot is grounded in compact block relay (Corallo, 2016, *BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*) and Prism (Bagaria et al., 2019, *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092); the combined hundredfold target remains unproved.
solved_when: A demonstrated relay scheme attains at least a hundredfold throughput or communication-efficiency gain over the baseline on fixed consumer hardware, with explicit adversarial security guarantees carried through the analysis.
why: It would make ambitious blockchain scaling claims comparable by giving a concrete, provably secure efficiency frontier against which future protocols can be measured.
key_works: Corallo (2016), *BIP 152: Compact Block Relay*; Bagaria et al. (2019), *Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits*, arXiv:1810.08092.

title: Randomized welfare-collusion frontier
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can a randomized transaction-fee mechanism remain truthful and miner-incentive compatible while resisting collusion, in a setting where colluders commit to their behavior before the randomization is revealed? More precisely, the goal is to characterize the class of randomized fee mechanisms satisfying truthfulness, miner incentives, and global welfare-collusion resistance under this interim-collusion timing.
status: The problem is explicitly open as of 2026 under interim collusion. Deterministic and scale-invariant impossibility results are known, and worst-case efficiency is at most 0.842 (Gafni and Yaish (2026), *Transaction Fee Mechanisms Robust to Welfare-Increasing Collusion*, DOI:10.1016/j.geb.2026.02.005).
solved_when: A full characterization is given of the randomized fee mechanisms that are truthful, miner-incentive compatible, and globally welfare-collusion resistant when colluders act before the randomness is revealed; any impossibility result must match or improve the known worst-case efficiency bound of 0.842.
why: It settles whether introducing randomness can circumvent the known impossibilities for deterministic mechanisms and permit any useful degree of collusion resistance.
key_works: Gafni and Yaish (2026), *Transaction Fee Mechanisms Robust to Welfare-Increasing Collusion*, DOI:10.1016/j.geb.2026.02.005.

title: Quantitative incentive-relaxation frontier
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can we characterize exactly how much welfare and revenue a transaction-fee mechanism can guarantee once exact incentive compatibility is relaxed — that is, when user, miner, and coalition deviation gains are each allowed to fall below an explicit approximation tolerance?
status: The target lies beyond exact impossibility results. Gafni's 2026 theorem equates 2-SCP and c-SCP under consistent tie-breaking. Key works include Chung, Roughgarden and Shi (2024–2025), *Collusion-Resilience in Transaction Fee Mechanism Design*, arXiv:2402.09321, and Gafni (2026), *Deterring A Small Collusion is All You Need*, DOI:10.1145/3774904.3792121.
solved_when: Tight bounds (matching upper and lower constructions) are established for welfare and revenue guarantees as a function of the approximation tolerances bounding user, miner, and coalition deviation gains.
why: It converts bare impossibility results into usable attack budgets, telling designers what loss must be tolerated and what can still be guaranteed.
key_works: Chung, Roughgarden and Shi (2024–2025), *Collusion-Resilience in Transaction Fee Mechanism Design*, arXiv:2402.09321; Gafni (2026), *Deterring A Small Collusion is All You Need*, DOI:10.1145/3774904.3792121.

title: Discrete fees with heterogeneous transaction sizes
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can collusion-resistant transaction-fee mechanisms designed for discrete fee values be extended to settings where transactions have unequal sizes, exhibit dependencies, and users can strategically split transactions to game the mechanism?
status: This is a research target following 2022–2024 constructions (Gafni and Yaish (2024), *Discrete & Bayesian Transaction Fee Mechanisms*, arXiv:2210.07793) that circumvented some continuous-domain impossibility results through discretization.
solved_when: A fee mechanism is constructed that retains discrete-value collusion-resistance guarantees while handling heterogeneous transaction sizes, inter-transaction dependencies, and strategic splitting, with no user able to gain by splitting or merging transactions.
why: It would connect the discrete guarantees recently achieved for idealized settings to realistic block-capacity constraints, where transactions genuinely vary in size.
key_works: Gafni and Yaish (2024), *Discrete & Bayesian Transaction Fee Mechanisms*, arXiv:2210.07793.

bib.title: Discrete fees with heterogeneous transaction sizes

title: Bayesian fees under correlated and drifting demand
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can Bayesian transaction-fee mechanisms retain their guarantees when users' valuations are correlated and the demand distribution drifts over time? The goal is to extend the existing framework to correlated, drifting valuations under limited distributional samples, making explicit the dependence assumptions required.
status: The state of the art is the 2025 multinomial-logit construction of Chen et al. (2025), *Bayesian Mechanism Design for Blockchain Transaction Fee Allocation* (DOI:10.1287/opre.2024.0865), which achieves an asymptotic constant-factor revenue approximation under independent values; correlated values, distribution drift, and limited samples remain open.
solved_when: A fee mechanism is constructed that preserves Bayesian incentive-compatibility and revenue guarantees (matching, at least asymptotically, the constant-factor revenue approximation of the independent-values baseline) under correlated and drifting demand, with stated dependence assumptions and a quantified sample budget for learning the distribution.
why: Transaction demand does not arrive independently — it clusters around shared events such as network congestion or market shocks, so independent-value fee mechanisms can misprice or lose revenue exactly when usage is highest.
key_works: Chen et al. (2025), *Bayesian Mechanism Design for Blockchain Transaction Fee Allocation*, DOI:10.1287/opre.2024.0865.

bib.title: Bayesian fees under correlated and drifting demand

title: Learning off-chain-influence-proof fees
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can a transaction-fee mechanism learn users' demand online while remaining robust to producers colluding through off-chain auctions — including cases where strategic behavior deliberately poisons the observations the learning relies on? Formally, the goal is a learning rule whose regret guarantee holds even when agents can manipulate the data it learns from.
status: This is a research target that goes beyond the January 2026 burn-identity characterization of off-chain-influence-proof transaction fee mechanisms and its prior-dependence restrictions (Ganesh, Thomas and Weinberg, 2026, *Characterizing Off-Chain Influence Proof Transaction Fee Mechanisms*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.65). Strategic data poisoning in online pricing is a related line of work.
solved_when: A fee mechanism is exhibited that learns demand without assuming a perfectly known prior and provably bounds producers' gains from off-chain influence, even under strategic poisoning of the learning observations.
why: It removes the field's dependence on a perfectly known prior, making incentive-compatible fee design realistic in settings where demand must be estimated from strategic behavior.
key_works: Ganesh, Thomas and Weinberg (2026), *Characterizing Off-Chain Influence Proof Transaction Fee Mechanisms*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.65.

title: Coalition-resistant leaderless fee sharing
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can a leaderless transaction-fee mechanism be extended to a setting with multiple producers who have private capacities, unequal costs, and the ability to coordinate on inclusion or duplicate transactions — while remaining resistant to such coalitions? Formally, the question is whether multi-producer fee allocation can be made incentive compatible and collusion-proof under this richer heterogeneity.
status: Following FPA-EQ's 2025 results on producer incentives, which achieve 63.2% of optimal expected welfare at equilibrium, the private-capacity, unequal-cost, coalition-prone setting remains open. Key work: Garimidi, Heimbach and Roughgarden (2025), *Transaction Fee Mechanism Design for Leaderless Blockchain Protocols*, arXiv:2505.17885.
solved_when: A multi-producer fee-sharing mechanism is designed and proven coalition-resistant in the setting with private capacities, unequal costs, and coordinated inclusion or duplication, improving on FPA-EQ's current guarantee of 63.2% of optimal expected welfare at equilibrium.
why: It would make shared (multi-producer) transaction production viable even when committee members are heterogeneous, so that collusion and asymmetry do not undermine the mechanism.
key_works: Garimidi, Heimbach and Roughgarden (2025), *Transaction Fee Mechanism Design for Leaderless Blockchain Protocols*, arXiv:2505.17885.

title: Strategic patient bidders
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: When transaction fee markets admit bidders who are willing to wait, how do strategic users bid and choose when to submit? In particular, characterize the equilibrium bids and submission timing of patient users and relate the welfare computed from declared bids to the welfare with respect to users' true values.
status: This is posed as an explicit challenge in the 2025–2026 patient-bidder work of Babaioff and Nisan (2025; revised 2026), *On the Welfare of EIP-1559 with Patient Bidders*, arXiv:2502.20031, where it is observed that algorithmic scheduling guarantees permit strategic bid shading.
solved_when: An equilibrium analysis of patient users' bids and submission timing is given, together with a quantitative relationship (bound or exact characterization) between declared-bid welfare and true-value welfare.
why: Real wallets routinely wait across several blocks before their transactions land, so welfare guarantees that ignore this patience and the strategic bid shading it permits may not reflect actual outcomes.
key_works: Babaioff and Nisan (2025; revised 2026), *On the Welfare of EIP-1559 with Patient Bidders*, arXiv:2502.20031.

title: Repeated base-fee manipulation with endogenous coalitions
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can a coalition of block producers that trades block rights and freely forms or dissolves memberships over time profitably manipulate EIP-1559-style base fees despite each block being individually honest? A formal characterization of when such repeated manipulation is sustainable, together with mitigations that remain stable against these endogenous coalitions, is the goal.
status: Attacks demonstrated by Azouvi et al. (2023), *Base Fee Manipulation In Ethereum's EIP-1559 Transaction Fee Mechanism*, arXiv:2304.11478, are profitable below majority control; characterizing repeated manipulation with endogenous coalitions and designing stable mitigations remains an open research target beyond 2023.
solved_when: A theorem characterizes the long-run (repeated-game) feasibility and profitability of base-fee manipulation by coalitions with endogenous membership and transferable block rights, and a mechanism or mitigation is proved stable against such coalitions — i.e., manipulation is no longer profitable, or is bounded, under the characterized conditions.
why: One-block honesty does not preclude manipulation sustained across a sequence of blocks, so short-horizon incentive-compatibility analysis of fee mechanisms misses attacks that are profitable even below majority control.
key_works: Azouvi et al. (2023), *Base Fee Manipulation In Ethereum’s EIP-1559 Transaction Fee Mechanism*, arXiv:2304.11478.

bib.title: Repeated base-fee manipulation with endogenous coalitions

title: Fee-controller robustness to bursts and strategic telemetry
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: How should a transaction-fee controller behave when congestion arrives in bursts and the bid stream feeding it is generated strategically rather than honestly? Formally, characterize bounds on congestion recovery time, price overshoot, and susceptibility to manipulation under abrupt demand shifts with strategic telemetry.
status: This remains a research target beyond the 2021 posted-price stability and welfare results of Ferreira et al. (2021), *Dynamic Posted-Price Mechanisms for the Blockchain Transaction Fee Market* (arXiv:2103.14144), which hold under regularity assumptions.
solved_when: A fee-controller design is given with provable bounds on congestion recovery time, price overshoot, and manipulation resistance under abrupt demand shifts and strategically generated bids, without relying on truthful demand reports.
why: It yields congestion response that does not depend on trusting demand reports, so a mechanism can remain stable even when participants game their bids.
key_works: Ferreira et al. (2021), *Dynamic Posted-Price Mechanisms for the Blockchain Transaction Fee Market*, arXiv:2103.14144.

bib.title: Fee-controller robustness to bursts and strategic telemetry

title: Spam-resistant zero-fee inclusion
subfield: Transaction-fee incentive compatibility and collusion
open: Can a transaction-fee mechanism admit zero-fee transactions in a meaningfully fair way while an adversary floods the system with Sybils, so that subsidized users get real access without destroying service for paying users?
status: The target goes beyond existing 2024 randomized fairness constructions; current work has not yet supplied the additional guarantees needed for admission scarcity and subsidy budgets under adversarial load. Key reference: Damle, Srivastava and Gujar (2024), *No Transaction Fees? No Problem! Achieving Fairness in Transaction Fee Mechanism Design*, arXiv:2402.04634.
solved_when: A mechanism is constructed that, under sustained adversarial load, simultaneously provides meaningful zero-fee inclusion, bounds the Sybil attacker's advantage over honest subsidized users, and preserves quality of service for paying transactions.
why: It would let protocols subsidize access for users who cannot pay fees without that subsidy becoming a vector for denial-of-service against everyone else.
key_works: Damle, Srivastava and Gujar (2024), *No Transaction Fees? No Problem! Achieving Fairness in Transaction Fee Mechanism Design*, arXiv:2402.04634.

title: Strategic resource-price learning
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: What happens to resource-price learning when the users it prices are strategic — can we bound both welfare regret and manipulation gains when forward-looking users adapt their demand, timing, and resource declarations in response to the mechanism?
status: Regret results as of 2024–2025 cover specified action sequences, but the strategic-manipulation setting remains an open research target. Related angles include performative prediction and strategic online convex optimization; see Angeris, Diamandis and Moallemi (2024), *Multidimensional Blockchain Fees are (Essentially) Optimal*, arXiv:2402.08661.
solved_when: A mechanism or algorithm is given with provable bounds on welfare regret and on the gains users can achieve through strategic manipulation of demand, timing, and resource declarations, going beyond regret guarantees that hold only for specified (non-strategic) action sequences.
why: Existing online optimization guarantees assume users behave as given; without robustness to strategic behavior, price-learning results do not carry over to actual economic implementation in blockchain fee markets.
key_works: Angeris, Diamandis and Moallemi (2024), *Multidimensional Blockchain Fees are (Essentially) Optimal*, arXiv:2402.08661.

title: Pricing persistent-state externalities
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: How should a transaction be priced when its effects outlive it — that is, can we design a fee schedule that charges transactions for the future state burdens they create? The target is a pricing rule that remains profitable to the protocol even against adversaries who split transactions, or delete and recreate state to dodge charges, while still keeping ordinary access to state affordable.
status: This is a research target extending 2024–2025 multidimensional pricing work, notably Angeris, Diamandis and Moallemi (2024), *Multidimensional Blockchain Fees are (Essentially) Optimal*, arXiv:2402.08661, to the setting of intergenerational costs.
solved_when: A formal fee mechanism exists that (i) charges for persistent-state externalities imposed by present transactions, (ii) leaves no profitable strategy involving splitting, deletion, and recreation cycles, and (iii) preserves usable (non-prohibitive) access to stored state — with proofs of each property.
why: Present transactions impose lasting infrastructure obligations on the system; without such pricing, these intergenerational costs go uncharged and accumulate as an unfunded burden.
key_works: Angeris, Diamandis and Moallemi (2024), *Multidimensional Blockchain Fees are (Essentially) Optimal*, arXiv:2402.08661.

title: Incentives for accurate dependency declarations
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: Can blockchain protocols elicit honest transaction dependency declarations — access lists and execution dependencies — when the declarant profits from misreporting? Formally: is there a fee/scheduling mechanism under which truthful declaration of access sets, including state-dependent ones, is a (dominant) equilibrium?
status: This is a research target arising after 2025 parallel-gas proposals, which assume access sets are known or conservatively estimated (Acilan et al. (2025), *Transaction Fee Market Design for Parallel Execution*, arXiv:2502.11964). Related literature exists on strategyproof scheduling with private resource requirements.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified in which reporting the true access list and execution dependencies (including state-dependent accesses) is strategyproof, or at least an equilibrium, so that overstatement, understatement, and concealment are all unprofitable; ideally with parallelism guarantees under strategic declarations.
why: Strategic declarations can destroy the parallelism these mechanisms are meant to enable, since transactions hide or inflate dependencies to game fees or scheduling priority.
key_works: Acilan et al. (2025), *Transaction Fee Market Design for Parallel Execution*, arXiv:2502.11964.

title: Choosing the execution-risk allocation
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: How should execution risk be optimally shared between users and schedulers when users are risk-averse, capital is limited, and failures are correlated? Concretely, characterize the welfare-optimal allocation of execution-risk along the user–scheduler risk frontier.
status: The problem became a research target after Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (2026), *Perils of Parallelism: Transaction Fee Mechanisms under Execution Uncertainty* (arXiv:2604.04193), established the user–scheduler risk frontier and mechanisms attaining its boundary. Related work concerns optimal risk sharing in reservation contracts.
solved_when: A mechanism (or characterization) is given that achieves welfare-optimal risk sharing between users and schedulers under risk aversion, limited capital, and correlated execution failures, matching or attaining the boundary of the risk frontier.
why: It converts a known tradeoff into usable design parameters, telling mechanism designers exactly how much execution risk each side should bear.
key_works: Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (2026), *Perils of Parallelism: Transaction Fee Mechanisms under Execution Uncertainty*, arXiv:2604.04193.

title: High-priority shill resistance under contingency
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: How much can a transaction scheduler pad its schedule when users draw priority fees from heavy-tailed distributions, and what are the tight tradeoffs among risk allocation, fee burning, and responsiveness in resisting shill attacks under such contingencies? Formally, the goal is to bound scheduler padding incentives when priority fees are heavy-tailed and to characterize the achievable frontier between shill resistance and execution responsiveness.
status: This is an open research target beyond the parameterized OW-TFM shill-resistance conditions of Perils' 2026 analysis (Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (2026), *Perils of Parallelism*, arXiv:2604.04193); no tight tradeoffs are known.
solved_when: Tight tradeoffs among risk allocation, burning, and responsiveness are derived under heavy-tailed priority fees, yielding bounds on scheduler padding that go beyond the parameterized OW-TFM shill-resistance conditions.
why: High-value congestion magnifies padding incentives, so without such bounds shill-driven scheduling manipulation becomes most profitable exactly when the chain is most valuable to users.
key_works: Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (2026), *Perils of Parallelism*, arXiv:2604.04193.

title: Collusive and malicious parallel-fee attacks
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: Can parallel-fee mechanism design survive collusion and malice — that is, what happens when users and schedulers coordinate off-chain, or when an attacker deliberately loses money to congest the system? Formally, this asks for a fee analysis extending beyond individually rational actors to coalitional and Byzantine adversaries in parallel-execution fee markets.
status: The current state of the art is the 2026 rational-individual analysis of Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (*Perils of Parallelism*, arXiv:2604.04193), which explicitly excludes malicious denial of service and off-chain collusion; no extension covering these settings exists.
solved_when: A model of parallel fees is extended beyond Perils' 2026 rational-individual analysis to cover user–scheduler coalitions and malicious denial-of-service attackers willing to sacrifice money to waste execution capacity, with availability guarantees characterizable in that setting.
why: Availability of parallel-execution systems requires more than individual incentive compatibility; a fee mechanism that is safe against lone rational users can still be broken by colluding schedulers or by attackers who do not mind losing money to waste capacity.
key_works: Wadhwa, Yaish, Zhang and Nayak (2026), *Perils of Parallelism*, arXiv:2604.04193.

title: Hardware-portable parallel gas accounting
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: Can validators on different machines be guaranteed to pay roughly the same real computational cost for the same transaction — that is, can we bound the actual validation work performed per unit of charged gas across supported hardware, caches, storage devices, and scheduling policies?
status: This remains a research target beyond 2025, which offered only weighted-area and makespan-based abstract cost models (Acilan et al. (2025), *Transaction Fee Market Design for Parallel Execution*, arXiv:2502.11964); related work exists in architecture-independent worst-case execution-time analysis.
solved_when: A cost-accounting scheme is demonstrated under which, for every supported hardware and scheduling configuration, the actual validation work per charged gas unit stays within an explicit bound across caches, storage devices, and scheduling policies.
why: Without such a bound, nodes on cheaper or slower hardware effectively subsidize or destabilize validation, so a solution is what keeps heterogeneous validator sets affordable and sustainable.
key_works: Acilan et al. (2025), *Transaction Fee Market Design for Parallel Execution*, arXiv:2502.11964.

title: Paying for speculative validation work
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: How can a protocol make senders pay for the simulation and bundle-evaluation work their transactions trigger, even when those transactions are never included, without allowing fabricated-work claims or fee theft?
status: The research target was sharpened in 2024 by ConditionalExhaust, MemPurge and GhostTX, documented in Yaish et al. (2024), *Speculative Denial-of-Service Attacks in Ethereum* (USENIX Security 2024).
solved_when: A fee or metering mechanism exists that bounds or charges for speculative validation work on excluded transactions, is robust against inflated work claims, and cannot be used to extract fees beyond work actually performed.
why: Without it, validators bear unpriced computational load from transactions that generate no revenue, and imposing such fees naively invites fabricated-work griefing and fee theft; a solution aligns imposed computation with collectible fees.
key_works: Yaish et al. (2024), [*Speculative Denial-of-Service Attacks in Ethereum*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/yaish).

title: Fair-ordering and execution-profit frontier
subfield: Multiresource fees and uncertain execution
open: How much fairness must a transaction scheduler give up to maximize execution profit, when transactions conflict with each other and their runtimes are uncertain? More precisely, what are the tight bounds relating fairness, throughput, and scheduler revenue in scheduling problems modeled by conflict graphs with uncertain runtimes?
status: The question was posed as a research target after the October 2026 Execution Dilemma study by Pugatsov, Ileri and Decouchant (2026), *The Execution Dilemma in Pessimistic Blockchains: Profitability XOR Fair Ordering* (DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.27), which measured a tradeoff that is not known to be a universal impossibility theorem. Related work exists on fairness-constrained multiprocessor scheduling.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on the achievable tradeoff between fairness, throughput, and scheduler revenue are established for conflict-graph models with uncertain runtimes — showing the measured tradeoff is either tight or improvable.
why: It separates the fundamental cost of fair ordering from the losses caused by weak heuristics, telling designers whether observed profit–fairness tradeoffs are inherent or merely artifacts of current schedulers.
key_works: Pugatsov, Ileri and Decouchant (2026), *The Execution Dilemma in Pessimistic Blockchains: Profitability XOR Fair Ordering*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.27.

title: Many-position preference auctions
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can private-position auctions be generalized from two positions to blocks with many valuable slots, and if so, what are the tight tradeoffs between welfare and communication? A satisfactory answer should characterize these tradeoffs while remaining resistant to false-name bidding and seller shill participation.
status: As of August 2026, two-position private-position auctions are known to achieve welfare guarantees of 1/2 and 1−1/e under different communication allowances (Wang and Yaish (2026), *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786; SSRN:7217199). Generalizing beyond two positions remains an open research target.
solved_when: A mechanism for blocks with many positions is given with provable welfare guarantees and communication costs that match the known two-position benchmarks of 1/2 and 1−1/e (achieved under different communication allowances as of August 2026), together with matching lower bounds showing the tradeoff is tight, all under false-name and seller-shill resistance.
why: Real blocks expose many valuable positions, while existing guarantees cover only the two-position case; without a many-position design, auctions cannot be deployed where ordering value is actually created.
key_works: Wang and Yaish (2026), *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786; SSRN:7217199.

title: Rich position-value curves
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can we design compact, truthful (or approximately truthful) auctions when bidders' values depend irregularly on their position in an ordering and include precedence preferences over others? That is, mechanism design for position-dependent valuations that go beyond what scalar fees or simple two-position models can express.
status: This remains a research target beyond Wang–Yaish's 2026 two-position specialist/generalist model (Wang and Yaish, 2026, *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786); related work exists in multidimensional mechanism design for priority services.
solved_when: A mechanism exists that handles irregular position-dependent values and precedence preferences with truthful or approximately truthful reporting, in a compact (succinct-bidding) format; this would extend the two-position specialist/generalist setting of Wang–Yaish (2026).
why: Scalar fees cannot express many ordering dependencies, so current order-auction designs leave valuable preference structure unpriced and misallocated.
key_works: Wang and Yaish (2026), *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786.

title: Repeated order auctions with private deadlines
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: How much welfare and revenue can be lost when users in a repeated order auction decide adaptively whether to bid now or wait, with private deadlines, budgets, and ordering preferences? Formally, the goal is to bound equilibrium losses (e.g., price-of-anarchy or revenue-gap measures) in this repeated setting with private arrival and deadline information.
status: This is a research target extending the 2026 one-round order-auction model of Wang and Yaish (2026), *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786; no results for the repeated setting are known. Related literature includes budgeted online advertising and strategic arrival and departure.
solved_when: Explicit bounds on equilibrium losses are established for the repeated order-auction setting with private deadlines, budgets, and ordering preferences, extending the 2026 one-round order-auction model.
why: Such bounds capture how adaptive bots and wallets actually participate in MEV auctions; without them, one-round guarantees may not survive once users can strategically time their participation.
key_works: Wang and Yaish (2026), *Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences*, arXiv:2608.00786.

title: Optimal MEV-auction closing rules
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: How should an MEV auction set its closing rules — deadlines and permitted bid updates — so that the outcome remains fair and efficient when bidders' private information changes during the auction? Formally, find closing mechanisms that balance latency fairness, proposer revenue, and incentives for strategic withholding under evolving private ordering preferences.
