status: No mechanism currently achieves this; it remains a research target beyond the empirical game-theoretic bidding studies of 2023–2024, including Wu et al. (2024), *Strategic Bidding Wars in On-chain Auctions*, arXiv:2312.14510.
solved_when: A closing rule (deadline and bid-update policy) is specified and analyzed, with provable guarantees on latency fairness, proposer revenue, and the mitigation of strategic withholding under changing private information.
why: Privileged timing advantages let fast, well-positioned bidders systematically capture MEV, concentrating extraction power; better closing rules would cap that concentration.
key_works: Wu et al. (2024), *Strategic Bidding Wars in On-chain Auctions*, arXiv:2312.14510.

title: Contribution-based searcher rewards beyond copied-code Sybils
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can contribution-based searcher reward schemes remain fair and Sybil-resistant when searchers disguise copied strategies through semantic variation, opportunities interact rather than arrive independently, and searchers collude with builders? In formal terms, this asks for reward guarantees that survive strategy disguises, combinatorial opportunity overlap, and searcher–builder coalitions.
status: As of October 2026, Shapley-capped guarantees are known only for the restricted model of copied-code Sybils and coalitions (Sarenche and Liu (2026), *Towards Decentralized Searcher Competition in MEV Markets*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.21); semantic variants, interacting opportunities, and searcher–builder coalitions remain open, with related work in Sybil-resistant cooperative cost sharing.
solved_when: A reward mechanism is constructed (or proven impossible) that grants contribution-based rewards robust to semantic strategy variants, interacting opportunities, and searcher–builder coalitions, going beyond the October 2026 Shapley-capped guarantees that hold only for modeled copied-code Sybils.
why: Existing guarantees break because sophisticated identity manipulation need not look like literal code copying, so today's Sybil defenses can be evaded by functionally identical but semantically distinct strategies.
key_works: Sarenche and Liu (2026), *Towards Decentralized Searcher Competition in MEV Markets*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.21.

bib.title: Contribution-based searcher rewards beyond copied-code Sybils

title: Competition between order-flow auctions
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: When wallets can submit their order flow to several competing order-flow auctions at once, what exclusive-versus-multihoming arrangements, rebate structures, and efficiency outcomes arise in equilibrium? A formal characterization of the equilibrium set — including which auctions win flow and at what rebates — in a model of competing OFAs with multihoming wallets is the goal.
status: This remains a research target beyond the 2025 two-stage OFA/PBS game of Ma, Tang and Yao (2025), *Analysis of the Order Flow Auction under Proposer-Builder Separation on Blockchain* (arXiv:2502.12026), in which the two-player case is solved; competition and multihoming in two-sided platforms is a related literature.
solved_when: A model of competing order-flow auctions with multihoming wallets is formulated and its equilibria are characterized in terms of exclusivity, rebates, and efficiency, extending the 2025 two-stage OFA/PBS game beyond the solved two-player case.
why: Order-flow auctions can create new intermediaries with market power, so understanding when competition disciplines or entrenches them determines whether OFAs improve or distort outcomes for users.
key_works: Ma, Tang and Yao (2025), *Analysis of the Order Flow Auction under Proposer-Builder Separation on Blockchain*, arXiv:2502.12026.

title: Rebate allocation for interacting order flow
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: When multiple transactions jointly create or compete for the same MEV opportunity, how should the extracted value be rebated among them? A satisfying allocation rule should be counterfactually transparent — each participant can see what their rebate would have been under alternative orderings — and robust against agents splitting or misreporting transactions to game the split.
status: The 2025 equilibrium analysis of the order flow auction under proposer-builder separation by Ma, Tang and Yao (arXiv:2502.12026) covers more restricted MEV opportunity structures; allocation among interacting flows remains a research target beyond that setting.
solved_when: A rebate allocation rule is given for interacting (overlapping or competing) order flow that provably provides counterfactual transparency and resists splitting (false-name manipulation), generalizing beyond the restricted opportunity structures analyzed in existing order flow auction work.
why: It would make refunds defensible for overlapping bundles, giving participants verifiable grounds for why they received the share they did rather than an arbitrary or gameable split.
key_works: Ma, Tang and Yao (2025), *Analysis of the Order Flow Auction under Proposer-Builder Separation on Blockchain*, arXiv:2502.12026.

bib.title: Rebate allocation for interacting order flow

title: Cross-domain order-auction settlement
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can an order-flow auction spanning domains with different finality rules be settled so that no party holds a free option to abandon the auction when settlement turns against them, and can the resulting privacy loss and capital requirements be quantified as an explicit tradeoff?
status: The problem has been an open research target since the 2023 systematization of cross-domain MEV (McMenamin (2023), *SoK: Cross-Domain MEV*, arXiv:2308.04159); no mechanism is known.
solved_when: A settlement mechanism for cross-domain order-flow auctions is given that eliminates free abandonment options under heterogeneous finality, together with a quantitative characterization of its privacy and capital tradeoffs.
why: It prevents hidden settlement subsidies in cross-domain execution, where the cost of abandonment risk is silently passed to other participants.
key_works: McMenamin (2023), *SoK: Cross-Domain MEV*, arXiv:2308.04159.

title: Manipulation-resistant MEV-burn price discovery
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can an auction mechanism infer a dependable lower bound on the total extractable MEV from the bids it receives, even when bidders are vertically integrated, move value through private channels, or deliberately suppress bids to keep the price low — and can the resulting estimate be turned into a burn rule that cannot be profitably gamed?
status: A research target since the 2023 MEV-burn proposals (Drake 2023, "MEV burn—a simple design"), with subsequent evidence of builder-market concentration (Yang, Nayak and Zhang 2025, *Decentralization of Ethereum's Builder Market*, arXiv:2405.01329) sharpening the relevance of manipulation resistance; no bound-yielding rule is known.
solved_when: A formally specified burn rule exists whose collected amount provably lower-bounds true available MEV under integration, private transfers, and coordinated bid suppression, together with a proof of the bound's tightness (or an impossibility result and characterization of when reliable lower bounds can exist at all).
why: Because strategic bids need not reveal available surplus, a naive burn rule undercharges whenever builders integrate or collude, letting participants keep MEV that protocol design intends to redistribute; a robust rule makes MEV-burn a credible revenue and fairness mechanism rather than an optional toll.
key_works: Drake (2023), [*MEV burn—a simple design*](https://ethresear.ch/t/mev-burn-a-simple-design/15590); Yang, Nayak and Zhang (2025), *Decentralization of Ethereum’s Builder Market*, arXiv:2405.01329.

title: Decentralized resale of execution rights
subfield: MEV auction design and private ordering preferences
open: Can advance execution rights be resold in a decentralized way without creating persistent reserve-price advantages for incumbents? More precisely, is there a resale mechanism that preserves efficiency and credible commitments while preventing an incumbent who acquires rights from entrenching a durable monopoly through endogenous secondary-market reserve pricing?
status: A 2024 analysis (Pai and Resnick, *Centralization in Attester-Proposer Separation*, arXiv:2408.03116) showed that adding resale alone does not eliminate centralization incentives; this problem remains an open research target.
solved_when: A mechanism for advance execution-right resale is designed and shown to (i) prevent persistent incumbent reserve-price advantages, (ii) preserve efficiency, and (iii) maintain credible commitments.
why: It keeps competitive access to previously allocated execution rights, blocking the emergence of a durable monopoly over block building and ordering.
key_works: Pai and Resnick (2024), *Centralization in Attester-Proposer Separation*, arXiv:2408.03116.

title: Causal effects of exclusive order flow
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: What actually causes a builder's success in PBS auctions — is it exclusive order flow, latency advantages, algorithmic quality, or deep integration — rather than these merely correlating with each other? The question is to causally decompose these contributions using credible interventions or quasi-experimental variation.
status: Research target beyond predictive associations in 2024 auction datasets. Key works: Öz et al. (2024), *Who Wins Ethereum Block Building Auctions and Why?*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2024.22. Related: causal identification of digital-platform market power.
solved_when: A study identifies the separate causal effects of exclusivity, latency, algorithms, and integration on builder success, using credible interventions rather than predictive associations.
why: It targets the causes of builder concentration, telling us which mechanisms drive market power rather than which features merely predict it.
key_works: Öz et al. (2024), *Who Wins Ethereum Block Building Auctions and Why?*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2024.22.

bib.title: Causal effects of exclusive order flow

title: Contestable builder entry with private inventories
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: Can a block-building market be designed so that new builders can realistically compete despite incumbents' advantages in capital, private inventory, and order-flow access, while still preserving the legitimate risk-management efficiencies those resources provide?
status: Open as a research target following 2025 builder-market analysis (Yang, Nayak and Zhang (2025), *Decentralization of Ethereum’s Builder Market*, arXiv:2405.01329) documenting integration and private-information advantages of incumbent builders. Related considerations include contestability under sunk information and financing costs.
solved_when: A formal model and mechanism are given that bound the entrant disadvantage arising from capital, inventory, and order-flow access, and in which entry remains viable without eliminating the legitimate risk-management efficiencies of integrated builders.
why: Without such a bound, permissionless entry into building is formal only, with no economic substance; a solution would characterize when decentralized builder markets can actually persist.
key_works: Yang, Nayak and Zhang (2025), *Decentralization of Ethereum’s Builder Market*, arXiv:2405.01329.

bib.title: Contestable builder entry with private inventories

title: Geographically neutral block-building incentives
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: Can block-building protocol timing and reward rules be designed so that no builder's expected payoff meaningfully depends on where in the world it operates, without sacrificing the network's resilience to regional failures?
status: This is a research target identified after 2026 latency-calibrated and mean-field analysis established location-dependent incentives in Ethereum's block-building paradigms (Yang et al. (2026), *Geographical Centralization Resilience in Ethereum's Block-Building Paradigms*, arXiv:2509.21475).
solved_when: A concrete timing-and-reward mechanism is specified whose latency-calibrated, mean-field analysis bounds location-dependent payoff differences, while maintaining the geographic-centralization resilience properties established in prior analysis.
why: Strong location-dependent payoffs push builders toward a few low-latency regions, eroding the geographic diversity that protects block production from regional outages and attacks.
key_works: Yang et al. (2026), *Geographical Centralization Resilience in Ethereum’s Block-Building Paradigms*, arXiv:2509.21475.

title: Coverage rewards with heterogeneous builder costs
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: Can builder-coverage reward games be extended to settings where builders have private costs, entry is endogenous, and outages are correlated, while still deterring builders from gaining by spinning up redundant identities?
status: The current state of the art is the October 2026 equilibrium, factor-2 price-of-anarchy, and concentration results of Öz, Wu, Correia, Yang, Mazorra and Leonardos (2026), *The Price of Decentralization in Block Building*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.25; the extensions to private costs, endogenous entry, and correlated outages remain open research targets. Related models include stochastic facility-location games with entry costs.
solved_when: A model of builder-coverage games is established covering private costs, endogenous entry, and correlated outages, with equilibrium and incentive analysis (analogous to the October 2026 equilibrium, factor-2 price-of-anarchy, and concentration results) that rules out beneficial redundant identities.
why: It would show that coverage rewards genuinely incentivize peripheral builders rather than being captured or gamed, informing robust builder-infrastructure design in PBS markets.
key_works: Öz, Wu, Correia, Yang, Mazorra and Leonardos (2026), *The Price of Decentralization in Block Building*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.25.

bib.title: Coverage rewards with heterogeneous builder costs

title: Censorship–throughput trade-offs with private mempools
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: What is the true trade-off curve between censorship resistance and throughput when multiple concurrent proposers hold different views of the transaction set, can be bribed at a cost, and the attacker adapts over time? More precisely, derive tight frontiers characterizing how much throughput a censoring adversary must sacrifice, as a function of proposers' information asymmetry and bribery costs.
status: This is a research target that goes beyond the October 2026 shared-mempool equilibrium and fee-sharing results of Saraf et al. (2026), *Price of Censorship: Censorship Resistance and Throughput Under Rational Concurrent Proposers*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.26; related work exists on budgeted interdiction of redundant service networks.
solved_when: Tight (matching upper and lower bound) censorship–throughput frontiers are derived for the setting of concurrent proposers with heterogeneous transaction views, bribery costs, and adaptive attackers.
why: When proposers see different transactions, redundancy no longer protects uniformly against censorship, so existing intuitions about replicating across proposers break down; tight frontiers would tell protocol designers exactly how much throughput must be paid for a given level of censorship resistance.
key_works: Saraf et al. (2026), *Price of Censorship: Censorship Resistance and Throughput Under Rational Concurrent Proposers*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.26.

title: False-name-resistant inclusion-list auctions
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: Can an inclusion-list auction mechanism be designed that resists manipulation through false identities — coordinated Sybils, duplicated submissions, and omission-contingent bribes — while still charging participants the resource costs their actions impose?
status: The current state of the art is AUCIL (Wadhwa et al. (2025), *AUCIL: An Inclusion List Design for Rational Parties*, IACR ePrint:2025/194), a 2025 correlated-equilibrium construction for rational parties. False-name resistance remains a research target beyond this result. Related directions include Sybil-resistant public-good procurement.
solved_when: A mechanism for inclusion-list auctions exists that provably cannot be profitably manipulated by coordinated identities, duplication, or bribes contingent on omitting listed transactions, and that charges resource costs; this improves on the correlated-equilibrium construction for rational parties given by AUCIL.
why: Inclusion lists are meant to protect users from builder censorship, but if the machinery itself can be captured by false identities and bribes, it becomes another surface for the very exclusion it was built to prevent.
key_works: Wadhwa et al. (2025), *AUCIL: An Inclusion List Design for Rational Parties*, IACR ePrint:2025/194.

title: Free-option-resistant PBS under strategic failures
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: How can a proposer–builder separation design be made resistant to the "free option" when builders or proposers hold outside positions that reward strategic failure? Concretely, how should payload-withholding opportunities be limited and collateral, payment, and fallback rules priced in such a setting?
status: This is a research target extending EIP-7732 (enshrined proposer–builder separation), which remained in Review status on the snapshot date. Related work includes D’Amato et al. (2024; evolving) and the problem connects to fair exchange with external contingent positions.
solved_when: A mechanism (extending the EIP-7732 framework) is specified in which payload withholding by builders or proposers with external contingent positions is unprofitable or optimally deterred, with the corresponding collateral, payment, and fallback rules derived and analyzed.
why: Trustless payment alone does not price every incentive to abandon or withhold, so strategic failures can extract value from the protocol; a solution would let PBS markets function safely even when participants hold outside exposure.
key_works: D’Amato et al. (2024; evolving), [*EIP-7732: Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation*](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7732).

title: Permissionless confidential block construction
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: Can a block-construction protocol admit any participant without permission while keeping transaction content confidential, with an ordering that remains auditable and recovery possible even if some execution environments are compromised?
status: BuilderNet, introduced in 2024 by Flashbots and collaborators, marked the first step toward distributed block construction; fully permissionless, confidential, compromise-resilient construction remains an engineering target beyond it and subsequent implementations. See Flashbots and collaborators (2024), [*Introducing BuilderNet*](https://buildernet.org/blog/introducing-buildernet).
solved_when: A deployed confidential distributed block-construction system is demonstrated that achieves open admission, auditable transaction ordering, and recovery from compromised execution environments — going beyond BuilderNet's 2024 introduction and subsequent implementations.
why: It would combine private order flow with competitive block construction, so users gain confidentiality without surrendering inclusion to a closed or trusted builder set.
key_works: Flashbots and collaborators (2024), [*Introducing BuilderNet*](https://buildernet.org/blog/introducing-buildernet).

title: Endogenous timing-game participation
subfield: PBS market structure, inclusion and builder infrastructure
open: How do timing games evolve when the players are not fixed — validators learn from experience, choose which relays to connect to, and invest in infrastructure in response to what their competitors do? The question is to characterize the stable timing policies, if any, that emerge in this endogenous setting.
status: The state of the art as of 2023 consists of timing-game models and early measurements of their adoption, as in Schwarz-Schilling et al. (2023), *Time Is Money: Strategic Timing Games in Proof-Of-Stake Protocols*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.30; treating participation, relay choice, learning, and infrastructure investment as endogenous remains an open research target. Related lines include evolutionary congestion games and endogenous speed investment.
solved_when: A characterization of stable (equilibrium or evolutionary) timing policies exists for a model in which validator participation, relay choice, learning, and infrastructure investment all respond endogenously to competitors' behavior — going beyond the fixed-player timing-game models current as of 2023 and beyond early adoption measurements.
why: If strategic delay becomes widespread because of these feedback loops, it directly reshapes validator rewards and the safety margins of the protocol.
key_works: Schwarz-Schilling et al. (2023), *Time Is Money: Strategic Timing Games in Proof-Of-Stake Protocols*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.30.

title: Economic guarantees from order fairness
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can the abstract order-fairness axioms proposed for Byzantine consensus be given a quantitative economic meaning — that is, can we derive explicit bounds on the value an adversary can extract, or the loss users suffer, directly from the fairness properties of the transaction ordering, while accounting for network skew and transaction dependencies?
status: Order fairness has been a research target since the 2020 order-fairness formulations of Kelkar et al. (2020), *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus* (IACR ePrint:2020/269); related work draws on quantitative information-flow security and adversarial market microstructure, but no such economic translation exists yet.
solved_when: A formal translation exists from an order-fairness axiom set (e.g., that of Kelkar et al., 2020) to quantitative bounds on extractable value or user loss, with the analysis explicitly incorporating network skew and transaction dependencies.
why: Without an economic interpretation, ordering guarantees remain syntactic properties with no demonstrated protection for users; with it, protocols could be compared and selected on the basis of measurable extractable-value and user-loss bounds.
key_works: Kelkar et al. (2020), *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*, IACR ePrint:2020/269.

title: Bounded damage from adversarial Condorcet cycles
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: How much delay and economic loss can a set of clients inflict by deliberately manufacturing Condorcet cycles in the observed receive order of transactions? In formal terms: find a fair-ordering protocol that bounds both the ordering delay and the economic harm caused by such cycles without ever exposing an arbitrarily large batch of reorderable transactions.
status: This remains an open research target beyond the 2023 Condorcet attack of Vafnar and Khabbazian (2023), *Condorcet Attack Against Fair Transaction Ordering*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.15, and the mitigations they evaluated; no bound of the desired form is known.
solved_when: A fair-ordering protocol is given, with proven bounds on the delay and the economic damage an adversary can cause via manufactured receive-order cycles, and a proof that no unboundedly large set of transactions is simultaneously left reorderable.
why: Every fairness guarantee has exceptions, and an adversary who can trigger those exceptions at will turns a fairness mechanism into an attack surface; without such bounds, fair-ordering protocols offer attackers a controlled window for extractive reordering.
key_works: Vafadar and Khabbazian (2023), *Condorcet Attack Against Fair Transaction Ordering*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.15.

bib.title: Bounded damage from adversarial Condorcet cycles

title: Equal opportunity with strategic client identities
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can an ordering protocol keep ordering opportunities fair when clients can invest in faster network routes, rotate identities, and submit correlated copies of the same message? Formally, can equal-opportunity guarantees be extended from the message level to the user level under strategic, Sybil-like behavior?
status: This is an open research target going beyond the equal-opportunity consensus construction of Zhang et al. (2025), *Ordered Consensus with Equal Opportunity* (arXiv:2509.09868); related directions include Sybil-resistant fair queueing.
solved_when: A consensus construction (or impossibility result) exists that provides ordering-fairness guarantees robust to clients purchasing network advantages, changing identities, and submitting correlated transactions — extending the 2025 equal-opportunity setting to strategic client identities.
why: Fairness between messages need not mean fairness between users: without user-level robustness, a wealthy or Sybil-capable client can convert ordering fairness into an unfair share of opportunities.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2025), *Ordered Consensus with Equal Opportunity*, arXiv:2509.09868.

bib.title: Equal opportunity with strategic client identities

title: Encrypted ordering with same-block user rebates
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can a protocol let block producers compute MEV-based rebates and pay users within the same block, on encrypted transactions, before any plaintext is revealed — while ensuring no party can extract value they are not authorized to? In formal terms, the question is whether private market-clearing computations over an encrypted mempool can authorize rebate extraction for users without also enabling unauthorized extraction by others.
status: The October 2026 analysis of Passerat-Palmbach (2026), *SoK: Encrypted Mempools Through the MEV Lens* (DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.22), identifies this as an explicit open direction, noting that binary decrypt-after-ordering suppresses useful auctions along with harmful extraction.
solved_when: A protocol exists that computes and distributes user rebates before plaintext revelation, admits the useful auctions that binary decrypt-after-ordering suppresses, and provably prevents unauthorized MEV extraction.
why: Without it, encrypted mempools face a forced choice between suppressing legitimate auctions and exposing users to harmful extraction; a solution preserves user refunds without giving up transaction privacy.
key_works: Passerat-Palmbach (2026), *SoK: Encrypted Mempools Through the MEV Lens*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.22.

bib.title: Encrypted ordering with same-block user rebates

title: Weighted decryption committees under churn and bribery
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can a weighted batch-decryption committee tolerate ongoing membership churn and periodic key refresh while remaining resistant to adversaries who bribe members to early-reveal or withhold their decryption shares? Formally, the goal is a construction achieving weighted threshold decryption under dynamic committees with share-refresh (proactive) security and bribe-resilience beyond what stake weights alone guarantee.
status: This remains a research target beyond the 2025 guarantees of quasilinear computation and weight-independent communication (Agarwal et al. (2025), *Weighted Batched Threshold Encryption with Applications to Mempool Privacy*, IACR ePrint:2025/2115); no construction currently combines those guarantees with committee churn, key refresh, and early-reveal/withholding bribe resistance.
solved_when: A construction (with proof) exists that combines weighted batched threshold decryption with membership changes, key refresh, and resistance to early-reveal and withholding bribes — matching or exceeding the 2025 state of the art, namely quasilinear computation and weight-independent communication.
why: Stake weights are a poor proxy for trust, because concentrated correlated ownership can hide behind many small-looking weights; without churn, refresh, and bribe-resistance, a weighted committee can be quietly captured and its mempool privacy broken.
key_works: Agarwal et al. (2025), *Weighted Batched Threshold Encryption with Applications to Mempool Privacy*, IACR ePrint:2025/2115.

bib.title: Weighted decryption committees under churn and bribery

title: Encrypted-mempool admission without blind spam
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can an encrypted mempool admit transactions only after verifying they are valid, solvent, and not deliberately costly to process — without decrypting, and thus without exposing content that attackers could exploit? Formally, this asks for an admission mechanism that combines validity and solvency checks with a pricing of computational expense, all under confidentiality.
status: This remains a research target beyond 2024 confidential batch-selection guarantees; related efforts include Choudhuri et al. (2024), *Mempool Privacy via Batched Threshold Encryption: Attacks and Defenses*, and zero-knowledge admission control for encrypted computation.
solved_when: A deployed or concretely specified admission mechanism exists that rejects or suitably prices invalid, insolvent, and deliberately expensive encrypted transactions while revealing no exploitable information about transaction content before inclusion.
why: Without such a mechanism, private admission is open to cheap resource exhaustion: anyone can flood the encrypted mempool with transactions that are invalid or ruinous to process, since validators cannot inspect them. Solving it makes encrypted mempools robust against spam at negligible attacker cost.
key_works: Choudhuri et al. (2024), [*Mempool Privacy via Batched Threshold Encryption: Attacks and Defenses*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/choudhuri).

title: Adaptive privacy across failed encrypted batches
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: How much transaction information leaks when encrypted-batch decryption fails and the system retries, possibly with a new committee or with reused ciphertexts that are later compromised? A composable, adaptive notion of privacy covering this stateful, multi-attempt execution would sharpen the question.
status: The state of the art is the 2025 epochless approach to batched threshold encryption for MEV prevention (Bormet et al., 2025, BEAT-MEV); bounding leakage in the stateful, adaptively composed setting of failed batches remains open.
solved_when: A formal security definition and proof bound the leakage of pending transactions across retries, committee changes, selective decryption failures, ciphertext reuse, and later compromise of ciphertexts — a target beyond what epochless batched threshold encryption (Bormet et al., 2025) currently provides.
why: Transactions may remain pending through several failures, so privacy guarantees proven only for a single epoch do not cover the operational reality of retries and committee churn.
key_works: Bormet et al. (2025), [*BEAT-MEV: Epochless Approach to Batched Threshold Encryption for MEV Prevention*](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/bormet).

bib.title: Adaptive privacy across failed encrypted batches

title: Tenfold end-to-end encrypted-mempool acceleration
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: Can the end-to-end performance of an encrypted mempool — counting setup, communication, admission, and retries — be improved tenfold over a frozen modern baseline, without weakening privacy or the corruption assumptions?
status: Currently a moonshot beyond existing 2025–2026 primitives; no construction is known that achieves the target once setup, communication, admission, and retries are all accounted for. Related key work includes Boneh, Laufer and Tas (2025), *Threshold Batch Identity-based Encryption without Epochs*, IACR ePrint:2025/1254.
solved_when: A full-path construction achieves at least a 10x improvement in throughput or latency relative to the frozen baseline, with all setup, communication, admission, and retry costs counted, while retaining the baseline's privacy guarantees and corruption assumptions.
why: It would make transaction privacy compatible with short block slots and affordable hardware, rather than forcing operators to choose between privacy and practical performance.
key_works: Boneh, Laufer and Tas (2025), *Threshold Batch Identity-based Encryption without Epochs*, IACR ePrint:2025/1254.

title: Network anonymity without timing centralization
subfield: Fair ordering, encrypted mempools and transaction privacy
open: How much extra latency must a network-anonymized mempool pay for privacy, and how large is the economic edge a user gains by sidestepping anonymity during periods of congestion and volatility? Formally, this asks for bounds on anonymity's latency costs and on the economic advantage of bypassing it under strategic traffic selection.
status: An open research target following the February 2026 network-anonymized mempool proposal; no bounds yet established. Key works: Flashbots (2026), [*Network Anonymized Mempools*](https://writings.flashbots.net/network-anonymized-mempools). Related threads include low-latency anonymity under strategic traffic selection and private relay deadlines.
solved_when: Quantitative bounds are established for both the latency overhead of network anonymity and the bypass advantage during congestion and volatility, showing whether remaining in the shared privacy system is incentive-compatible.
why: Without such bounds, users have no reason to stay in shared privacy systems, and anonymity infrastructure risks unraveling exactly when congestion makes bypassing most profitable.
key_works: Flashbots (2026), [*Network Anonymized Mempools*](https://writings.flashbots.net/network-anonymized-mempools).

title: Auditable full-cost searcher profitability
subfield: MEV measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: How profitable are MEV searchers once every real cost — exchange trades, financing, infrastructure, failed bids, and private transfers — is counted? The goal is an auditable estimate of full-cost searcher profitability, using rigorous bounds wherever the underlying observations are incomplete.
status: No full accounting yet exists; the 2025 CEX–DEX study by Wu et al. (2025), *Measuring CEX-DEX Extracted Value and Searcher Profitability: The Darkest of the MEV Dark Forest* (arXiv:2507.13023), provides extensive but partially inferred accounting, making a complete, auditable estimate an open research target beyond that work.
solved_when: A profitability estimate exists that incorporates exchange trades, financing, infrastructure, failed bids, and private transfers, with explicit bounds quantifying uncertainty from incomplete observations, and is auditable in methodology.
why: It distinguishes genuine searcher efficiency from profitability inflated by omitted costs and hidden subsidies, which matters for anyone using MEV profitability figures to assess market efficiency.
key_works: Wu et al. (2025), *Measuring CEX-DEX Extracted Value and Searcher Profitability: The Darkest of the MEV Dark Forest*, arXiv:2507.13023.

title: Cross-chain benchmark for speculative MEV load
subfield: MEV measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Do optimistic rollups such as Arbitrum, Base and Optimism, when running matched workloads, actually convert speculative MEV-driven demand into useful execution, or does it displace ordinary users? A rigorous cross-chain benchmark would compare useful execution against speculative probes, failures and user displacement under matched workloads and adapting strategies.
status: No such benchmark exists yet; the data target lies beyond 2025 optimistic-MEV measurements on Arbitrum, Base and Optimism (Solmaz et al. (2025), *Optimistic MEV in Ethereum Layer 2s: Why Blockspace Is Always in Demand*, arXiv:2506.14768).
solved_when: A benchmark dataset and methodology exist that measure useful execution, speculative probes, failure rates and user displacement across Arbitrum, Base and Optimism under matched workloads with adapting strategies, extending the 2025 optimistic-MEV measurements.
why: It separates genuinely productive scaling from demand that is merely subsidized search activity, which is essential for judging whether current Layer-2 blockspace growth reflects real adoption.
key_works: Solmaz et al. (2025), *Optimistic MEV in Ethereum Layer 2s: Why Blockspace Is Always in Demand*, arXiv:2506.14768.

bib.title: Cross-chain benchmark for speculative MEV load

title: Sustainable independent auction telemetry
subfield: MEV measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: How can measurement of blockchain auctions and mempools be sustained as a public good rather than left to whoever happens to collect it — with stable schemas, retained history, privacy protections, and auditable records of what is missing?
status: The current state of the art consists of public relay APIs and individual datasets, available since 2022 (Flashbots 2022–2026; [MEV-Boost Relay API Specs](https://github.com/flashbots/relay-specs)); no independently funded telemetry infrastructure with the above guarantees yet exists.
solved_when: Independent auction and mempool telemetry is durably funded and operating beyond what public relay APIs and individual datasets (available since 2022) provide, with stable schemas, retained history, privacy protections, and auditable missingness.
why: Durable telemetry underpins research on market power and censorship; without it, such studies depend on transient, privately held data.
key_works: Flashbots (2022–2026), [*MEV-Boost Relay API Specs*](https://github.com/flashbots/relay-specs).

title: Fully decentralized stablecoin participation conjecture
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can a fully decentralized stablecoin sustain long-run participation when it has distinct stakeholder classes and sufficiently flexible governance? More precisely, determine whether such participation is achievable under realistic parameter and governance restrictions, or prove an impossibility.
status: The problem has been an explicit conjecture since 2020, raised by Klages-Mundt, Harz, Gudgeon, Liu and Minca (2020), *Stablecoins 2.0: Economic Foundations and Risk-based Models*, arXiv:2006.12388; any resolution must formalize the realistic parameter and governance restrictions.
solved_when: A rigorous resolution — proof of sustainability or an impossibility/refutation — is given for fully decentralized stablecoins with distinct stakeholder classes and sufficiently flexible governance, with realistic parameter and governance restrictions formalized.
why: It identifies exactly where external enforcement or restricted governance becomes necessary, delimiting what decentralized designs can achieve on their own.
key_works: Klages-Mundt, Harz, Gudgeon, Liu and Minca (2020), *Stablecoins 2.0: Economic Foundations and Risk-based Models*, arXiv:2006.12388.

title: Distributionally robust stablecoin collateral
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: How much collateral must a stablecoin hold so that its probability of depegging stays below a specified level, when the distributions of tails and jumps are uncertain and liquidation slippage is endogenous to the protocol's own actions? Formally: characterize the minimum collateral ratio guaranteeing a depeg bound over an explicit distributional uncertainty set, extending the 2022 stochastic stability framework.
status: No solution yet; this is a research target extending the 2022 stochastic stability bounds of Klages-Mundt and Minca (2022), *While stability lasts*, DOI:10.1111/mafi.12357, to explicit distributional uncertainty sets. Related tools include distributionally robust optimization, rare-event estimation, and ruin theory.
solved_when: A theorem (and ideally a computable rule) gives the minimum collateral level ensuring depeg probability at most the specified bound, robust over the stated uncertainty sets for tails, jumps magnitudes, and endogenous liquidation slippage.
why: It would let collateral requirements be set by risk level rather than by convention, making different stablecoin designs directly comparable at equal risk — the difference between efficient backing and either runs or idle capital.
key_works: Klages-Mundt and Minca (2022), *While stability lasts*, DOI:10.1111/mafi.12357.

title: Adaptive stabilization without time inconsistency
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can a stablecoin protocol adapt its stabilization parameters — the rules governing issuance and redemption — over time in response to changing conditions, without this flexibility becoming an invitation to opportunistic revisions that destroy the credibility of its commitments? Formally, is there an adaptive mechanism whose adjustments are time-consistent, so that the protocol has no incentive to deviate from its promised backing and redemption behavior at any point along the path?
status: This is a research target beyond the 2022–2026 results on commitment failure and decentralized issuance, including d’Avernas, Maurin and Vandeweyer (2026), *Can Stablecoins Be Stable?*, DOI:10.1287/mnsc.2024.06992.
solved_when: A mechanism is exhibited (or proven impossible) that permits useful parameter adaptation while preserving credible issuance and redemption commitments against opportunistic revisions, with a proof that revisions are either infeasible or non-beneficial ex post.
why: Without this, every adjustment to a stablecoin's rules risks triggering a run or a collapse in confidence, so protocols face a stark trade-off between rigidity and credibility; a solution lets stabilization mechanisms evolve with market conditions without undermining the promises that make them stable.
key_works: d’Avernas, Maurin and Vandeweyer (2026), *Can Stablecoins Be Stable?*, DOI:10.1287/mnsc.2024.06992.

title: Collusion-resistant open redemption
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: How should a stablecoin's redemption mechanism be designed so that coalitions cannot manipulate secondary-market prices or deliberately withhold arbitrage during periods of stress? More formally, the goal is a redemption-access and terms structure for which no coalition of redeemers has a profitable manipulation strategy that destabilizes the peg or worsens run risk.
status: This remains a research target beyond the established 2023–2026 arbitrage-concentration stability/run-risk tradeoff; the closest work is Ma, Zeng and Zhang (2026), *Stablecoin Runs and the Centralization of Arbitrage*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhag072. Related literatures include ETF authorized-participant concentration and bank-run coordination games.
solved_when: A redemption mechanism is specified — who may redeem directly and on what terms — together with a proof that it is coalition-resistant, in that no coalition can profit by manipulating secondary prices or withholding arbitrage during stress, within the established 2023–2026 arbitrage-concentration stability/run-risk tradeoff framework.
why: A solution directly determines who should redeem directly and on what terms, closing a governance gap that currently leaves stablecoins exposed to concentrated-arbitrageur manipulation during runs.
key_works: Ma, Zeng and Zhang (2026), *Stablecoin Runs and the Centralization of Arbitrage*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhag072.

title: Reserve liquidity with endogenous redemption capacity
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: How should a stablecoin issuer jointly choose its reserves, capital, and redemption capacity when its own asset sales move prices and the payment intermediaries it relies on become constrained? Formally, this asks for a characterization of the jointly optimal policy in a dynamic issuer model where both fire-sale price impact and intermediary capacity are endogenous.
status: This is an open research target extending Li and Mayer's dynamic issuer model (*Financial Intermediation with Fragile Seigniorage: A Dynamic Model of Stablecoin Issuers*, SSRN:3757083, 2020, revised), in which the extension was initiated; related directions include liquidity-adjusted asset allocation and endogenous fire sales.
solved_when: A dynamic model is provided in which reserve composition, capital, and redemption capacity are jointly optimized under price-moving sales and constrained intermediaries, with a characterization of the optimal policy.
why: It would tie the issuer's reserve composition to its actual capacity to meet withdrawals, rather than treating redemption capacity as given.
key_works: Li and Mayer (2020; revised), *Financial Intermediation with Fragile Seigniorage: A Dynamic Model of Stablecoin Issuers*, SSRN:3757083.

bib.title: Reserve liquidity with endogenous redemption capacity

title: Disclosure schedules under strategic signaling
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: How should a stablecoin issuer schedule and calibrate its reserve disclosures when it privately chooses asset quality and holders read every announcement strategically? Formally, what disclosure policy over timing and precision minimizes run risk given the signaling equilibrium it induces?
status: Open research target. A 2024 analysis (Ahmed, Aldasoro and Duley, *Public information and stablecoin runs*, BIS Working Paper 1164) showed that transparency can either raise or lower run risk; related literatures include Bayesian persuasion and bank stress-test disclosure.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the optimal reserve-disclosure schedule — its timing and precision — in a model where the issuer chooses quality and holders condition run decisions on announcements, including conditions under which more transparency raises versus lowers run risk.
why: It turns transparency from a slogan into a testable design variable, telling issuers and regulators when revelation stabilizes and when it invites runs.
key_works: Ahmed, Aldasoro and Duley (2024), *Public information and stablecoin runs*, BIS Working Paper 1164.

title: Stablecoin-bank contagion with settlement calendars
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Do contagion models that combine continuous trading, bank closures, shared custodians, and redemption queues accurately reproduce the dynamics of stablecoin–bank stress? In particular, can such models distinguish losses caused purely by settlement-timing frictions from those caused by actual insolvency?
status: The research target was sharpened by a 2026 Federal Reserve analysis of intermediation and integration risks: Carapella, Lubis and Vardoulakis (2026), *Stablecoins in 2025: Developments and Financial Stability Implications*, DOI:10.17016/2380-7172.4020. Related literatures include payment gridlock and queueing networks with server vacations.
solved_when: A validated contagion model is demonstrated that jointly incorporates continuous trading, bank closure windows, shared custodians, and redemption queues, and can empirically separate operational delay effects from insolvency-driven losses.
why: It separates operational delay from insolvency, telling us which stablecoin–bank stress episodes reflect fixable settlement frictions rather than balance-sheet failure.
key_works: Carapella, Lubis and Vardoulakis (2026), *Stablecoins in 2025: Developments and Financial Stability Implications*, DOI:10.17016/2380-7172.4020.

title: Diversified baskets under correlated depegs
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can a composite stablecoin backed by a diversified basket of pegged assets preserve its diversification when the underlying pegs fail together, or when traders unload weak constituents into the composite? Formally, is there a basket design whose stability guarantees survive correlated depegs and adverse-selection-driven redemption flows?
status: The problem has been an explicit research direction since 2020 composite-design and adverse-selection analysis (Klages-Mundt et al. (2020), *Stablecoins 2.0*, arXiv:2006.12388); related concerns appear in structured-credit correlation breakdown and adverse selection in redeemable funds, but no construction resolving it is known.
solved_when: A basket-construction or mechanism design is given whose diversification and stability properties provably survive correlated constituent depegs and strategic redemption of weak constituents into the composite stablecoin.
why: Without it, ostensibly diversified backing concentrates into failure precisely when it is needed, so the composite stablecoin inherits the fragility of its weakest constituents.
key_works: Klages-Mundt et al. (2020), *Stablecoins 2.0*, arXiv:2006.12388.

title: Redemption throttles with vanishing market liquidity
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: When do redemption throttles actually stabilize a stablecoin issuer if dealers withdraw their capital from secondary markets and leveraged holders are forced to sell into those thinning markets? In other words, characterize the conditions under which redemption limits remain effective when the market liquidity that previously supported them vanishes.
status: This is a research target beyond the 2026 models of Gersbach, van Buggenum and Zelzner (2026), *Stablecoins as private money: a policy agenda*, DOI:10.1007/s42521-026-00208-0, in which secondary-market liquidity supports stabilizing redemption barriers; the case of vanishing dealer liquidity and forced sales by leveraged holders remains unmodeled. Related phenomena include money-market-fund gates and suspension of convertibility.
solved_when: A theoretical characterization exists of the settings in which redemption throttles do or do not stabilize the issuer when dealers withdraw capital and leveraged holders must sell — going beyond the 2026 models that rely on secondary-market liquidity to support stabilizing redemption barriers.
why: It tests whether redemption controls function during simultaneous liquidity crises, rather than only when secondary markets are deep; without it, throttles may be presumed safe precisely when they fail.
key_works: Gersbach, van Buggenum and Zelzner (2026), *Stablecoins as private money: a policy agenda*, DOI:10.1007/s42521-026-00208-0.

bib.title: Redemption throttles with vanishing market liquidity

title: Stablecoin growth and reserve-yield feedback
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: How large can a stablecoin grow when its own expansion moves the Treasury market it depends on — do issuer scale, reserve revenue, and government yields settle at a fixed point, and is it unique? Formally, characterize the equilibrium in which issuance flows affect Treasury yields and those yields feed back into issuer revenue and reserve policy.
status: A research target following Ahmed and Aldasoro (2025; revised 2026), *Stablecoins and safe asset prices*, BIS Working Paper 1270, whose 2025–2026 estimates established state-dependent yield responses to stablecoin flows.
solved_when: A model (or empirical characterization) of the fixed point between stablecoin issuance scale, Treasury yields, and issuer revenue/reserve policy is established, with existence and determinacy of the equilibrium scale resolved.
why: A stablecoin's stability rests on revenues from its reserves, so growth endogenous to yields can undermine the very backing that supports it — or, conversely, the feedback may bound growth well below what partial-equilibrium analysis suggests.
key_works: Ahmed and Aldasoro (2025; revised 2026), *Stablecoins and safe asset prices*, BIS Working Paper 1270.

title: Separating liquidity depegs from insolvency
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can we identify, in real time, what is driving a stablecoin depeg — distinguishing genuine reserve losses from redemption frictions, flow imbalance, or exchange segmentation? The goal is an experimental identification strategy, drawing on market-microstructure identification and online change-point detection, that separates these causes as a depeg unfolds.
status: Evidence through 2020–2023 on arbitrage stabilization — notably Lyons and Viswanath-Natraj (2023), *What keeps stablecoins stable?* (DOI:10.1016/j.jimonfin.2022.102777) — remains the state of the art; real-time causal attribution of depegs is an open research target beyond that literature, with structural market-microstructure identification and online change-point detection suggested as relevant approaches.
solved_when: A method exists that attributes an ongoing depeg to its cause (reserve losses vs. redemption frictions vs. flow imbalance vs. exchange segmentation) in real time, going beyond the 2020–2023 arbitrage-stabilization evidence and demonstrably distinguishing these mechanisms on real depeg episodes.
why: Different depeg causes demand different responses; misattributing an illiquidity event to insolvency (or vice versa) leads to inappropriate interventions, so causal attribution in real time enables appropriately targeted responses.
key_works: Lyons and Viswanath-Natraj (2023), *What keeps stablecoins stable?*, DOI:10.1016/j.jimonfin.2022.102777.

title: Multi-currency stablecoin market equilibrium
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can a market of stablecoins pegged to different currencies persist when arbitrageurs who keep the pegs tight are capital constrained? A formal model of competing pegging currencies should derive conditions under which non-dollar pegs survive rather than collapse to dollar dominance.
status: No such model exists; this is a research target beyond 2026 evidence covering four dollar stablecoins and 27 fiat currencies (Aldasoro, Beltran and Grinberg (2026), *Stablecoin Inflows and Spillovers to FX Markets*, DOI:10.5089/9798229042246.001).
solved_when: A theoretical model of capital-constrained arbitrage across competing pegs yields checkable conditions characterizing when persistent non-dollar stablecoin pegs are an equilibrium.
why: It tests whether stablecoin markets can sustain currency diversity, or whether structural forces push them toward dollar dominance.
key_works: Aldasoro, Beltran and Grinberg (2026), *Stablecoin Inflows and Spillovers to FX Markets*, DOI:10.5089/9798229042246.001.

title: Continuously verifiable encumbered reserves
subfield: Stablecoin backing, stabilization and runs
open: Can a stablecoin issuer prove, in a way that updates continuously rather than at discrete attestations, that its encumbered reserves genuinely cover its liabilities — including liens and other claims on those reserves — without revealing sensitive portfolio details and without being able to embellish the picture at snapshot time?
status: The current state of the art is the 2015 line of cryptographic solvency proofs, exemplified by Dagher, Bünz, Bonneau, Clark and Boneh (2015), *Provisions: Privacy-preserving proofs of solvency for Bitcoin exchanges*, IACR ePrint:2015/1008, which establish statements only about the records supplied. Continuous verification of encumbered reserves remains an open engineering research target beyond these techniques, with related threads in continuous auditing and hidden-liability verification.
solved_when: A construction exists that proves reserve ownership net of encumbrances against total liabilities, with freshness that holds between attestations (continuous verification rather than point-in-time snapshots), while preserving privacy of the underlying portfolio.
why: Existing solvency proofs only certify whatever records the issuer chooses to supply at a given moment, so assurance evaporates immediately after each attestation; continuous verifiability would make the guarantee meaningful exactly when holders depend on it.
key_works: Dagher, Bünz, Bonneau, Clark and Boneh (2015), *Provisions: Privacy-preserving proofs of solvency for Bitcoin exchanges*, IACR ePrint:2015/1008.

title: Incentive-compatible liquidation penalties
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: How should a lending protocol set its liquidation bonus and close factor when liquidators can invest strategically in monitoring and transaction costs? A formal answer would characterize the penalty schedule that remains incentive-compatible under endogenous liquidator effort and expenditure.
status: This remains a theoretical research target beyond the 2020–2021 empirical liquidation literature, e.g. Perez, Werner, Xu and Livshits (2021), *Liquidations: DeFi on a Knife-edge*, arXiv:2009.13235.
solved_when: A mechanism (bonus/close-factor schedule) is specified with a proof that it induces strategic liquidators to monitor and execute liquidations, reducing bad debt without imposing excessive losses on borrowers.
why: It determines whether protocols can avoid accumulation of bad debt while not over-penalizing borrowers — the central trade-off in automated lending.
key_works: Perez, Werner, Xu and Livshits (2021), *Liquidations: DeFi on a Knife-edge*, arXiv:2009.13235.

title: Cross-protocol cascade forecasting
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can we predict, ahead of time, liquidation and withdrawal cascades that propagate across multiple DeFi protocols and custodial venues, using reconstructed balance sheets as the starting point?
status: No method yet exists; the current state of the art is 2023–2026 Compound-specific contagion reconstruction and simulations, as in Tovanich, Marcassa, Kitzler, Makridis and Prat (2025; revised 2026), *Shock Propagation in Decentralized Lending Networks: Evidence from the Compound Protocol*, SSRN:5380164.
solved_when: A method exists that, from reconstructed cross-protocol balance sheets, forecasts liquidation and withdrawal cascades across protocols and custodial venues beyond the scope of the 2023–2026 Compound-specific contagion reconstruction and simulations.
why: It measures risks that isolated collateral ratios hide, exposing contagion channels invisible to single-protocol analysis.
key_works: Tovanich, Marcassa, Kitzler, Makridis and Prat (2025; revised 2026), *Shock Propagation in Decentralized Lending Networks: Evidence from the Compound Protocol*, SSRN:5380164.

title: Stable strategic interest-rate controllers
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can an interest-rate controller for a lending pool remain stable and welfare-preserving once borrowers and lenders strategically migrate among pools while acting on delayed observations of rates and liquidity?
status: A research target extending lending-market models and measurements developed since 2020, drawing on Gudgeon, Werner, Perez and Knottenbelt (2020), *DeFi Protocols for Loanable Funds: Interest Rates, Liquidity and Market Efficiency*, arXiv:2006.13922; related lines include strategic-agent control and cobweb dynamics.
solved_when: A formal model and proof establish rate-controller stability and welfare guarantees under strategic cross-pool migration with delayed observations.
why: It prevents liquidity oscillations that amplify stress in lending markets.
key_works: Gudgeon, Werner, Perez and Knottenbelt (2020), *DeFi Protocols for Loanable Funds: Interest Rates, Liquidity and Market Efficiency*, arXiv:2006.13922.

title: Clock-safe lending economics
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can we guarantee that a loan's interest charges remain correct and bounded when blocks arrive irregularly, timestamps are uncertain, or the protocol migrates between chains — and can implementations be verified to comply with those guarantees? Formally, the goal is a set of bounds on interest-accrual outcomes under adverse timing conditions, together with a verification method for deployed lending code.
status: The research target has been sharpened by the 2026 taxonomy of timing and interest-design vulnerabilities in DeFi lending, given in Kotzer, Azoulay, Abels, Yaish and Rottenstreich (2026), *SoK: DeFi Lending and Yield Aggregation Protocol Taxonomy, Empirical Measurements, and Security Challenges*, IACR ePrint:2026/675.
solved_when: Provable bounds on interest accrual are established under irregular block production, timestamp uncertainty, and chain migration, and a verification procedure demonstrates that a lending implementation complies with those bounds.
why: Consensus-clock irregularities should not silently alter what borrowers owe or what lenders earn; without such bounds, credit terms can drift from their intended economics without any party being at fault.
key_works: Kotzer, Azoulay, Abels, Yaish and Rottenstreich (2026), *SoK: DeFi Lending and Yield Aggregation Protocol Taxonomy, Empirical Measurements, and Security Challenges*, IACR ePrint:2026/675.

title: Zero-liquidation lending without hidden subsidies
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: When collateral values fall and borrowers are free to repay whenever it benefits them, what do solvency and welfare look like in a lending market with no liquidations? The goal is a full characterization that explicitly prices the repayment-timing option embedded in such contracts.
status: This remains a research target beyond the zero-liquidation products surveyed in the 2026 lending taxonomy of Kotzer et al. (2026), *SoK: DeFi Lending and Yield Aggregation Protocol Taxonomy, Empirical Measurements, and Security Challenges*, IACR ePrint:2026/675.
solved_when: A characterization of equilibrium solvency and welfare is obtained for zero-liquidation lending under optimally delayed repayment by borrowers, with the embedded repayment option explicitly priced and no hidden subsidy sustaining the arrangement.
why: It reveals where the risk avoided by foregoing liquidations actually goes — showing which parties silently absorb losses that liquidation mechanisms would otherwise force onto borrowers.
key_works: Kotzer et al. (2026), *SoK: DeFi Lending and Yield Aggregation Protocol Taxonomy, Empirical Measurements, and Security Challenges*, IACR ePrint:2026/675.

title: Unsecured credit under costly pseudonyms
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can unsecured lending be sustained in a decentralized setting where borrowers can discard their identity and start fresh, but doing so carries a measurable cost and the future value of a good reputation is uncertain? Formally, characterize the feasible set of unsecured credit arrangements — or prove they are empty — when identity replacement is costly and reputation payoff streams are stochastic.
status: Framed as a research target extending 2021–2022 DeFi security analysis (Werner et al. (2022), *SoK: Decentralized Finance (DeFi)*, arXiv:2101.08778) and the literature on limited-commitment concerns; related work covers strategic default, reputation whitewashing, and limited-commitment lending.
solved_when: A characterization of when unsecured credit is feasible given a positive identity-replacement cost and uncertain future reputation value is established, or an impossibility result shows no such arrangement can be sustained under those conditions.
why: It delineates the credible routes to lending beyond overcollateralization, which currently bottlenecks capital efficiency in DeFi credit markets.
key_works: Werner et al. (2022), *SoK: Decentralized Finance (DeFi)*, arXiv:2101.08778.

title: Certified approximate optimal DeFi execution
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can a DeFi executor produce a machine-checkable certificate that its plan for joint borrowing, swapping and liquidation is within a stated gap of optimal — a proof carried out entirely with integer arithmetic over a model that includes gas costs, transaction failures and state changes?
status: An open research target beyond the 2023–2024 optimization of common DeFi primitives; the key prior work is Yaish, Dotan, Qin, Zohar and Gervais (2023; revised 2024), *Suboptimality in DeFi*, IACR ePrint:2023/892. Related directions include certified nonlinear optimization and planning under execution uncertainty.
solved_when: A certificate system exists that, given a candidate execution plan over borrowing, swapping and liquidation, verifies in exact integer arithmetic an approximation gap for the plan's value relative to the modeled optimum under gas, failure and state-change effects.
why: It makes execution-optimality claims independently checkable, so users and protocols need not trust a central solver's assertion that an execution path is near-optimal.
key_works: Yaish, Dotan, Qin, Zohar and Gervais (2023; revised 2024), *Suboptimality in DeFi*, IACR ePrint:2023/892.

title: Oracle-aware adaptive borrowing limits
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: How should a lending protocol set its collateral and borrowing limits when it can observe how expensive it is to manipulate the price oracles it depends on — accounting for the fact that an attacker can recycle capital across venues and that liquidity migrates between them?
status: This remains a research target beyond 2024 safeguards such as SecPLF (Arora, Li, Feng and Xu (2024), *SecPLF: Secure Protocols for Loanable Funds against Oracle Manipulation Attacks*, arXiv:2401.08520).
solved_when: A formal model of cross-venue manipulation costs, including capital recycling and liquidity migration, is given together with an adaptive borrowing-limit rule whose safety can be proven with respect to that model.
why: Credit exposure should respect the economic security of the underlying oracle; without it, borrowing limits can exceed what manipulating prices would actually cost an attacker.
key_works: Arora, Li, Feng and Xu (2024), *SecPLF: Secure Protocols for Loanable Funds against Oracle Manipulation Attacks*, arXiv:2401.08520.

title: Liquid-staking collateral run feedback
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: Can we build a unified model of liquid staking in which staking-side degradation — falling collateral quality, receipt-token discounts, and redemption queues — interacts with lending-market liquidations while traders simultaneously short the assets involved? A formal treatment would characterize when these coupled channels amplify a validator shock into a collateral run.
status: No such unified model exists; current work extends only to low-stake attack strategies and simulated monetization, per Yang, Yaish, Gervais and Zhang (2026), *Your Loss is My Gain: Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools*, arXiv:2605.01025. The coupled liquidation–short-selling feedback remains open.
solved_when: A model exists that jointly captures staking degradation, receipt-token discounts, redemption queues, and lending liquidations under simultaneous short-selling, with conditions (analytic or simulated) for run versus stable outcomes.
why: It would connect validator-level risk directly to leveraged credit markets, showing how protocol-side staking shocks propagate into lending cascades rather than staying contained.
key_works: Yang, Yaish, Gervais and Zhang (2026), *Your Loss is My Gain: Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools*, arXiv:2605.01025.

title: Rehypothecation-aware yield aggregation
subfield: Lending, liquidation and composable credit
open: When collateral is rehypothecated through nested vaults and receipt tokens, can a system trace each unit of collateral back to its ultimate owner and correctly aggregate the contingent liabilities it backs? In particular, the goal is an accounting construction that follows ultimate collateral through arbitrary nesting without double-counting diversification across layers.
status: This is a research target extending 2021–2023 composability and contagion models; no solution is recorded in the census. Key works: Werner et al. (2022), *SoK: Decentralized Finance*, arXiv:2101.08778; Tovanich et al. (2023), *Contagion in Decentralized Lending Protocols: A Case Study of Compound*, DOI:10.1145/3605768.3623544.
solved_when: An engineering construction exists that tracks ultimate collateral and contingent liabilities through nested vaults and receipt tokens and provably avoids double-counting diversification.
why: It makes common exposures visible, so that risk concentrated through chains of rehypothecation can be measured rather than hidden inside layered receipts.
key_works: Werner et al. (2022), *SoK: Decentralized Finance*, arXiv:2101.08778; Tovanich et al. (2023), *Contagion in Decentralized Lending Protocols: A Case Study of Compound*, DOI:10.1145/3605768.3623544.

title: Robust learning of dynamic AMM fees
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Can an automated market maker learn its fee schedule online with meaningful regret guarantees when volatility, demand, and arbitrageur behavior are unknown, nonstationary, and themselves influenced by the fees it sets?
status: Currently an open research target; the state of the art consists of optimal controls derived for specified stochastic models, notably Baggiani, Herdegen and Sánchez-Betancourt (2025; revised 2026), *Optimal Dynamic Fees in Automated Market Makers*, arXiv:2506.02869, with no regret-based learning guarantee known under unknown, nonstationary, strategic conditions.
solved_when: A learning rule for dynamic AMM fees is given whose regret against a suitable benchmark is bounded despite nonstationary, strategically responsive environments, with the guarantee proven rather than assumed.
why: It would make dynamic fees reliable outside the narrow setting where the stochastic model has been calibrated in advance, replacing model-specific optimal controls with provable robustness.
key_works: Baggiani, Herdegen and Sánchez-Betancourt (2025; revised 2026), *Optimal Dynamic Fees in Automated Market Makers*, arXiv:2506.02869.

bib.title: Robust learning of dynamic AMM fees

title: Equilibrium among competing fee-changing pools
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: What happens when multiple automated market makers compete for liquidity while dynamically adjusting their curves and pricing policies — can we characterize the resulting equilibrium in entry, liquidity provision, routing, and fees? Formally, this asks for a game-theoretic equilibrium notion and its characterization in a market where CFMMs are strategic players choosing both their trading functions and fee schedules over time.
status: Open; this research target goes beyond the 2025 CFMM two-sided-market analysis of Fabi and Prat (2025), *The economics of Constant Function Market Makers*, DOI:10.1016/j.jcorpfin.2025.102737.
solved_when: A well-defined equilibrium of competing fee-changing AMMs exists and is characterized: specifying which pools enter, how liquidity is allocated across them, how order flow routes among them, and what fee/curve policies arise in equilibrium.
why: Individually appealing pools may collectively fragment liquidity; an equilibrium analysis tells us when competition consolidates or splinters liquidity and what market structure participants should expect.
key_works: Fabi and Prat (2025), *The economics of Constant Function Market Makers*, DOI:10.1016/j.jcorpfin.2025.102737.

title: Dynamic equilibrium of concentrated liquidity providers
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: What equilibrium emerges when many heterogeneous liquidity providers repeatedly choose price ranges in a concentrated-liquidity market maker, each paying gas costs and receiving fees that depend on where the others place liquidity? A satisfactory answer would characterize the dynamic equilibria of this repeated range-allocation game with endogenous fee sharing.
status: Work through 2021–2024 has developed single-provider optimization and exogenous-price models; the multi-provider dynamic game remains an open target. See Fan, Marmolejo-Cossío, Moroz, Neuder, Rao and Parkes (2023), *Strategic Liquidity Provision in Uniswap V3*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.25.
solved_when: A characterization (existence, and ideally uniqueness or structure) of equilibria in repeated range-allocation games with heterogeneous LPs, nonzero gas costs, and endogenously determined fee shares is obtained.
why: It explains the aggregate shape of liquidity in concentrated-liquidity AMMs and the distribution of returns across providers, which single-provider and exogenous-price models cannot capture.
key_works: Fan, Marmolejo-Cossío, Moroz, Neuder, Rao and Parkes (2023), *Strategic Liquidity Provision in Uniswap V3*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.25.

bib.title: Dynamic equilibrium of concentrated liquidity providers

title: Attainable hedging benchmarks for LP profitability
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: How much excess return can a liquidity provider in an automated market maker actually capture when hedges must be executed under real trading, funding, and settlement costs? The goal is to construct empirically attainable hedging benchmarks for LP profitability, going beyond frictionless measures.
status: This is an experimental research target extending the 2022–2026 loss-versus-rebalancing framework of Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022; revised 2026), *Automated Market Making and Loss-Versus-Rebalancing*, arXiv:2208.06046; no attainable-cost benchmark yet exists in it.
solved_when: A hedging benchmark is implemented and LP excess returns are measured against hedges executed at actual trading, funding, and settlement costs, yielding an empirical assessment of attainable profitability under those frictions.
why: Frictionless benchmarks can misstate attainable profitability, so measuring against implementable hedges tells us what LPs can realistically earn rather than what idealized theory predicts.
key_works: Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022; revised 2026), *Automated Market Making and Loss-Versus-Rebalancing*, arXiv:2208.06046.

bib.title: Attainable hedging benchmarks for LP profitability

title: Dynamic routing with uncertain execution costs
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Can we design an AMM routing algorithm that remains near-optimal when the world does not hold still — gas costs are uncertain, pool states change while a transaction is in flight, venues charge fixed costs, and settlement is non-atomic? Formally, the question is to extend convex static routing to a dynamic setting with uncertain execution costs and per-venue fixed costs.
status: The current state of the art is the 2022 convex static routing framework of Angeris, Chitra, Evans and Boyd (2022), *Optimal Routing for Constant Function Market Makers*, arXiv:2204.05238, which handles neither fixed costs nor the dynamic, uncertain setting; this problem remains open beyond that baseline. Related tools include stochastic network flows and robust mixed-integer optimization.
solved_when: A routing method is given that provably approximates the optimal execution under uncertain gas prices, time-varying pool states, fixed venue costs, and non-atomic settlement, generalizing the convex static routing framework of Angeris, Chitra, Evans and Boyd (2022), arXiv:2204.05238.
why: It would let traders and protocols execute with explicit failure risk priced in, rather than assuming frictionless, atomic settlement — improving real-world execution quality.
key_works: Angeris, Chitra, Evans and Boyd (2022), *Optimal Routing for Constant Function Market Makers*, arXiv:2204.05238.

bib.title: Dynamic routing with uncertain execution costs

title: Replicating AMMs with jumps and trading frictions
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Which payoffs can an automated market maker approximately replicate when prices can jump, trades incur transaction costs, and collateral is limited — and how large is the resulting tracking error?
status: This remains a research target extending beyond the 2021–2023 CFMM/payoff correspondence literature, with no existing characterization of approximate replication under jumps, frictions, and collateral limits; the closest foundational work is Angeris, Evans and Chitra (2023), *Replicating market makers*, DOI:10.1007/s42521-023-00082-0.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the payoffs replicable (in the approximate sense) under jumps, transaction costs, and collateral limits, together with explicit tracking-error bounds.
why: It would allow decentralized derivatives to be reliably collateralized, so users can trust that promised payoffs are backed even under adverse market moves.
key_works: Angeris, Evans and Chitra (2023), *Replicating market makers*, DOI:10.1007/s42521-023-00082-0.

bib.title: Replicating AMMs with jumps and trading frictions

title: AMM privacy versus quote accuracy
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Can a modified automated market maker keep its users' trading activity private against an adaptive adversary who repeatedly probes for quotes, and if so, at what cost in quote accuracy and settlement delay? The goal is to derive tight tradeoffs among privacy, accuracy, and delay for such AMMs under adaptive probing, together with constructions that match the lower bounds.
status: The problem extends beyond the 2021 privacy impossibility results of Angeris, Evans and Chitra (2021), *A Note on Privacy in Constant Function Market Makers*, arXiv:2103.01193, which apply to ordinary CFMM implementations; no matching tradeoffs or constructions for modified AMMs are known.
solved_when: Quantitative tradeoff curves relating privacy, quote accuracy, and delay are proven, with matching AMM constructions achieving them.
why: A solution pinpoints exactly which market observables privacy mechanisms must alter, telling designers what information leakage is unavoidable and where accuracy or delay must be sacrificed.
key_works: Angeris, Evans and Chitra (2021), *A Note on Privacy in Constant Function Market Makers*, arXiv:2103.01193.

title: Economic composition guarantees for AMM hooks
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: When arbitrary hooks can be attached to an automated market maker, can we statically guarantee that any composition of those hooks still respects withdrawal rights, keeps fees within declared bounds, and matches its declared risk profile? The goal is such a guarantee for a restricted hook language, holding across all supported compositions and token behaviors.
status: An open research target following Uniswap v4's 2024 architecture (Adams et al. (2024), [*Uniswap v4 Core*](https://app.uniswap.org/whitepaper-v4.pdf)); related techniques include effect systems, compositional verification, and financial-contract semantics.
solved_when: A restricted hook language is specified together with a verification method that proves withdrawal rights, bounded fees, and declared risk for every supported composition and token behavior.
