why: It would make customizable market economics auditable — pool deployers and users could reason about hook-augmented AMMs before capital is committed, rather than trusting unaudited hook code.
key_works: Adams et al. (2024), [*Uniswap v4 Core*](https://app.uniswap.org/whitepaper-v4.pdf).

bib.title: Economic composition guarantees for AMM hooks

title: Tenfold risk-adjusted liquidity efficiency
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Can an automated market maker sustain ten times the executable depth per unit of loss-absorbing capital, at a fixed tail-risk tolerance, once hedging and rebalancing costs are fully accounted for?
status: This is a proposed moonshot going beyond concentrated-liquidity optimization (e.g., Fan et al. (2023), *Strategic Liquidity Provision in Uniswap V3*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.25); nominal depth alone does not meet the target.
solved_when: A mechanism is exhibited whose executable depth per unit of loss-absorbing capital is at least 10× that of the baseline, with tail risk held fixed and all hedging and rebalancing costs included in the accounting.
why: It would sharply reduce the capital cost of providing resilient exchange liquidity, the main economic bottleneck of on-chain market making.
key_works: Fan et al. (2023), *Strategic Liquidity Provision in Uniswap V3*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.25.

title: Out-of-sample LP tail-risk benchmarks
subfield: Automated market makers and liquidity economics
open: Do liquid-provider (LP) strategies actually make money once every real-world friction is counted? The goal is a prospective benchmark of LP strategies with complete costs, hedges, failed assets, and inactive positions across market regimes.
status: This is a data target beyond existing LVR modeling and its 2025 option-based extensions, including Singh et al. (2025), *Modeling Loss-Versus-Rebalancing in Automated Market Makers via Continuous-Installment Options*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2025.6.
solved_when: A benchmark dataset and evaluation exist covering LP strategies prospectively, accounting for complete costs, hedges, failed assets, and inactive positions, and spanning multiple market regimes.
why: Removes survivorship and accounting advantages that make LP strategies look more profitable than they are, so tail-risk comparisons become meaningful.
key_works: Singh et al. (2025), *Modeling Loss-Versus-Rebalancing in Automated Market Makers via Continuous-Installment Options*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2025.6.

title: ASIC valuation with endogenous computing capacity
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: How should ASIC hardware be priced and mining investment scheduled when chip manufacturers act strategically in how much capacity they supply, so that hardware prices, miner investment, and network difficulty are determined together in equilibrium?
status: The target combines Yaish–Zohar's option-based ASIC pricing (Yaish and Zohar, 2023, *Correct Cryptocurrency ASIC Pricing: Are Miners Overpaying?*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.2) with equilibrium models of the mining market such as Prat and Walter (2021), *An Equilibrium Model of the Market for Bitcoin Mining*, DOI:10.1086/714445; no such joint model with strategic manufacturers yet exists.
solved_when: A model exists that jointly endogenizes hardware prices, mining investment decisions, and difficulty, with manufacturers strategically choosing supply, and yields equilibrium characterizations (ideally closed-form or computable) connecting these quantities.
why: It connects equipment finance to security investment, showing how manufacturers' supply choices feed back into the cost of securing the network.
key_works: Yaish and Zohar (2023), *Correct Cryptocurrency ASIC Pricing: Are Miners Overpaying?*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.2; Prat and Walter (2021), *An Equilibrium Model of the Market for Bitcoin Mining*, DOI:10.1086/714445.

bib.title: ASIC valuation with endogenous computing capacity

title: Incomplete-market ASIC hedging
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: How should an ASIC be valued and hedged when the risks that drive its cash flows — electricity prices, network difficulty, downtime, and eventual resale — cannot all be traded away? The goal is to compute valuation intervals and hedging strategies in an incomplete-market setting where these risks are only imperfectly tradable.
status: The current state of the art is the 2023 no-arbitrage pricing result of Yaish and Zohar (2023), *Correct Cryptocurrency ASIC Pricing: Are Miners Overpaying?* (DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.2), which holds within its specified replication model; the incomplete-market extension remains an open research target.
solved_when: A method exists for computing valuation intervals (bounds) and explicit hedges for ASICs under imperfectly tradable electricity, difficulty, downtime, and resale risk, going beyond the 2023 no-arbitrage pricing result within its specified replication model.
why: It prices the risks miners actually retain, which complete-replication models assume away, exposing how much of an ASIC's value is unhedgeable in practice.
key_works: Yaish and Zohar (2023), *Correct Cryptocurrency ASIC Pricing: Are Miners Overpaying?*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.2.

title: Strategic ASIC supply and technology withholding
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: Can a game-theoretic model of the ASIC supply chain capture a manufacturer that holds private technology, makes delivery commitments, and has the option to mine on its own hardware — and if so, when does that manufacturer find it profitable to strategically restrict supply?
status: This is an open research target extending mining-investment models from 2017–2021, with Prat and Walter (2021), *An Equilibrium Model of the Market for Bitcoin Mining* (DOI:10.1086/714445), as the key prior work; related literatures include semiconductor capacity competition and vertical foreclosure.
solved_when: A model is built that characterizes the manufacturer's private technology, delivery commitments, and own-mining options, and yields testable evidence (or a refutation) of strategic supply restriction, extending the 2017–2021 mining-investment literature.
why: The security of proof-of-work blockchains rests on an upstream hardware market whose structure is largely unmodeled; understanding when manufacturers can profitably withhold technology or capacity clarifies how concentrated that market threatens the system.
key_works: Prat and Walter (2021), *An Equilibrium Model of the Market for Bitcoin Mining*, DOI:10.1086/714445.

bib.title: Strategic ASIC supply and technology withholding

title: Idle ASIC inventories and credible attack costs
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: How much idle ASIC mining capacity exists in the world, how quickly could it be activated, and at what cost could an attacker acquire it — and how should uncertainty in these quantities be folded into credible bounds on attack costs?
status: This data target has been highlighted by economic-security work spanning 2018–2025, including Budish (2025), *Trust at Scale: The Economic Limits of Cryptocurrencies and Blockchains*, DOI:10.1093/qje/qjae033.
solved_when: A data-driven estimate is produced of idle ASIC inventories, activation delays, and attainable acquisition costs, with these uncertainties explicitly incorporated into quantitative attack-cost bounds.
why: Active hashrate does not measure all available supply, so attack-cost estimates based on it alone can materially understate the true cost of mounting an attack.
key_works: Budish (2025), *Trust at Scale: The Economic Limits of Cryptocurrencies and Blockchains*, DOI:10.1093/qje/qjae033.

bib.title: Idle ASIC inventories and credible attack costs

title: Hedged attacks with endogenous market impact
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: When an attacker takes a short position to profit from a security failure, does the attack still pay once their own entry, liquidation, and exit move the market against them and financing is constrained?
status: The problem lies beyond current work, which consists of 2026 liquid-staking simulations and historical performance-return associations, e.g. Yang, Yaish, Gervais and Zhang (2026), *Your Loss is My Gain: Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools*, arXiv:2605.01025. Related literature includes predatory trading, derivatives manipulation, and limits to arbitrage.
solved_when: A model or characterization of attack profitability is obtained that endogenizes the price impact of short-position entry, liquidation, and exit together with financing constraints on the attacker.
why: Security analysis must price the attacker's realistically attainable outside payoffs; ignoring market impact and financing constraints can overstate the profitability — and thus the threat — of hedged attacks.
key_works: Yang, Yaish, Gervais and Zhang (2026), *Your Loss is My Gain: Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools*, arXiv:2605.01025.

bib.title: Hedged attacks with endogenous market impact

title: Mining-pool competition with switching frictions
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: When miners face real frictions — costs of switching pools, proprietary firmware locking them to particular operators, and bundled credit arrangements — under what conditions can fee competition among pools still restrain concentration of hash power, and when does it fail? The goal is a full characterization of pooling equilibria in an oligopoly model with these switching frictions.
status: No solution yet; this is a research target beyond the decentralizing forces identified in Cong–He–Li's 2019–2021 baseline (Cong, He and Li 2021, *Decentralized Mining in Centralized Pools*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhaa040).
solved_when: A characterization exists of pool-competition equilibria with switching costs, proprietary firmware, and credit ties, specifying the conditions under which fee competition restrains mining-power concentration and those under which it does not.
why: It identifies the precise conditions that make pooling dangerous for blockchain decentralization, telling regulators and protocol designers when market forces alone suffice and when concentration becomes entrenched.
key_works: Cong, He and Li (2021), *Decentralized Mining in Centralized Pools*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhaa040.

title: Solvent low-variance mining payouts
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: Can a mining-pool payout scheme be designed so that miners receive predictable rewards while the pool remains solvent even when bad events — block withholding, miner outages, and reward shocks — occur in a correlated fashion rather than independently? Formally, the goal is a payout rule and reserve policy whose ruin probability stays bounded under correlated withholding, outage, and reward-shock processes.
status: This is an open research target extending the line of payout-method analyses begun with Rosenfeld (2011), *Analysis of Bitcoin Pooled Mining Reward Systems* (arXiv:1112.4980); related foundations come from insurance-solvency and correlated-claim ruin theory.
solved_when: A payout mechanism with an explicit reserve policy is specified, together with a proof (or tight analysis) of solvency — i.e., bounded ruin probability — under a model allowing correlated withholding, outages, and reward shocks, while preserving low payout variance for miners.
why: A solvent, low-variance payout design lets pools self-insure against correlated shocks, reducing the ecosystem's dependence on a few large insurers as backstops.
key_works: Rosenfeld (2011), *Analysis of Bitcoin Pooled Mining Reward Systems*, arXiv:1112.4980.

title: Miner refinancing and security feedback
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: How do miners' balance sheets — equipment-backed debt, margin calls, and refinancing constraints — transmit cryptocurrency price declines into hashrate loss and further valuation changes? A formal model is sought in which these financing frictions generate a feedback loop layered on top of established price–security equilibria.
status: Price–security equilibria over 2018–2022 are established, notably in Pagnotta (2022), *Decentralizing Money: Bitcoin Prices and Blockchain Security*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhaa149; adding miner balance sheets to these equilibria remains an open research target.
solved_when: A tractable model of miner equipment debt, margin calls, and refinancing constraints exists that reproduces the transmission channel from price declines to hashrate loss to further valuation changes, consistent with the price–security equilibria established for the 2018–2022 period.
why: It would connect credit distress in mining finance to settlement-layer security, showing how collateral spirals and financial accelerators can amplify shocks that existing price–security models treat as exogenous.
key_works: Pagnotta (2022), *Decentralizing Money: Bitcoin Prices and Blockchain Security*, DOI:10.1093/rfs/hhaa149.

title: Incentive-compatible mining demand response
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: Can a mechanism be designed that induces Bitcoin miners to truthfully report how much load they can curtail as hashprice and mining efficiency fluctuate, and that either guarantees delivery of the promised curtailment or prices shortfalls explicitly?
status: The target has been sharpened by 2026 Texas evidence that hashprice moderates the electricity demand response of Bitcoin miners (Majumder 2026, *Hashprice moderates the electricity demand response of Bitcoin miners*, arXiv:2606.00587).
solved_when: A mechanism exists in which miners' reported curtailment capacity is truthfully elicited as a function of hashprice and efficiency, with delivery made credible or shortfalls priced; success is a stated design with incentive-compatibility (and delivery or shortfall-pricing guarantees) proved.
why: It converts miners' promised flexibility into a dependable grid resource, so demand-response programs can rely on miner curtailment rather than treating it as speculative.
key_works: Majumder (2026), *Hashprice moderates the electricity demand response of Bitcoin miners*, arXiv:2606.00587.

title: Verifiable hashrate delivery contracts
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: Can a mining contract be designed so that delivered hashrate — promised, actually submitted, and usefully contributing — can be audited without exposing the miner's proprietary business data, and with only bounded gain available to parties who selectively report their work?
status: No such mechanism exists yet; the target sits beyond current pooled-work accounting techniques and beyond the funded audit infrastructure that OpenSats began supporting in 2025 (OpenSats, *Fifteenth Wave of Bitcoin Grants*). Classical pooled-mining reward accounting, as analyzed by Rosenfeld (2011), *Analysis of Bitcoin Pooled Mining Reward Systems*, arXiv:1112.4980, addresses share accounting but not the auditing, confidentiality, and selective-reporting constraints posed here.
solved_when: A contract and auditing mechanism exists that verifiably reconciles promised hashrate with submitted and useful delivered work, keeps business data confidential, and provably bounds the advantage from selective reporting.
why: It would underpin transparent hashpower finance, letting hashrate be collateralized, sold, or audited as a commodity rather than on trust.
key_works: Rosenfeld (2011), *Analysis of Bitcoin Pooled Mining Reward Systems*, arXiv:1112.4980; OpenSats (2025), [*Fifteenth Wave of Bitcoin Grants*](https://opensats.org/blog/fifteenth-wave-of-bitcoin-grants).

title: Global marginal emissions accounting for mining
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: When a new mine comes online somewhere in the world, how much additional pollution and disease does it actually cause — through shifted electricity dispatch, curtailed renewables, displaced activity, and newly built generation? The goal is a causal global estimate of the marginal emissions and health effects of added mining.
status: Research target beyond 2025 US power-plant attribution and industry surveys; the closest existing work is Guidi et al. (2025), *The environmental burden of the United States’ bitcoin mining boom*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58287-3.
solved_when: A validated method delivers causal global estimates of the marginal emissions and health effects of additional mining, accounting for dispatch, curtailment, relocation, and new generation.
why: It measures the induced consequences of mining rather than assigning average emission labels, which is what determines the true environmental and health burden of expanding mining activity.
key_works: Guidi et al. (2025), *The environmental burden of the United States’ bitcoin mining boom*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58287-3.

bib.title: Global marginal emissions accounting for mining

title: Mining policy and causal security effects
subfield: Mining finance, energy markets and economic security
open: What happens to security, fees, and mining ownership once the industry has fully adapted to policy interventions — restrictions, subsidies, or forced relocation? The goal is a credible estimate of the long-run causal effects of mining policy, rather than its immediate impact.
status: The current evidence base, from Scharnowski and Shi (2026), *Bitcoin blackout: Proof-of-work and the risks of mining centralization* (DOI:10.1016/j.jfs.2026.101569), documents only short-lived effects stemming from a local electricity shock; long-run post-adaptation effects remain unmeasured and are a research target beyond 2026.
solved_when: A study provides causal estimates of the long-run (post-adaptation) effects of mining restrictions, subsidies, and relocation on security, fees, and ownership, going beyond existing evidence of short-lived effects from a local electricity shock.
why: It would let us tell whether policy genuinely reduces systemic risk or merely displaces it — a distinction on which any sound mining or energy-security regulation depends.
key_works: Scharnowski and Shi (2026), *Bitcoin blackout: Proof-of-work and the risks of mining centralization*, DOI:10.1016/j.jfs.2026.101569.

bib.title: Mining policy and causal security effects

title: Bounded-information Sybil-proof inequality
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: How much additional information beyond pseudonymous records is needed to estimate beneficial-owner inequality with bounded error, when agents can freely split or merge identities? Formally, characterize the minimal information required for a Sybil-proof, bounded-error inequality estimator, or prove no such bound is achievable.
status: The target lies beyond the 2025–2026 Sybil-proof characterization and canonical-axiom impossibility of Yaish, Chemaya, Malkhi and Cong (2026), *Inequality in the Age of Pseudonymity* (DOI:10.1609/aaai.v40i20.38781); related work includes partial identification and privacy-preserving statistics.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the minimal extra information that suffices for bounded-error beneficial-owner inequality estimates under identity splitting and merging, or an impossibility result showing no such information bound can be met.
why: It makes inequality claims about pseudonymous populations interpretable — without it, such estimates can be arbitrarily manipulated by Sybil behavior and carry no meaning.
key_works: Yaish, Chemaya, Malkhi and Cong (2026), *Inequality in the Age of Pseudonymity*, DOI:10.1609/aaai.v40i20.38781.

title: Ownership through nested financial contracts
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: When tokens sit inside vaults, custodians, and layered receipt-token arrangements, can we determine who ultimately owns what — attributing exposure through arbitrarily nested contracts without counting the same asset twice, and quantifying uncertainty when some beneficiaries cannot be observed?
status: Stated as a research target extending 2025–2026 corrections for complex Ethereum holdings, in the line of Chemaya, Yaish, Yacouel, Malkhi and Cong (2025; revised 2026), *Quantifying Inequality in Blockchain Networks*, SSRN:5540258; related work includes beneficial-ownership accounting and latent-variable identification.
solved_when: A method exists that traces ultimate exposure through nested receipt tokens, vaults, and custodial structures on Ethereum, provably avoids double counting of the underlying assets, and returns explicit uncertainty estimates for hidden or unobservable beneficiaries.
why: Contract structure can masquerade as redistribution: without a correct unwinding of nested holdings, measured inequality and ownership concentration can be grossly misstated.
key_works: Chemaya, Yaish, Yacouel, Malkhi and Cong (2025; revised 2026), *Quantifying Inequality in Blockchain Networks*, SSRN:5540258.

title: Control concentration that predicts failures
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can we build a single concentration measure for blockchain control that combines ownership, operational dependence, and delegation, and shows it actually predicts correlated failures and control events?
status: The current state of the art is large-scale Bitcoin attribution as of 2021, exemplified by Makarov and Schoar (2021), *Blockchain Analysis of the Bitcoin Market*, NBER Working Paper 29396; the combined validated measure remains a research target beyond that. Related directions include corporate-control networks and common-cause reliability.
solved_when: Such a combined concentration measure is validated empirically against observed correlated failures and control events, beyond the large-scale Bitcoin attribution work of 2021.
why: It would give decentralization metrics predictive meaning — turning static concentration statistics into forecasts of when systems actually fail or lose control.
key_works: Makarov and Schoar (2021), *Blockchain Analysis of the Bitcoin Market*, NBER Working Paper 29396.

title: Investor outcomes beyond address-level portfolios
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can we measure crypto investors' true portfolio choices once we look past individual addresses to the full entity behind them? The goal is an evaluation of portfolio decisions at the entity level, incorporating liabilities, hidden hedges, and executable costs, that separates what investors prefer from what they are constrained to hold.
status: This is a research target lying beyond the 2026 analysis of over 116 million Ethereum accounts by Vynyavskyy, Kitzler, Haslhofer and Yaish (2026), *Modern Portfolio Theory in the Crypto-Wilderness*, arXiv:2605.20528. Related work spans household finance, revealed preference, and portfolio selection bias.
solved_when: Portfolio decisions can be evaluated using entity-level liabilities, hidden hedges and executable costs, with preferences cleanly separated from constraints — going beyond the 2026 analysis of over 116 million Ethereum accounts.
why: Address-level accounts are imperfect proxies for investors, so conclusions about portfolio behavior drawn from them may misattribute constraints (such as liabilities or hedges held elsewhere) to preferences.
key_works: Vynyavskyy, Kitzler, Haslhofer and Yaish (2026), *Modern Portfolio Theory in the Crypto-Wilderness*, arXiv:2605.20528.

title: Cross-incident stablecoin run benchmark
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can we build a harmonized cross-incident dataset of stablecoin runs, pairing each run and near-run with surviving controls and recording reserves, redemption rules, market depth, and contemporaneous information in a common format?
status: Analysis beyond the Terra case has begun, starting with the Terra Luna run study of Liu, Makarov and Schoar (2023), *Anatomy of a Run: The Terra Luna Crash*, NBER Working Paper 31160, and its 2026 replication package; no harmonized multi-incident benchmark exists yet.
solved_when: A benchmark dataset exists covering multiple run and near-run incidents alongside surviving stablecoin controls, with reserves, redemption rules, market depth, and contemporaneous information harmonized across incidents and made publicly available in a replication package.
why: With such a benchmark, models of stablecoin runs become falsifiable and comparable across different coin designs rather than testable only on a single episode.
key_works: Liu, Makarov and Schoar (2023), *Anatomy of a Run: The Terra Luna Crash*, NBER Working Paper 31160; [2026 replication data](https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/j5d8n7hzdy/2).

title: Adversarially robust wash-trading labels
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can wash-trading labels remain calibrated when manipulators actively imitate natural trade distributions and split their activity across venues to defeat detection? The goal is a labeling method whose accuracy guarantees survive such adversarial adaptation.
status: The target lies beyond the 2020–2023 statistical studies covering 29 exchanges, such as Cong, Li, Tang and Yang (2023), *Crypto Wash Trading*, DOI:10.1287/mnsc.2021.02709; it connects to adaptive fraud detection and adversarial statistics.
solved_when: A labeling procedure exists that produces calibrated wash-trading labels on data in which manipulators imitate natural trade distributions and distribute activity across venues, with calibration demonstrated against such adversarial behavior.
why: Without adversarially robust labels, liquidity and adoption measurements built on them can be deliberately inflated or distorted by manipulators, undermining the empirical study of exchanges.
key_works: Cong, Li, Tang and Yang (2023), *Crypto Wash Trading*, DOI:10.1287/mnsc.2021.02709.

title: Counterfactual behavioral benchmark for DeFi users
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can the execution shortfalls of DeFi users be explained by observable constraints — information, latency, risk limits, and computation — rather than by irrationality, when measured against feasible counterfactual actions? Formally, this asks for a behavioral benchmark that attributes each user's shortfall to these constraints using counterfactuals restricted to actions the user could actually have taken.
status: Evidence from 2023–2024 (Yaish, Dotan, Qin, Zohar and Gervais, *Suboptimality in DeFi*, IACR ePrint:2023/892) documents unrealized profit among users despite sophisticated tools being available; explaining those shortfalls via counterfactual analysis remains an open research target.
solved_when: An experimental benchmark exists that, for real DeFi user executions, constructs feasible counterfactual actions and quantitatively decomposes execution shortfalls into contributions from information, latency, risk limits, and computation.
why: It grounds the rational-user assumption underlying most DeFi economic models in actual behavior, telling modelers when that assumption is safe and when it fails.
key_works: Yaish, Dotan, Qin, Zohar and Gervais (2023–2024), *Suboptimality in DeFi*, IACR ePrint:2023/892.

bib.title: Counterfactual behavioral benchmark for DeFi users

title: Causal evaluation of stablecoin reserve rules
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: What actually happens when a specific stablecoin reserve rule is imposed — do run losses fall, and how do access, entry, and substitution across payment instruments respond — once the effect of the regulation itself is separated from the market shocks hitting at the same time?
status: Posed as a research target following the 2026 theoretical work on reserve-policy welfare tradeoffs by Li, Mancini-Griffoli, Miccoli, Tan and Zhang (2026), *Making Stablecoins Stable*, DOI:10.5089/9798229044349.001.
solved_when: A causal evaluation credibly isolates the effects of a reserve rule on run losses, access, entry, and substitution, disentangling the regulation from concurrent market shocks.
why: It tests whether specific reserve rules achieve their intended outcomes rather than merely shifting risk elsewhere in the payment system.
key_works: Li, Mancini-Griffoli, Miccoli, Tan and Zhang (2026), *Making Stablecoins Stable*, DOI:10.5089/9798229044349.001.

bib.title: Causal evaluation of stablecoin reserve rules

title: Sustainable neutral economic-data infrastructure
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: How can the research community sustain a neutral economic-data infrastructure that keeps reproducible datasets alive — with historical labels, deleted assets, versioned methods, correction rights, and independent reproduction — rather than letting them decay with vendor interest?
status: The current frontier is the 2025 graph datasets and funded analytics infrastructure — Schnoering and Vazirgiannis (2025), *Bitcoin research with a transaction graph dataset*, DOI:10.1038/s41597-025-04684-8, and OpenSats's *Bitcoin Research Kit* — and sustainability beyond that point remains an unfunded target.
solved_when: Datasets of the kind exemplified by the 2025 Bitcoin transaction graph dataset are maintained beyond 2025 under a durable funding model, together with funded analytics infrastructure, supporting historical labels, deleted assets, versioned methods, correction rights and independent reproduction.
why: Without it, research depends on disappearing vendor histories, so results cannot be checked or extended once the underlying data vanishes.
key_works: Schnoering and Vazirgiannis (2025), *Bitcoin research with a transaction graph dataset*, DOI:10.1038/s41597-025-04684-8; OpenSats, [*Bitcoin Research Kit*](https://opensats.org/projects/bitcoinresearchkit).

title: Independent funding for economic-security audits
subfield: Economic measurement, benchmarks and research infrastructure
open: Can economic-security audits be funded in a way that is independent of the sponsors whose systems are being audited? A concrete step is to evaluate sponsor-independent replication programs, measuring their cost per resolved claim and their coverage of neglected mechanisms.
status: No such evaluation is funded yet; current support stops at 2023 data-gap reports (FSB, 2023, *The Financial Stability Risks of Decentralised Finance*) and 2025 infrastructure grants (OpenSats, 2025, *Fifteenth Wave of Bitcoin Grants*).
solved_when: An evaluation exists of sponsor-independent replication programs reporting cost per resolved claim and coverage of neglected mechanisms, with dedicated funding beyond the 2023 data-gap reports and 2025 infrastructure grants.
why: It converts arguments about auditor incentives into regularly checked evidence, so claims about economic security can be verified rather than trusted.
key_works: FSB (2023), [*The Financial Stability Risks of Decentralised Finance*](https://www.fsb.org/2023/02/the-financial-stability-risks-of-decentralised-finance/); OpenSats (2025), *Fifteenth Wave of Bitcoin Grants*.

title: Demand-adaptive payment-network formation
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: When participants in a payment-channel network each choose which channels to open under directional, heterogeneous demand and real liquidity costs, what topologies arise in equilibrium? More precisely, characterize the channel-topology equilibria that emerge when directional demand, liquidity costs, and opening decisions evolve together.
status: The problem remains open and beyond current techniques; existing work consists of the 2019–2020 creation-game and symmetric-demand optimization results of Avarikioti et al. (2020), *Ride the Lightning: The Game Theory of Payment Channels*, arXiv:1912.04797, and Sali and Zohar (2020), *Optimizing Off-Chain Payment Networks in Cryptocurrencies*, arXiv:2007.09410; related directions include dynamic network-creation games and stochastic facility location.
solved_when: A characterization of equilibrium channel topologies is proved for a model in which directional demand, liquidity costs, and channel-opening decisions co-evolve, going beyond the 2019–2020 setting of static creation games and symmetric-demand optimization.
why: It settles whether efficient payment networks form through self-interested channel openings alone, without any central coordination of topology.
key_works: Avarikioti et al. (2020), *Ride the Lightning: The Game Theory of Payment Channels*, arXiv:1912.04797; Sali and Zohar (2020), *Optimizing Off-Chain Payment Networks in Cryptocurrencies*, arXiv:2007.09410.

title: Strategic routing fees with endogenous rebalancing
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: What routing fees arise in equilibrium when payment-channel intermediaries both set prices and independently rebalance their capital, so that each routed payment reshapes the future capacity available to others? A satisfactory answer characterizes efficient routing-price equilibria in this setting where pricing and liquidity management are endogenous and coupled over time.
status: This is an open research target bridging the 2017 work of Khalil and Gervais (2017), *Revive: Rebalancing Off-Blockchain Payment Networks* (IACR ePrint:2017/823), on rebalancing with the 2025 optimization-based routing prices of Sankagiri and Hajek (2025), *Pricing for Routing and Flow-Control in Payment Channel Networks* (DOI:10.1109/TON.2025.3588049). Related areas include dynamic congestion games and inventory-dependent pricing.
solved_when: A characterization of efficient routing-price equilibria is obtained for networks in which intermediaries set routing prices and rebalance capital endogenously, with payments affecting future channel capacity.
why: It would connect intermediary profitability to sustainable network throughput, explaining when self-interested pricing and rebalancing still support a payment network that keeps routing liquidity available over time.
key_works: Khalil and Gervais (2017), *Revive: Rebalancing Off-Blockchain Payment Networks*, IACR ePrint:2017/823; Sankagiri and Hajek (2025), *Pricing for Routing and Flow-Control in Payment Channel Networks*, DOI:10.1109/TON.2025.3588049.

bib.title: Strategic routing fees with endogenous rebalancing

title: Liquidity-private routing guarantees
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a routing algorithm in a payment-channel network still guarantee good success probability and low fees when channel balances are private and change while the algorithm is probing them? Formally, quantify the achievable routing-success and fee bounds under an adversary (or stochastic process) controlling liquidity that mutates during discovery.
status: This remains an open research target beyond Pickhardt and Richter's 2021 probabilistic-flow optimization (Pickhardt and Richter (2021), *Optimally Reliable & Cheap Payment Flows on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2107.05322). Related directions include partial-information online routing and private active learning.
solved_when: Provable bounds on routing success probability and fee cost are established for a setting with limited probing of private balances that change during the discovery process; any concrete quantitative targets stated in such a result should be matched or improved.
why: It reconciles reliable payment delivery with financial privacy: today, reliability generally requires learning channel liquidity, which leaks information about balances that parties wish to keep private.
key_works: Pickhardt and Richter (2021), *Optimally Reliable & Cheap Payment Flows on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2107.05322.

title: Coordinated channel-jamming resistance
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a payment-channel network that combines fees and reputation mechanisms withstand coordinated jamming attackers, and if so at what cost? Concretely, establish — or experimentally falsify — network-wide bounds on the attack cost when fee-based and reputation-based defenses are deployed together against colluding participants.
status: A longstanding target; hybrid fee-and-reputation defenses reached detailed simulation and specification work in 2025–2026, notably in the Project Updates: Hybrid Channel Jamming Mitigation (Kirk-Cohen, Shikh-Gelman and collaborators; lightning/bolts issue #1218) and the bitcoinproblems.org channel-jamming writeup.
solved_when: A proof or reproducible experimental evaluation yields network-wide attack-cost bounds for the combined fee-plus-reputation defense against coordinated jamming, either confirming such bounds exist or demonstrating falsifying attacks.
why: Without such bounds, attackers can cheaply deny liquidity across the network, rendering hybrid jamming mitigations deployable only on faith rather than evidence.
key_works: Kirk-Cohen, Shikhelman and collaborators, [*Project Updates: Hybrid Channel Jamming Mitigation*](https://github.com/lightning/bolts/issues/1218); [*Channel jamming*](https://bitcoinproblems.org/problems/channel-jamming.html).

title: Jamming-resistant reputation without newcomer exclusion
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a payment-channel reputation system resist jamming attacks without locking out honest users who have no history? Formally, can we bound the advantage an attacker gains from resetting into fresh identities (Sybil resets) while still guaranteeing useful service to newcomers?
status: Currently a research target accompanying 2025–2026 reputation and accountability proposals, notably Lightning contributors' [*Outgoing reputation and HTLC Accountability*](https://github.com/lightning/bolts/pull/1280). Related lines of work include anonymous reputation cold start and fair online admission, but the problem itself remains open.
solved_when: A reputation design (with analysis) exists in which the Sybil-reset advantage is bounded and honest participants without payment history are guaranteed useful service.
why: Without such a design, any jamming defense based on history either fails against identity resets or permanently privileges incumbents, excluding legitimate new participants from the network.
key_works: Lightning contributors (2025–2026), [*Outgoing reputation and HTLC Accountability*](https://github.com/lightning/bolts/pull/1280).

title: Clock-free compensation for held payments
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a payment-channel design charge routers for the HTLC slots and liquidity their payments occupy, without relying on trusted fine-grained clocks and without creating incentives to deliberately delay payments?
status: This is an explicit design direction in the channel-jamming literature; existing fee approaches suffer from different incentive failures (Bitcoin Problems contributors, [*Channel jamming*](https://bitcoinproblems.org/problems/channel-jamming.html)).
solved_when: A concrete fee mechanism is specified that meters occupied slot time and liquidity, requires no trusted clock, and provably (or convincingly by analysis) removes the incentive to delay payments.
why: It makes attackers pay for the resources their unsuccessful routing attempts consume, closing the channel-jamming attack economically.
key_works: Bitcoin Problems contributors, [*Channel jamming*](https://bitcoinproblems.org/problems/channel-jamming.html).

title: Ground-truth payment-routing benchmark
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can we construct a benchmark of real payment-routing activity — consented traces of payment attempts, hidden directional liquidity, chosen routes, failures, and rebalancing — that comes with a quantified bound on the privacy lost by participants?
status: The target lies beyond what is available from public topology data and probabilistic routing models; relevant background includes Pickhardt and Richter (2021), *Optimally Reliable & Cheap Payment Flows on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2107.05322, and Chaincode Labs, [*Introduction to Bitcoin Research*](https://research.chaincode.com/research-intro/).
solved_when: A released dataset exists containing consented traces of attempts, hidden directional liquidity, routes, failures, and rebalancing, together with an explicit quantification of privacy loss.
why: It would enable comparable, ground-truth evaluation of routing success rates, which current public-topology and probabilistic-routing models cannot support.
key_works: Pickhardt and Richter (2021), *Optimally Reliable & Cheap Payment Flows on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2107.05322; Chaincode Labs, [*Introduction to Bitcoin Research*](https://research.chaincode.com/research-intro/).

title: Safe mass exits under endogenous fees
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Which channel populations can still exit safely when closing a channel itself drives up transaction fees, and adversaries can deliberately time congestion to worsen the damage? More precisely, characterize the sets of participants whose cooperative closure remains safe when exit transactions endogenously raise fees under attacker-induced congestion.
status: This remains a research target, posed beyond the systemic attack described by Harris and Zohar (2020), *Flood & Loot: A Systemic Attack on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2006.08513; no characterization is known.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the channel populations that can safely close when exit transactions raise fees and attackers time congestion — going beyond the Flood & Loot systemic attack scenario — with the safety condition stated checkably for a given population.
why: It determines whether individual exit rights remain usable during system stress, or whether congestion and fee endogeneity make mass closure self-defeating.
key_works: Harris and Zohar (2020), *Flood & Loot: A Systemic Attack on the Lightning Network*, arXiv:2006.08513.

bib.title: Safe mass exits under endogenous fees

title: Competitive and accountable watchtower markets
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can a market of paid watchtowers for payment channels be designed so that monitoring remains trustworthy even when cheating is rare, outages are correlated, and watchtowers can collude with the counterparties they are supposed to catch? Formally, is there an incentive-compatible payment mechanism sustaining honest, timely watchtower behavior under collusion and correlated failure?
status: Open beyond current art; the closest reference point is Outpost (Nadahazzi correction: Nadahalli, Khabbazian and Wattenhofer, 2019, [Outpost: A Responsive Lightweight Watchtower](https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/entities/publication/d1a9979f-b97d-41ff-b2f9-80d437379a0c)), which provides lightweight monitoring and payment evidence but no competitive, collusion-resistant market design.
solved_when: A mechanism (protocol plus payment/incentive scheme) is specified and proved to sustain honest watchtower monitoring under the stated adversarial conditions — rare cheating, correlated outages, and watchtower–counterparty collusion — with provable guarantees on accountability and liveness.
why: It would make safe offline custody economically sustainable, so users can delegate channel monitoring without trusting any single watchtower.
key_works: Nadahalli, Khabbazian and Wattenhofer (2019), [*Outpost: A Responsive Lightweight Watchtower*](https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/entities/publication/d1a9979f-b97d-41ff-b2f9-80d437379a0c).

title: Channel-factory coalition exit incentives
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: Can the savings, collateral, and exit costs of a channel factory be allocated among its participants so that no coalition can gain by threatening premature closure or holding liquidity hostage? Formally, is there a cost-sharing rule for shared channel-factory funding under which no coalition has a profitable deviation via exit threats or liquidity hostage-taking?
status: This remains an open research target beyond the 2018 funding-efficiency results of Burchert, Decker and Wattenhofer (2018), *Scalable funding of Bitcoin micropayment channel networks*, DOI:10.1098/rsos.180089.
solved_when: An allocation rule (or an impossibility result) is proved for the savings, collateral, and exit costs of a channel factory such that coalition deviations through premature-closure threats or liquidity hostage-taking are unprofitable.
why: Without such an allocation, any participant or coalition inside a factory can extort value by threatening to strand others' liquidity, undermining shared funding as an economic arrangement; with it, shared funding becomes economically safe.
key_works: Burchert, Decker and Wattenhofer (2018), *Scalable funding of Bitcoin micropayment channel networks*, DOI:10.1098/rsos.180089.

title: Atomic-swap premiums under endogenous settlement risk
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: How should an atomic-swap protocol compensate a party for the risk of cancellation when exchange-rate jumps, transaction fees, and censorship all jointly shape both the decision to exercise the swap and whether settlement actually completes? Formally, this asks for a pricing theory of cancellation compensation in which exercise and settlement frictions are endogenous rather than taken as exogenous.
status: This remains a research target beyond the analysis of Han, Lin and Yu (2019), *On the optionality and fairness of Atomic Swaps* (DOI:10.1145/3318041.3355460), which addressed atomic-swap optionality and premium repairs but left endogenous settlement risk unpriced; related threads include strategic American-option exercise and incomplete-market risk sharing.
solved_when: A model and formula (or characterization) is provided that prices cancellation compensation under exchange-rate jumps, fees, and censorship endogenously determining exercise and settlement — extending the 2019 treatment of atomic-swap optionality and premium repairs.
why: It preserves economic fairness between swap counterparties during volatility, ensuring neither side systematically bears the cost of cancellation risk created by market jumps or protocol frictions.
key_works: Han, Lin and Yu (2019), *On the optionality and fairness of Atomic Swaps*, DOI:10.1145/3318041.3355460.

bib.title: Atomic-swap premiums under endogenous settlement risk

title: Strategic virtual-channel provisioning
subfield: Payment-channel routing and liquidity economics
open: How should virtual channels be placed in a payment-channel network when the intermediaries whose capital is needed hold private prices for that capital and can strategically veto the channel's setup? Formally, is there an approximation mechanism for virtual-channel placement that remains near-optimal in the presence of such self-interested veto players?
status: No mechanism is known; the problem sits beyond the 2024–2025 literature on on-path-adversary optimization and snapshot evaluation. The closest work is Aumayr et al. (2025), *Optimizing virtual payment channel establishment in the face of on-path adversaries*, DOI:10.1016/j.comcom.2025.108155.
solved_when: A mechanism (with provable approximation guarantees for virtual-channel placement) is given that works despite intermediaries who privately price capital and can strategically obstruct setup, without requiring strategic subsidies; and it advances the state of the art beyond 2024–2025 on-path-adversary optimization and snapshot evaluation.
why: It reduces the recurring routing and capital costs of payment-channel operation without resorting to strategic subsidies — a form of network-design procurement with veto players that current approaches sidestep.
key_works: Aumayr et al. (2025), *Optimizing virtual payment channel establishment in the face of on-path adversaries*, DOI:10.1016/j.comcom.2025.108155.

title: Heterogeneous proof-task procurement
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can we design a truthful, budget-respecting mechanism that allocates heterogeneous proof tasks — tasks with interdependencies — across provers whose hardware costs, capacities, and deadlines are all private information? Formally, the goal is a procurement mechanism for dependent proof tasks that retains truthfulness and budget guarantees despite the richer, heterogeneous setting.
status: This remains a research target beyond Prooφ’s 2024–2025 batch-market model (Wang et al. (2025), *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism*, arXiv:2404.06495); the problem connects to combinatorial procurement and unrelated-machine scheduling.
solved_when: A mechanism is given that allocates dependent proof tasks over private costs, capacities, and deadlines while provably preserving truthfulness and budget guarantees; this extends Prooφ’s 2024–2025 batch-market model to the heterogeneous case.
why: It would let proof markets support realistic mixed workloads, enabling genuine competition across heterogeneous provers rather than only homogeneous batch settings.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism*, arXiv:2404.06495.

title: Proof-market entry and backlog dynamics
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: When new provers can enter a proof market and low-value tasks accumulate in a backlog, does competition emerge and persist, or do entry barriers and queue dynamics lock in exclusionary pricing? Formally, characterize the long-run equilibria of a market with endogenous prover entry and task backlog.
status: Long-run entry and backlog are explicit future-work directions in the Prooφ mechanism of Wang et al. (2025), *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism* (arXiv:2404.06495); the question remains open.
solved_when: A characterization (or counterexample) is given of the long-run market outcome — convergence to competitive pricing versus persistent exclusion or recurring price cycles — under endogenous prover entry and accumulating low-value tasks.
why: It tests whether proof-market competition is durable over time, or whether backlog dynamics undermine the market mechanisms that ZK proof systems rely on.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), *Prooφ: A ZKP Market Mechanism*, arXiv:2404.06495.

title: Attack-resistant proof-work contracts
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can a proving service price a submitted task cheaply — before running the full proof — so that adversarial "prover-killer" tasks cannot consume disproportionate compute for a negligible fee?
status: An open engineering target arising from 2025 pricing attacks on blockchain rollups documented by Chaliasos et al. (2025), *Unaligned Incentives: Pricing Attacks Against Blockchain Rollups*, arXiv:2509.17126; no mechanism is yet known.
solved_when: A pricing mechanism exists that estimates the cost of an arbitrary proving task without performing the full proof, and cheap adversarial tasks can no longer trigger disproportionate compute consumption on the prover.
why: Without such pricing, an attacker can spend pennies to force provers into expensive work, effectively disabling them; a solution makes proof markets robust to this cheap-shutdown vector.
key_works: Chaliasos et al. (2025), *Unaligned Incentives: Pricing Attacks Against Blockchain Rollups*, arXiv:2509.17126.

title: Reproducible proof-market cost benchmark
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can the community produce and publish full-cost proof traces — including amortization, retries, memory, queueing, verification, and missed deadlines — so that proof-market mechanisms are evaluated on complete, reproducible cost data rather than partial measurements?
status: This is currently a data target beyond zk-Bench's 2024 primitive and proof-system benchmarking (Ernstberger et al. (2024), [*zk-Bench: A Toolset for Comparative Evaluation and Performance Benchmarking of SNARKs*](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10198741/)).
solved_when: A publicly reproducible benchmark dataset exists that captures full cost traces for proof-market workloads, covering amortization, retries, memory, queueing, verification, and missed deadlines, going beyond zk-Bench's 2024 primitive- and proof-system-level benchmarking.
why: It separates the merits of proof-market mechanisms from favorable hardware selection, allowing mechanism design to be judged on its own terms.
key_works: Ernstberger et al. (2024), [*zk-Bench: A Toolset for Comparative Evaluation and Performance Benchmarking of SNARKs*](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10198741/).

title: Coalition-proof fraud-proof compensation
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can a fraud-proof reward scheme be designed so that honest, independent challengers always recover their true costs of challenging, even when a malicious proposer can spin up fake identities, trigger reward races, or run side auctions to drain the compensation pool?
status: The problem is posed as a research target beyond Lee (2025), *Hollow Victory: How Malicious Proposers Exploit Validator Incentives in Optimistic Rollup Dispute Games* (arXiv:2504.05094), which documented the exploits and proposed escrow and commitment repairs. Related lines include contest sabotage and false-name-proof rewards.
solved_when: A mechanism (or proof of impossibility) exists in which no coalition led by the proposer, using identity creation, reward races, or side auctions, can prevent a correct challenger from recovering its actual verification costs.
why: Without cost recovery, correct challenges become unprofitable and rational verifiers stop challenging invalid fraud proofs, breaking the security of optimistic rollups.
key_works: Lee (2025), *Hollow Victory: How Malicious Proposers Exploit Validator Incentives in Optimistic Rollup Dispute Games*, arXiv:2504.05094.

title: Challenge solvency during settlement congestion
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: When many disputes are opened at once on an adversarially congested parent chain, how much capital and how large a fee budget must honest challengers post to still get their challenges resolved? Formally, the goal is to bound honest challengers’ capital and fee requirements under concurrent disputes combined with adversarial parent-chain congestion.
status: This remains a research target beyond the delay guarantees of BoLD (Alvarez et al. (2024), *BoLD: Fast and Cheap Dispute Resolution*, arXiv:2404.10491). Related directions include adversarial queueing and liquidity-constrained security games.
solved_when: Provable bounds exist on the capital locked and fees paid by honest challengers as a function of the number of concurrent disputes and the degree of parent-chain congestion, going beyond BoLD’s 2024 protocol delay guarantees.
why: Permissionless challenge systems only work if honest parties can actually afford to see a dispute through; without such bounds, timely and affordable execution of challenges cannot be guaranteed.
key_works: Alvarez et al. (2024), *BoLD: Fast and Cheap Dispute Resolution*, arXiv:2404.10491.

title: Economically meaningful utility gaps for rational proofs
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can rational proofs be constructed so that a prover's payoff advantage from telling the truth exceeds the realistic costs of computation and capital it must commit, even when the prover is only boundedly rational or risk-averse? Formally, the goal is a construction in the rational-proof framework whose truthful-strategy utility gap stays above these costs under such relaxations of perfect rationality.
status: This is an open research target extending the 2012 rational-proof complexity framework of Azar and Micali (2012), [*Rational Proofs*](https://people.csail.mit.edu/silvio/Selected%20Scientific%20Papers/Proof%20Systems/RationalProofs.pdf).
solved_when: An explicit rational-proof construction is given whose truthful-payoff gap exceeds realistic computation and capital costs while remaining robust under bounded rationality or risk aversion.
why: It would turn the mere existence of incentive-compatible verification into services that can actually be implemented and priced, closing the gap between the theory of rational proofs and deployable proof markets.
key_works: Azar and Micali (2012), [*Rational Proofs*](https://people.csail.mit.edu/silvio/Selected%20Scientific%20Papers/Proof%20Systems/RationalProofs.pdf).

bib.title: Economically meaningful utility gaps for rational proofs

title: Minimal collateral for repeated fair computation
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: How little collateral suffices to keep repeated multiparty computation fair when the set of participants changes over time and aborting yields only bounded external gains? Formally, derive tight tradeoffs between the collateral parties must post and the communication cost of the protocol in this setting.
status: No results yet; this target goes beyond penalty-based fairness as established from 2014 onward, e.g. Bentov and Kumaresan (2014), *How to Use Bitcoin to Design Fair Protocols*, IACR ePrint:2014/129.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on the collateral–communication tradeoff are established for repeated MPC with changing membership and bounded external abort benefits.
why: Lower collateral requirements cut the capital parties must lock up to securely join joint computation, making protected multiparty protocols practical for participants without deep pockets.
key_works: Bentov and Kumaresan (2014), *How to Use Bitcoin to Design Fair Protocols*, IACR ePrint:2014/129.

bib.title: Minimal collateral for repeated fair computation

title: Composable penalty mechanisms under side contracts
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: When do monetary penalties still deter misbehavior if participants can insure, hedge, or otherwise reimburse each other's slashing losses through side contracts? Characterize the conditions under which penalty-based incentive mechanisms remain sound in the presence of such external financial arrangements.
status: This is a research target connecting the 2014 penalty protocols of Bentov and Kumaresan (2014), *How to Use Bitcoin to Design Fair Protocols*, IACR ePrint:2014/129, with the 2022–2025 exchange guarantees of Chung et al. (2025), *Rapidash*, IACR ePrint:2022/1063; no characterization is known.
solved_when: A characterization exists — necessary and sufficient conditions under which penalty protocols (in the style of Bentov–Kumaresan 2014) preserve their incentive guarantees when composed with side contracts, ideally with a composable framework connecting to Rapidash's exchange guarantees.
why: External finance can invalidate local deterrence, so protocols that appear secure in isolation may fail once participants can insure away their penalties.
key_works: Bentov and Kumaresan (2014), *How to Use Bitcoin to Design Fair Protocols*, IACR ePrint:2014/129; Chung et al. (2025), *Rapidash*, IACR ePrint:2022/1063.

bib.title: Composable penalty mechanisms under side contracts

title: Incentive-compatible threshold-signing availability
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can a threshold-signing protocol pay and select its signers so that deliberately delaying or selectively aborting a signing session is never profitable, while preserving asynchronous robustness and not disadvantaging slower participants? Formally, the goal is a payment-and-selection rule under which honest-but-slow behavior weakly dominates delay and selective-abort strategies in an asynchronous threshold-signing environment.
status: This is a research target going beyond the robustness guarantee of Ruffing et al. (2022), *ROAST: Robust Asynchronous Schnorr Threshold Signatures* (IACR ePrint:2022/550), which achieves honest-quorum robustness in asynchronous Schnorr threshold signing but does not address incentive-compatible payment or signer selection. Related directions include reliability auctions and mechanism design for unverifiable delays.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified together with a proof that deviation (delays, selective aborts) is unprofitable, that asynchronous robustness at the level of ROAST's honest-quorum guarantee is retained, and that slower honest participants are not sacrificed (no correctness or reward loss imposed on them).
why: It makes signing committees economically accountable, so that protocol security does not rest on assuming away rational misbehavior by committee members.
key_works: Ruffing et al. (2022), *ROAST: Robust Asynchronous Schnorr Threshold Signatures*, IACR ePrint:2022/550.

title: Coalition-resilient private equilibrium mediation
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can correlated recommendations for many players be delivered privately and robustly in a decentralized setting — even when coalitions of players may adaptively collude and any participant may gain by aborting after seeing their recommendation? The goal is a mechanism implementing repeated multi-player correlated equilibrium with private signals that remains resilient to adaptive coalition deviations and bounds post-recommendation abort incentives.
status: The current frontier is the 2025 result of Barakbayeva, Cai, Goharshady and Keyparloo, *Smart Contracts for Trustless Sampling of Correlated Equilibria* (DOI:10.24963/ijcai.2025/416), which achieves trustless two-player correlated-equilibrium sampling; the many-player coalition-resilient setting remains open.
solved_when: A construction (or existence proof) exists for repeated many-player correlated-recommendation sampling with private signals, adaptive-coalition resilience, and bounded post-recommendation abort incentives, with a proof of its incentive guarantees.
why: It would extend trustless cryptographic mediation beyond two players, enabling decentralized strategic coordination among many parties without a trusted mediator.
key_works: Barakbayeva, Cai, Goharshady and Keypoor (2025), *Smart Contracts for Trustless Sampling of Correlated Equilibria*, DOI:10.24963/ijcai.2025/416.

title: Credible combinatorial auctions with cheap commitments
subfield: Proof markets, verification incentives and cryptographic mechanisms
open: Can we design credible combinatorial auctions that remain efficient when bidders value bundles of goods complements each other, or when the feasibility constraint is a non-matroid set system? A satisfactory construction should jointly bound the communication needed to run the auction, the collateral participants must lock up, and the incentives to abort the protocol.
status: This remains a research target beyond 2025 matroid results and October 2026 constant-round MPC constructions. Key works: Ferreira and Weinberg (2020), *Credible, Truthful, and Two-Round (Optimal) Auctions via Cryptographic Commitments*, arXiv:2004.01598; Ganesh and Zhang (2025), *Truthful, Credible, and Optimal Auctions for Matroids via Blockchains and Commitments*, arXiv:2507.04592; Ferreira (2026), *Credible Auctions via MPC Gadgets: Bounding Information Leakage Under Abort*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.18.
solved_when: A mechanism exists for complementary multidimensional valuations (or non-matroid feasibility) with explicit, quantitative bounds on communication complexity, collateral requirements, and abort incentives — extending the 2025 matroid case and the October 2026 constant-round MPC constructions.
why: It would make markets for bundled resources (e.g., spectrum or compute packages) credibly enforceable without a trusted auctioneer, since today's techniques only cover the matroid-feasible single-dimensional setting.
key_works: Ferreira and Weinberg (2020), *Credible, Truthful, and Two-Round (Optimal) Auctions via Cryptographic Commitments*, arXiv:2004.01598; Ganesh and Zhang (2025), *Truthful, Credible, and Optimal Auctions for Matroids via Blockchains and Commitments*, arXiv:2507.04592; Ferreira (2026), *Credible Auctions via MPC Gadgets: Bounding Information Leakage Under Abort*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2026.18.

bib.title: Credible combinatorial auctions with cheap commitments

title: Optimal randomized discounted scheduling
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: What is the optimal competitive ratio of randomized algorithms for online packet scheduling with time discounts, for each discount factor, and how does the answer differ between adaptive and oblivious adversaries? In particular, closing the gaps left by current algorithms and lower bounds — including at the classical randomized endpoint — would settle the power of randomization in this setting.
status: The 2026 RDISC algorithm and its accompanying lower bounds leave gaps, including at the classical randomized endpoint; see Gafni and Yaish (2024–2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549.
solved_when: For every discount factor, matching upper and lower bounds on the randomized competitive ratio are established, with the adaptive-adversary and oblivious-adversary cases each resolved, including the classical randomized endpoint.
why: A resolution quantifies exactly how much value randomization adds in discounted scheduling, separating what adaptive adversaries can nullify from what oblivious adversaries cannot.
key_works: Gafni and Yaish (2024–2026), *Online Packet Scheduling With Time Discounts*, arXiv:2402.08549.

title: Competitive authenticated-state adaptation
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can an authenticated data structure adapt its shape to a changing sequence of accesses, queries, and updates while provably performing within a constant factor (or with bounded regret) of the best shape chosen in hindsight? In other words, is there an analogue of dynamic optimality for search trees that holds under authentication constraints and jointly charges queries, updates, reshaping, and shifts in access frequencies?
status: Currently a research target with no bounds known; the motivating work is Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads* (arXiv:2608.25206), whose 2026 Huffman-Merkle trees are evaluated only by measured average performance. Related lines include dynamic optimality of search trees and online data structures.
solved_when: A competitive-ratio or regret bound is proved for a data structure that jointly accounts for the costs of queries, updates, and reshaping under arbitrary access sequences, including changing access frequencies.
why: It would upgrade adaptive authenticated data structures from heuristics with measured average performance to objects with worst-case guarantees, giving principled adaptive-state security and efficiency for dynamic workloads.
key_works: Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads*, arXiv:2608.25206.

title: Manipulation-resistant hot-state promotion
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can a frequency-aware authenticated data structure, such as a cache or sketch-based tier migration scheme, resist a cheap adversarial workload that forces constant rebuilding or eviction, while still adapting well to honest access patterns? In other words, we want provable or well-measured bounds on attacker-induced rebuild and eviction costs without sacrificing the adaptation benefits these layouts provide.
status: An engineering research target prompted by 2026 HMT sketches, caches and tier migration; related problems include cache pollution and adversarial streaming algorithms. Key work: Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads*, arXiv:2608.25206.
solved_when: A hot-state promotion scheme is exhibited whose attacker-induced rebuild and eviction costs are bounded (quantitatively) relative to the attacker's work, while retaining the adaptation benefits of frequency-aware layouts under honest workloads.
why: Without such bounds, adaptive layouts become denial-of-service targets: an adversary with cheap writes can force expensive rebuilding and eviction, turning the system's own adaptation mechanism against it.
key_works: Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads*, arXiv:2608.25206.

title: Access-pattern privacy of adaptive commitments
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can an adaptively updated authenticated data structure hide which items are being accessed — through both proof lengths and tier changes — while still delivering meaningful savings for skewed workloads? Formally, is there a scheme whose observable access pattern (proof-size and tier-migration traces) is independent of the request sequence, or leaks only a quantified, bounded amount, without giving up the workload-aware efficiency gains?
status: This is an open research target beyond the workload-aware efficiency results of Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads* (arXiv:2608.25206); related lines include oblivious RAM lower bounds and leakage-aware data structures.
solved_when: A construction and analysis exist showing that adaptive-storage savings are preserved while the leakage from proof lengths and tier changes is either eliminated or bounded by an explicitly characterized function; conversely, a matching lower bound showing a fundamental trade-off between savings and leakage would equally resolve the question.
why: Activity frequency can be sensitive information — an adversary observing proof lengths or tier changes can infer which data items are hot, so without such a scheme the efficiency benefits of workload-aware structures come at the cost of privacy.
key_works: Shangguan, Yaish and Malkhi (2026), *Authenticated Data Structures for Dynamic Workloads*, arXiv:2608.25206.

title: Jointly private and fee-efficient coin selection
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can one design an online UTXO coin-selection policy that simultaneously achieves explicit long-run guarantees on fees, fragmentation, and privacy when payments and fee levels arrive unpredictably? In other words, is there a strategy whose greedy fee savings today do not force higher costs or linkage leakage tomorrow, under uncertainty about future transactions and fee shocks?
status: A practical research target since at least 2016, extending the empirical evaluation of coin-selection strategies in Erhardt (2016), [*An Evaluation of Coin Selection Strategies*](https://murch.one/erhardt2016coinselection.pdf); no formal joint guarantees on fees, fragmentation, and privacy are known.
solved_when: An online coin-selection algorithm is given, together with a formal analysis establishing long-run bounds on accumulated fees, wallet fragmentation, and privacy leakage (e.g., address clustering exposure) under stochastic or adversarial sequences of payments and fee shocks.
why: A solution would let wallets spend cheaply now without paying for it later — in literal transaction fees, in a fragmented UTXO set that raises future costs, or in coin linkages that erode privacy.
key_works: Erhardt (2016), [*An Evaluation of Coin Selection Strategies*](https://murch.one/erhardt2016coinselection.pdf).
