title: Incentive-preserving contract compilation
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we build a compiler that takes a strategic specification — a contract written with explicit fees, timeouts, failure branches, and scheduling of moves — and emits executable code together with a proof that the compiled artifact preserves the payoffs and equilibrium bounds the specification promised?
status: This is a research target that would integrate 2018-era sound compilation techniques (Bartoletti and Zunino, 2018, *BitML: A Calculus for Bitcoin Smart Contracts*, IACR ePrint:2018/122) with quantitative payoff analysis of smart contracts (Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner, 2018, *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_6). No such incentive-preserving compilation pipeline currently exists.
solved_when: A working compilation pipeline exists that, for input contracts with stated payoff and equilibrium bounds, produces deployed bytecode (or equivalent low-level code) plus a machine-checkable or rigorous argument that fees, timeouts, failures, and scheduling in the compiled output preserve those bounds.
why: It would close the gap between incentive theorems proved on paper and the bytecode actually deployed, so that game-theoretic guarantees of a contract survive translation into executable form.
key_works: Bartoletti and Zunino (2018), *BitML: A Calculus for Bitcoin Smart Contracts*, IACR ePrint:2018/122; Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner (2018), *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_26.

title: Economic liquidity of recursive contracts
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we prove that funds locked in recursive, renegotiable contracts can be recovered at acceptable cost, when counterparties act strategically and settlement channels are congested? Formally, this asks for a quantitative notion of economic liquidity — accounting for strategic continuation choices and congestion costs — that is verifiable for recursive contracts.
status: The state of the art is the 2020–2022 line of work on logical-liquidity verification for the studied BitML models, notably Bartoletti, Lande, Murgia and Zunino (2022), *Verifying liquidity of recursive Bitcoin contracts*, arXiv:2011.14165; the present target goes beyond those results.
solved_when: A verification method (or accompanying counterexample) exists for recursive renegotiable contracts establishing that fund recovery is affordable — i.e., technically reachable exits are also economically viable — under strategic continuation and congested settlement.
why: A contract exit that is reachable in principle may be prohibitively expensive in practice, so purely logical liquidity guarantees do not protect participants; an economic-liquidity criterion closes this gap.
key_works: Bartoletti, Lande, Murgia and Zunino (2022), *Verifying liquidity of recursive Bitcoin contracts*, arXiv:2011.14165.

title: Automatic models with certified economic fidelity
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we automatically extract a sound economic model directly from a virtual machine's code for a given contract fragment and time horizon? The model must faithfully capture callback semantics and external-token behavior, so that reasoning over it is valid for the actual program.
status: Clockwork Finance (Babel, Daian, Kelkar and Juels, 2023, arXiv:2109.04347) performs exhaustive economic reasoning, but only over models supplied to it; automatic extraction of certified models from code remains an open target. Related directions include sound abstraction generation and translation validation.
solved_when: A tool exists that, given a specified VM, contract fragment, and horizon, produces an economic model certified sound with respect to callbacks and external-token semantics.
why: It connects economic-security guarantees proved on a model to the code that actually runs, closing the gap between modeled and deployed behavior.
key_works: Babel, Daian, Kelkar and Juels (2023), *Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts*, arXiv:2109.04347.

bib.title: Automatic models with certified economic fidelity

title: Scalable economic-attack upper bounds
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we certify useful upper bounds on the exploit value available to an attacker across a large set of interacting contracts, without enumerating every possible ordering and trajectory? Formally, the goal is a scalable method that bounds achievable adversarial profit over composed contract semantics.
status: The state of the art as of 2021–2023 consists of exhaustive modeled-semantics analyses and case studies, exemplified by Babel et al. (2023), *Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts*, arXiv:2109.04347; scalable certification remains an open research target. Related directions include abstract-interpretation precision and compositional optimization certificates.
solved_when: A method exists that computes certified exploit-value upper bounds for large interacting contract sets, avoiding exhaustive enumeration of orderings and trajectories, while remaining informative enough to rule out meaningful attacker profits.
why: Such bounds let defenders evaluate security mechanisms by the profits they provably rule out, turning economic security from case-by-case studies into a checkable property.
key_works: Babel et al. (2023), *Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts*, arXiv:2109.04347.

title: Economic-security bounds under model uncertainty
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we establish a bound on the exploit value available to an attacker that remains valid when the verification model itself is uncertain — in the oracle's pricing errors, the external liquidity available, transaction fees, and the attacker's capital? Formally, the goal is a construction and proof extending conditional extractable-value verification so that its security certificate degrades gracefully across a quantified uncertainty set over these market parameters.
status: This is a research target extending 2021–2023 work on conditional extractable-value verification; the closest key work is Babel et al. (2023), *Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts* (arXiv:2109.04347). Related directions include distributionally robust optimization and uncertain-environment verification.
solved_when: A proven upper bound on exploit value that holds uniformly over the specified uncertainties (oracle errors, external liquidity, fees, and attacker capital), extending the 2021–2023 conditional extractable-value verification framework; no quantitative budgets are specified in the record, so the natural criterion for this problem type applies.
why: It would yield security certificates for economic-security analyses that remain valid as market conditions shift, rather than breaking the moment fees, liquidity, or oracle behavior depart from the verified assumptions.
key_works: Babel et al. (2023), *Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts*, arXiv:2109.04347.

title: Cross-VM preservation of economic properties
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can incentive properties — such as strategy-proofness or equilibrium guarantees — be preserved when a contract is ported across execution environments with fundamentally different semantics, for example from the EVM to object-based or parallel-execution virtual machines? The goal is a transfer methodology that soundly accounts for divergent abort and fee semantics between source and target platforms.
status: This remains a research target predicated on cross-platform production-verification experience expected beyond 2026, per Georgiev (2026), *Scaling Formal Verification Across DeFi Ecosystems*, DOI:10.4230/OASIcs.FMBC.2026.1; no transfer method achieving it is on record.
solved_when: A method exists that transfers incentive properties of contracts across EVM, object-based, and parallel-execution platforms while provably accounting for differences in abort and fee semantics, demonstrated on cross-platform production-verification experience beyond 2026.
why: Ports can silently change strategic behavior: a mechanism that is incentive-safe on its native VM may admit new manipulations once abort and fee semantics differ, so verifiers need a guarantee that the ported contract retains the original economic properties.
key_works: Georgiev (2026), *Scaling Formal Verification Across DeFi Ecosystems*, DOI:10.4230/OASIcs.FMBC.2026.1.

title: Strategic-security regression corpus
subfield: Online algorithms and formal economic security
open: Can we build a curated corpus of executable code changes — each introducing or removing a profitable deviation, with certified payoffs and explicit attacker capabilities — that serves as a regression benchmark for economic security of smart contracts?
status: Proposed as a data target extending 2018 quantitative contract analysis (Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner, 2018, *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_26) and subsequent economic verification work; related efforts include formal-methods benchmark coverage and counterexample-guided testing.
solved_when: A corpus exists containing executable code changes that create or remove profitable deviations, where each entry includes a certified payoff and a specification of attacker capabilities.
why: It would let researchers test whether verification and testing tools catch incentive regressions, not just recognizable exploits, providing a shared measure of progress in economic security analysis.
key_works: Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner (2018), *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_26.

title: Causal long-run effects of airdrops
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Do the rules governing how an airdrop distributes tokens causally shape participants' long-run engagement — durable participation, genuinely useful activity, and governance involvement — even when spillovers between participants complicate identification?
status: The state of the art is the 2023–2025 study (revised) by Messias, Yaish and Livshits, *Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems*, arXiv:2312.02752, which examined nine major airdrops and found rapid token selling; the causal long-run question remains an open research target.
solved_when: A credible causal estimate of the effect of distribution rules on durable participation, useful activity, and governance under spillovers is produced, extending beyond the 2023–2025 study of nine major airdrops and rapid token selling.
why: It reveals whether giveaways buy sustainable participation rather than transient recipients who quickly sell.
key_works: Messias, Yaish and Livshits (2023; revised 2025), *Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems*, arXiv:2312.02752.

title: Competing platforms with strategic airdrop farmers
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: When multiple platforms run competing airdrop campaigns and farmers strategically coordinate across them (including through resale markets), what reward schemes and entry decisions arise in equilibrium? Formally, characterize the joint reward-setting and entry equilibria of competing platforms facing coordinated, strategic airdrop farmers.
status: Open research target extending a 2025 result (Hałaburda, Livshits and Yaish (2025), *Platform Building With Fake Consumers: On Double Dippers and Airdrop Farmers*, DOI:10.2139/ssrn.5364583) showing that platforms can benefit from farmers without identifying fake accounts; the competitive multi-platform setting with coordinated farmers remains uncharacterized.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the equilibria of competing platforms choosing reward schemes while strategic farmers coordinate across campaigns and resale markets — showing which reward and entry configurations can be sustained.
why: It embeds user-acquisition incentives in a genuinely competitive environment, showing how platform rivalry reshapes the strategic behavior of airdrop farmers that platforms may actually want to keep.
key_works: Hałaburda, Livshits and Yaish (2025), *Platform Building With Fake Consumers: On Double Dippers and Airdrop Farmers*, DOI:10.2139/ssrn.5364583.

title: Ground-truth farmer and genuine-user labels
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can we build a dataset of consented ground-truth labels that distinguishes ownership transfers, airdrop farming, legitimate automation, and genuine multi-account use by real users? Such labels would come from participants' own verified attestations across campaigns rather than inferred behavioral signals.
status: This remains a data target beyond the behavioral heuristics employed in 2023–2025 airdrop studies, including Messias, Yaish and Livshits (2023–2025), *Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems*, arXiv:2312.02752. Related directions include weakly supervised entity resolution and benchmark contamination.
solved_when: A publicly available, consented, cross-campaign label set exists in which each account is annotated as ownership transfer, farming, legitimate automation, or genuine multi-account use.
why: Without ground-truth labels, anti-Sybil mechanisms are evaluated against the same behavioral heuristics they were designed around, making the evaluation circular; real labels break that loop.
key_works: Messias, Yaish and Livshits (2023–2025), *Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems*, arXiv:2312.02752.

title: Personhood credentials resistant to rental
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can a personhood credential system remain meaningful when the credential itself can be rented, delegated, or extracted under coercion — all without any transfer of the private key? More precisely, what privacy and anti-collusion guarantees are achievable, and what is impossible, for unique-person credentials under such "use without transfer" attacks?
status: This remains a research target beyond existing proof-of-personhood constructions, which date to 2017 with Borge et al. (2017), [*Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies*](https://bford.info/pub/dec/pop.pdf); adjacent literature includes coercion-resistant voting and anonymous-credential nontransferability.
solved_when: A formal characterization exists of which combinations of privacy and anti-collusion (anti-rental, anti-delegation, anti-coercion) guarantees are simultaneously achievable for unique-person credentials and which are provably impossible, in an adversary model that includes rental, delegation, and coercion without key transfer.
why: Uniqueness alone does not prevent purchased influence — a credential that cannot be copied can still be wielded on behalf of whoever pays or coerces its holder.
key_works: Borge et al. (2017), [*Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies*](https://bford.info/pub/dec/pop.pdf).

title: Quadratic funding under coordinated donations
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: How much welfare and matching budget can be lost when donors coordinate identities and side payments across related projects in a quadratic funding mechanism? A formal bound on these losses under coordinated donations is the goal.
status: This has been an open research target since the 2018 introduction of quadratic funding in Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl (2018), *Liberal Radicalism: A Flexible Design for Philanthropic Matching Funds*, SSRN:3243656, which requires explicit pseudonymous anti-collusion assumptions. Related directions include coalition-proof public goods and false-name-proof mechanisms.
solved_when: A quantitative bound is proven on the welfare loss and matching-budget loss that quadratic funding suffers when donors collude via identity manipulation and side payments across related projects, together with explicit pseudonymous anti-collusion assumptions under which it holds.
why: Without such bounds, manufactured support can capture matching funds, diverting public-goods subsidies away from genuine contributions.
key_works: Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl (2018), *Liberal Radicalism: A Flexible Design for Philanthropic Matching Funds*, SSRN:3243656.

title: Funding complementary protocol public goods
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: How should a recurring grant pool be allocated across complementary public goods — maintenance, audits, documentation, and research — whose benefits arrive late and resist attribution to any single contributor? A formal mechanism is needed that goes beyond the matching-and-contribution-signal designs of 2018.
status: The state of the art remains the 2018 matching mechanisms of Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl (2018), *Liberal Radicalism: A Flexible Design for Philanthropic Matching Funds*, SSRN:3243656, which rely on contribution signals; no mechanism beyond these exists for this setting.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified that allocates recurring grants among such complementary tasks and demonstrably handles delayed, hard-to-attribute benefits, improving on the 2018 matching mechanisms and their contribution signals.
why: Components critical to a protocol's health can attract almost no visible usage, so contribution-based funding signals systematically starve them; without a dedicated mechanism, essential maintenance, audit, and research work goes unfunded.
key_works: Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl (2018), *Liberal Radicalism: A Flexible Design for Philanthropic Matching Funds*, SSRN:3243656.

title: Governance participation subsidies without vote farming
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can a mechanism reimburse the costs of meaningful participation in decentralized governance without thereby subsidizing fake turnout, redundant delegation, or vote-buying that farms the subsidy?
status: Open research target prompted by 2023 evidence linking participation, concentration, and gas costs in decentralized governance (Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267).
solved_when: A formally specified subsidy mechanism is proved (or empirically demonstrated) to reimburse genuinely meaningful participation while ruling out fake turnout, redundant delegation, and bribe-funded subsidy extraction.
why: Cheap voting alone does not create informed participation; without such a mechanism, subsidies either fail to move real engagement or get extracted by attackers.
key_works: Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267.

title: Strategic vote timing with delegation and quorum
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: When voters can delegate, revise earlier commitments, and react strategically to quorum or supermajority thresholds, at what times do they actually cast their votes? That is, characterize the voting-time equilibria that emerge once these richer strategic options are layered onto a public-tally setting.
status: No results yet exist beyond the 2024 public-tally model of Yaish, Abramova and Böhme (*Strategic Vote Timing in Online Elections With Public Tallies*, arXiv:2402.09776), which established mixed timing and last-minute voting; delegation, revised commitments, and quorum or supermajority effects remain open extensions.
solved_when: A characterization of equilibrium vote-timing behavior exists for a model that includes delegation, revision of prior commitments, and strategic quorum or supermajority effects, extending the mixed-timing and last-minute-voting findings of the 2024 public-tally model.
why: It would explain why votes concentrate at deadlines and why participation failures occur, connecting observed behavior to the underlying strategic incentives rather than treating them as anomalies.
key_works: Yaish, Abramova and Böhme (2024), *Strategic Vote Timing in Online Elections With Public Tallies*, arXiv:2402.09776.

bib.title: Strategic vote timing with delegation and quorum

title: Optimal disclosure of interim governance tallies
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: How much information about interim governance-vote tallies should a protocol reveal while voting is still open, when public tallies both enable coordination and invite strategic manipulation? Formally, characterize the disclosure policy that optimally trades off manipulation resistance and wasted participation costs against coordination and verifiability.
status: The target was motivated by 2024 public-tally analysis, notably Yaish, Abramova and Böhme (2024), *Strategic Vote Timing in Online Elections With Public Tallies*, arXiv:2402.09776; related frameworks include Bayesian persuasion and collective-decision information design.
solved_when: A disclosure mechanism (or policy family) is specified whose interim-tally information release provably limits strategic manipulation and wasted participation costs while preserving coordination and verifiability, with an optimality or near-optimality guarantee for the chosen objective.
why: It would elevate tally visibility from an implementation accident to an explicit, tunable mechanism-design choice for on-chain governance.
key_works: Yaish, Abramova and Böhme (2024), *Strategic Vote Timing in Online Elections With Public Tallies*, arXiv:2402.09776.

title: Governance security against borrowed voting power
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: When attackers can combine token loans, derivatives, delegation, and delayed execution, how much capital is genuinely at risk to seize governance control? A formal bound is needed for the true cost of mounting such a coordinated governance attack.
status: The target lies beyond 2023 empirical governance-attack analysis, as in Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267; related issues include empty voting in corporate finance and derivative-financed control.
solved_when: A provable bound exists on the capital an attacker must genuinely put at risk to acquire decisive voting power using any combination of token loans, derivatives, delegation, and delayed execution.
why: It measures the real cost of seizing control rather than nominal token capitalization, which can overstate how expensive a governance takeover actually is.
key_works: Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267.

title: Delegation equilibria with paid influence
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can we characterize how delegation and recall behave in liquid democracy when influence can be bought and sold, when uncertainty among voters generates delegation cycles, and when participants can exit before decisions are executed? Formally, the task is to characterize the equilibrium structure of delegation and recall under monetized influence, cyclic delegation induced by uncertainty, and the option of pre-execution exit.
status: This is a research target beyond the 2026 model of Brill et al. (2026), *Cycles in Liquid Democracy: A Game-Theoretic Justification* (DOI:10.24963/ijcai.2026/372), which explains equilibrium delegation cycles; the combined setting with paid influence and pre-execution exit remains uncharacterized.
solved_when: A characterization exists of delegation-and-recall equilibria in a model incorporating paid influence, uncertainty-driven delegation cycles, and voter exit before execution — extending the equilibrium account of delegation cycles beyond the 2026 model.
why: It would support accountable delegation when economic incentives are in play, showing when paid influence destabilizes or sustains liquid-democracy outcomes.
key_works: Brill et al. (2026), *Cycles in Liquid Democracy: A Game-Theoretic Justification*, DOI:10.24963/ijcai.2026/372.

title: Governance capture through proposal bundling
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can governance mechanisms be designed so that unpopular transfers cannot be smuggled through by bundling them with necessary upgrades, while still allowing genuinely complementary technical changes to be decided together? In formal terms, this asks for an agenda-formation rule (or proof of impossibility) that separates transfer decisions from upgrade decisions without sacrificing the efficiency gains of joint consideration for complementary proposals.
status: The problem is posed as a research target extending 2023 governance-security evidence — notably Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267 — to the setting of agenda control, with connections to strategic agenda setting and combinatorial social choice.
solved_when: A mechanism (or impossibility result) is established that provably prevents adoption of bundled packages containing unpopular transfers while permitting bundles of technically complementary changes; the natural criterion is a rigorous theorem, model, or deployed design extending the 2023 governance-security evidence to agenda control.
why: Whoever controls which proposals reach a vote can wield power exceeding their voting share, so bundling is a channel through which governance capture occurs despite formally fair voting.
key_works: Dotan et al. (2023), *The Vulnerable Nature of Decentralized Governance in DeFi*, arXiv:2308.04267.

title: Coordinated disclosure for ownerless financial protocols
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: How can an external party verify that a privately submitted vulnerability report is real, and coordinate a rewarded fix, when the vulnerable financial protocol has no responsive owner — all without publicizing information that creates an exploitation or front-running opportunity? Formally, the challenge is to design a disclosure and remediation mechanism that is privately verifiable yet reveals nothing that moves markets before the fix lands.
status: This is a research target following 2025 closed-source-contract evidence; existing organizational disclosure guidelines provide only part of the solution. Key works include Yang, Qin, Yaish and Zhang (2025; accepted CCS 2026), *Insecurity Through Obscurity: Veiled Vulnerabilities in Closed-Source Contracts*, arXiv:2504.13398, and Schaffer et al. (2023), *Recommendations for Federal Vulnerability Disclosure Guidelines*, DOI:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-216.
solved_when: A working mechanism exists that verifies private vulnerability reports against ownerless protocols and coordinates rewarded remediation while provably not exposing an exploitation or front-running opportunity.
why: It makes responsible discovery actionable when there is no owner to respond, closing the gap between finding a vulnerability in an ownerless financial protocol and safely getting it fixed.
key_works: Yang, Qin, Yaish and Zhang (2025; accepted CCS 2026), *Insecurity Through Obscurity: Veiled Vulnerabilities in Closed-Source Contracts*, arXiv:2504.13398; Schaffer et al. (2023), *Recommendations for Federal Vulnerability Disclosure Guidelines*, DOI:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-216.

title: Maintained adversarial-economics testbeds
subfield: Governance, pseudonymous participation and research public goods
open: Can we establish and maintain independent testbeds — with real clients, reproducible market and network conditions, and a durable archive of negative results across protocol upgrades — for adversarial-economics research?
status: Current efforts consist of individual implementations and research guides, such as Chaincode Labs' [*Introduction to Bitcoin Research*](https://research.chaincode.com/research-intro/) and analyses like Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner (2018), *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_26; continuity and neutral operation require dedicated governance beyond these, making this a funding problem.
solved_when: A continuously operated, neutrally governed testbed exists that researchers can use to reproduce significant incentive claims before deployment, with market conditions, network conditions, and negative results retained across upgrades.
why: Without such infrastructure, significant incentive claims cannot be reproducibly tested before real deployments, and lessons from failed experiments are lost at each upgrade.
key_works: Chaincode Labs, [*Introduction to Bitcoin Research*](https://research.chaincode.com/research-intro/); Chatterjee, Goharshady and Velner (2018), *Quantitative Analysis of Smart Contracts*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_26.
